# seedfall


<!-- docs/agents.md -->

# Using seedfall from AI coding agents

`seedfall mcp` serves seedfall's core operations over the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) on stdio. An agent such as Claude Code, Cursor or Codex can then sweep seeds, replay a failure and shrink it on its own, then use the exact fault schedule and trace to fix the bug and prove the fix. No API key and no hosted service are involved: the agent you already use does the reasoning.

## Setup

Install the binary first. Every integration below runs it:

```sh
go install github.com/kunalgoesbyken/seedfall/cmd/seedfall@latest
```

### Claude Code plugin

One command installs the MCP server, the four skills and the opt-in Stop hook:

```sh
claude plugin install seedfall --marketplace kunalgoesbyken/seedfall
```

Inside a session, `/plugin install seedfall --marketplace kunalgoesbyken/seedfall` does the same. On Claude Code versions before 2.1.275, add the marketplace first with `/plugin marketplace add kunalgoesbyken/seedfall`, then run `/plugin install seedfall@seedfall`. The skills then run as `/seedfall:seedfall-setup` and so on, and Claude also loads them on its own when a task matches.

### Skills for other agents

The skills follow the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/specification) format, so any agent that reads `SKILL.md` files can use them. To install them with the [`skills` CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills):

```sh
npx skills add kunalgoesbyken/seedfall
```

### MCP server only

Claude Code:

```sh
claude mcp add seedfall -- seedfall mcp
```

Cursor, or any client that reads an `mcpServers` file:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "seedfall": { "command": "seedfall", "args": ["mcp"] }
  }
}
```

Config paths in tool calls are resolved against the server's working directory, which is normally your project root. Every tool that takes `config` also takes an optional `profile` and a `set` list of `path=value` overrides, the same as `-profile` and `-set` on the command line ([config.md](config.md)).

## Tools

| Tool | Arguments | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `seedfall_init` | optional `dir`, `config`, `nodes`, `workload`, `dry_run` | The module's `main` packages and which become nodes, the packages that block a `GOOS=wasip1` build (compile errors and cgo, each with its import chain and the shim that covers it), `compat_shims` for every dependency `compat_overlay` would swap, the starter config and its starter profiles, the files written, and the next steps. See [onboarding](#onboarding-a-new-module) |
| `seedfall_run` | `config`, `seeds` (for example `1-200`), optional `rotate`, `check`, `skip_pinned`, `until_novelty`, `batch`, `timeout` | First the [pinned regressions](verify.md#pinned-regressions), stopping at one that fails again. Then seeds passed, the lowest failing seed with its reason, [classification](reports.md#classification), the faults before the failure, the trace tail, a replay command and `artifacts_dir` ([failure artifacts](reports.md#failure-artifacts)), plus property coverage, `seeds_per_second`, `virtual_seconds_per_wall_second` and `utilization` ([reports.md](reports.md#utilization)), and, with `faults.buggify` on, `buggify_sites` ([buggify](buggify.md#coverage)). With `until_novelty`, `stopped` and the `exploration` growth table ([explore.md](explore.md#stopping-a-plain-sweep)) |
| `seedfall_explore` | `config`, optional `seeds`, `rounds`, `batch`, `until_novelty`, `budget`, `explore_seed`, `keep_going`, `corpus` | Feedback-guided search: every round with the new signals and functions it added, the stop reason, the corpus size, property coverage, throughput, and the first failure with `artifacts_dir` and a replay command ([explore.md](explore.md)) |
| `seedfall_replay` | `config`, `seed`, optional `faults` file | The same failure view for one seed, or the trace tail if it passes, with a `note` when a shrunk schedule's shorter duration ended the run before the workload finished. A failure view of a run that recorded operations also names its `history_file` and, on a linearizability violation, its `timeline_file`. Every result has the run's `determinism_hash` and its `events` from `sim.Event` or `lifecycle.SendEvent` |
| `seedfall_logs` | `config`, `seed`, optional `faults`, `node`, `grep`, `from`, `to`, `net_trace`, `limit` | The run's trace lines filtered by node, regular expression and virtual time, each with its node, instance and time, and a node's slog JSON output parsed into `fields`, plus how many lines matched ([timeline.md](timeline.md#logs)) |
| `seedfall_trace_search` | `config`, `seed`, `pattern`, optional `faults`, `context` (default 3), `node`, `from`, `to`, `net_trace`, `limit` | Each line that matches the regular expression (on the given nodes, inside the virtual time window) with `context` trace lines of every node before and after it, as windows of numbered lines with their virtual time, node and instance, overlapping windows merged, plus how many lines matched ([timeline.md](timeline.md#searching-the-trace)) |
| `seedfall_debug` | `config`, `seed`, optional `faults`, `at`, `net_trace`, `commands` | Replays to `at`, runs each debugger command (`where`, `net`, `faults`, `ls`, `stat`, `cat`, `step`, `until <regex>`, `to <time>`, `branch`, `log`, `grep`) and returns each output and the final state of every node ([timeline.md](timeline.md#debugger)) |
| `seedfall_shrink` | `config`, `seed`, optional `faults` (a schedule file, for a failure found by `seedfall_explore`), `budget` (runs such as `300`, or time such as `10m`) | The original and minimal sizes (faults, duration and, with [`sim.Budget`](properties.md#workload-size), workload operations), the runs used, whether the budget ran out, the path of the saved schedule, and the failure view under that schedule with its replay command ([shrinking](how-it-works.md#shrinking)) |
| `seedfall_faults_edit` | `config`, `seed`, optional `faults`, `remove`, `shift`, `add`, `out` | Edits a fault schedule to test a hypothesis: `remove` takes positions counting from 1, `shift` takes `{"fault": 2, "by": "-50ms"}` (a count such as `"+2"` for a fault that fires at a disk operation, read, buggify hit, counted call or udp datagram), `add` takes faults in the [schedule format](faults.md#editing-a-schedule). Starts from `faults`, else `.seedfall/seed-N.faults.json`, else the seed's own faults, checks every fault against the config and writes nothing if one is wrong. Returns the numbered schedule, the file written (`out`, or the file it came from) and the replay command |
| `seedfall_inspect` | `config`, `seed`, optional `faults`, `at`, `node`, `path` | Every node's disk at the failure or at virtual time `at`: per file the live and durable sizes, the byte ranges a crash would lose, whether its directory entry is durable, the last torn write, and removed entries a crash would bring back. With `path`, one file's durable content as text or a hex dump ([inspect.md](inspect.md)) |
| `seedfall_check` | `history`, optional `model` | Re-checks a recorded history file against a model: the verdict, each anomaly with its cycle, and on a linearizability violation the HTML timeline file ([properties.md](properties.md#history-files)) |
| `seedfall_verify` | `config`, `seed` and optional `faults`, and/or `report`; optional `seeds`, `check_seeds`, `mutate`, `app_mutants` | Whether the fix holds: each replayed schedule, the fresh sweep with its confidence, the determinism check and the mutants, plus a Markdown proof block for the PR ([verify.md](verify.md)) |
| `seedfall_mutate` | `config`, optional `seeds` (default `1-100`), `only`, `app`, `mutants` | Sweeps the seeds unmutated, then once per [mutant](mutate.md) (disk, rename, truncate, network and clock guarantees), or with `app` once per [source mutant](mutate.md#source-mutants) of the node packages: each mutant's `outcome` (`killed`, `survived`, `not exercised` or `did not build`), its `location` and change for source mutants, the seed and reason that killed it, and how often the operation was weakened |
| `seedfall_pin` | `config`, `seed`, optional `faults` | Pins the seed's schedule (the one `seedfall_shrink` saved, the given file, or else the seed's own faults) into `seedfall-regressions/` as a permanent regression, and returns the file and whether it passes now, with the failure view if not ([verify.md](verify.md#pinned-regressions)) |
| `seedfall_doctor` | none | Checks the Go version, `GOOS=wasip1` builds, `net_overlay` against the installed Go, a writable build cache and working directory, and free memory, returning the seedfall build and each check as `ok`, `warn`, `fail` or `skip` with a fix ([install.md](install.md#check-the-install)) |
| `seedfall_findings` | optional `report` (default `.seedfall/report.html`), `history`, `status` (comma separated: `new`, `ongoing`, `regressed`, `resolved`, `not seen`) | Reads a triage report from `seedfall run -report` without running anything, the same as `seedfall findings`: each finding with the given statuses with its status, failing seeds, rate, classification and example failure with replay and shrink commands, findings not seen this time, unmet properties, and the run history of that config from `.seedfall/history.jsonl` ([reports.md](reports.md)) |
| `seedfall_cause` | `config`, `seed`, optional `points`, `branches` | The probability of failing from each moment of the run, with the faults between moments, so the agent can see which event made the failure inevitable ([cause.md](cause.md)) |

Every result is structured JSON, so the agent can read the seed, the faults and the trace directly.

### The same operations on the command line

Every tool has a command, so a person can repeat what the agent did and an agent without MCP can shell out:

| Tool | Command |
|---|---|
| `seedfall_init`, `seedfall_run`, `seedfall_explore`, `seedfall_replay`, `seedfall_logs`, `seedfall_debug`, `seedfall_shrink`, `seedfall_cause`, `seedfall_inspect`, `seedfall_check`, `seedfall_verify`, `seedfall_mutate`, `seedfall_pin` | `seedfall init`, `run`, `explore`, `replay`, `logs`, `debug`, `shrink`, `cause`, `inspect`, `check`, `verify`, `mutate`, `pin` |
| `seedfall_trace_search` | `seedfall trace grep -seed N -e re [-context 3]` |
| `seedfall_faults_edit` | `seedfall faults -seed N [-remove 2] [-shift 1=-50ms] [-add '{...}'] [-out file]` |
| `seedfall_findings` | `seedfall findings [-status new,regressed] [-json]` |
| `seedfall_doctor` | `seedfall doctor [-json]` |

`seedfall schema` prints the whole surface as JSON: every command with each flag's name, type, default and usage, and every MCP tool with its description and input and output JSON Schemas, plus the prompts and resources. Generate client bindings or check an agent's calls against it:

```sh
seedfall schema | jq '.commands[] | select(.command == "seedfall faults") | .flags[].name'
seedfall schema | jq '.mcp_tools[] | select(.name == "seedfall_faults_edit") | .inputSchema'
```

## Prompts and resources

The server also serves what an agent needs in order to work without guessing:

| Kind | Name | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt | `seedfall-setup`, `seedfall-properties`, `seedfall-triage`, `seedfall-fix-and-prove` | The four [skills](#skills), so MCP clients without skill support get the same workflows |
| Resource | `seedfall://schema/config` | JSON Schema of `seedfall.json`, generated from the config types, with every field's default |
| Resource | `seedfall://docs/<name>` | Each page of these docs, for example `seedfall://docs/properties` for the property API and `seedfall://docs/faults` for what each fault does |

## Onboarding a new module

`seedfall init` (MCP: `seedfall_init`) is the first step in a repository that has never run seedfall:

```sh
seedfall init -n                     # report only
seedfall init                        # write seedfall.json and seedfall/workload/main.go
seedfall init -node ./cmd/server     # choose the nodes yourself; repeatable
seedfall init -json                  # the same report as JSON
```

It runs `go list` twice. The first run uses `GOOS=wasip1 -export -deps`, so every package is compiled for wasip1, and any package that fails is reported with its compiler error and the import chain from the node that pulls it in. The second uses `GOOS=linux CGO_ENABLED=1` and lists the dependencies that contain cgo files. Every `main` package that imports `net` becomes a node. `net_overlay` is turned on unless every node already uses `sim`.

The scaffolded workload follows the pattern every example shares: write keys, remember which ones were acknowledged, then read each one back after the faults. Its `put` and `get` return `errors.ErrUnsupported` until the agent implements them against the service's API. Until then the sweep fails with `the workload got acknowledged writes` never true, so an unwired workload can never pass. Existing files are never overwritten.

On a fresh copy of `examples/kvlog` with its configs removed, `seedfall init -node ./server` writes a config and a workload. Wiring `put` and `get` to kvlog's line protocol takes about twenty lines. The first sweep then fails on seed 1 with `acknowledged write lost`, and shrink brings it down to the same two faults as the [getting started guide](getting-started.md).

## Skills

The `skills/` directory holds four skills. They follow the order of a real adoption, and every command in them runs as written:

| Skill | Use it to |
|---|---|
| `seedfall-setup` | Install, run `seedfall init`, clear the wasip1 blockers, wire the workload and run the first sweep |
| `seedfall-properties` | Read the storage and replication code, write `sim` properties for its durability and consistency promises, and grade them with `seedfall mutate` until every exercised mutant is killed |
| `seedfall-triage` | Classify, shrink, find the decisive fault with `cause`, inspect the disk, and confirm the explanation with a replay of an edited schedule |
| `seedfall-fix-and-prove` | Fix the cause, replay the saved schedule, sweep, run `seedfall verify -mutate -md proof.md` and paste the proof into the pull request |

## Stop hook

The Claude Code plugin registers a Stop hook that runs `seedfall hook`. It does nothing unless you opt in by setting `SEEDFALL_HOOK_SEEDS`, for example in `.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{ "env": { "SEEDFALL_HOOK_SEEDS": "1-20" } }
```

When Claude finishes a turn in a directory that has `seedfall.json` (or the file named by `SEEDFALL_HOOK_CONFIG`), the hook sweeps those seeds, under the profile named by `SEEDFALL_HOOK_PROFILE` if it is set. On a failure or an unmet property, it blocks the stop and hands Claude the seed and the replay and shrink commands. To avoid loops, it skips a stop that a hook has already continued once.

## Docs for models

The site serves [`llms.txt`](https://seedfall-lemon.vercel.app/llms.txt), an index of these docs and the skills, and [`llms-full.txt`](https://seedfall-lemon.vercel.app/llms-full.txt), their full text. `bash scripts/site-llms.sh` generates both from `docs/` and `skills/`.

## A verification loop

Ask the agent to treat a seed sweep as the definition of done for storage or replication changes:

1. Run `seedfall_run` over a few hundred seeds before changing anything, to record the baseline.
2. When a seed fails, run `seedfall_shrink` and read the minimal fault schedule. It usually names the exact window: "crash during disk op #56", then "crash". `seedfall_cause` shows which of those faults made the failure likely, and `seedfall_faults_edit` with `out` plus `seedfall_replay` tests a guess, such as dropping a fault or moving a crash one disk operation earlier.
3. Fix the code, then `seedfall_replay` the saved schedule until it passes.
4. Run `seedfall_verify` with the seed and schedule and paste its `markdown` proof block into the pull request.

Shrunk schedules are small enough that an agent can reason about them step by step. `examples/kvlog` is a good first exercise: its `seedfall.always.json` shrinks to two faults.


<!-- docs/antithesis.md -->

# Running Antithesis SDK code

Code instrumented with the [Antithesis Go SDK](https://github.com/antithesishq/antithesis-sdk-go) runs under seedfall unchanged. Assertions become seedfall properties, `lifecycle.SetupComplete` becomes seedfall's setup signal, and `random.GetRandom` draws from the seed.

`examples/ledger` has no seedfall imports at all. It uses plain `net` (through `net_overlay`) and only the Antithesis SDK:

```go
lifecycle.SetupComplete(map[string]any{"ledger": addr})
amount := int(random.GetRandom()%100) + 1
assert.Sometimes(unacked > 0, "a crash interrupted a deposit", nil)
lifecycle.SendEvent("deposits finished", map[string]any{"total": total, "acked": acked, "unacked": unacked})
assert.AlwaysGreaterThanOrEqualTo(total, acked, "ledger total covers every acknowledged deposit", map[string]any{"unacked": unacked})
assert.AlwaysLessThanOrEqualTo(total, acked+unacked, "ledger total holds no deposit that was never sent", nil)
assert.SometimesAll([]assert.NamedBool{{First: "interrupted", Second: unacked > 0}, {First: "kept", Second: total > acked}}, "an unacknowledged deposit survived a crash", nil)
```

```
$ seedfall run -c seedfall.json -seeds 1-20
property       seeds reached  seeds true
  sometimes              20          18  a crash interrupted a deposit
  sometimes              20           2  an unacknowledged deposit survived a crash
  always                 20          20  ledger total covers every acknowledged deposit  (smallest margin 0)
  always                 20          20  ledger total holds no deposit that was never sent  (smallest margin 0)
  sometimes              20           5  recovery dropped a partial entry

ok  20 seeds passed (0 hit the time horizon) in 908ms

$ seedfall run -c seedfall.json -profile nofsync -seeds 1-20
FAIL seed 1 at t=2.940793302s (618 scheduler steps, 336ms real)
  client#1: ledger total covers every acknowledged deposit: {"left":4203,"right":5608,"unacked":1729}
```

## How it works

On `wasip1` the SDK has no native Antithesis library to talk to, so it writes each event as a JSON line to the file named by `ANTITHESIS_SDK_LOCAL_OUTPUT`. seedfall sets that variable for every node and serves the path as a virtual file. Each line is decoded as it is written:

| SDK call | seedfall property |
|---|---|
| `assert.Always` | `always`: fails the seed when false, fails the sweep if never reached |
| `assert.AlwaysOrUnreachable` | `always_or_unreachable`: fails the seed when false |
| `assert.Sometimes` | `sometimes`: fails the sweep if never true |
| `assert.Reachable` | `reachable`: fails the sweep if never reached |
| `assert.Unreachable` | `unreachable`: fails the seed when reached |
| `assert.AlwaysGreaterThan`, `AlwaysGreaterThanOrEqualTo`, `AlwaysLessThan`, `AlwaysLessThanOrEqualTo` | `always`, with the smallest margin in the property table |
| `assert.SometimesGreaterThan`, `SometimesGreaterThanOrEqualTo`, `SometimesLessThan`, `SometimesLessThanOrEqualTo` | `sometimes`, with the largest margin in the property table |
| `assert.AlwaysSome` | `always`: at least one named boolean is true |
| `assert.SometimesAll` | `sometimes`: every named boolean is true |
| `lifecycle.SetupComplete` | ends the setup phase when `faults_after_setup` is on |
| `lifecycle.SendEvent` | an [event](properties.md#events): a trace line with the details as JSON, returned by `seedfall_replay` |

The SDK's details map appears as JSON in the failure message; the numeric variants add `left` and `right`, and the grouped variants add each named boolean. seedfall's source catalog recognizes every `assert.*` call above with a constant message, so Antithesis assertions that never run are reported too.

The margin of a numeric assertion comes from the SDK's own guidance records. Like Antithesis, the SDK only reports a new value when it gets closer to failing (for `Always`) or closer to true (for `Sometimes`), so the smallest and largest margins are exact. The SDK also reports each assertion only the first time it passes and the first time it fails in a process, so the number of hits is lower than with `sim` assertions; seeds reached and seeds true are unaffected.

`sim` has the same variants with the same names ([properties.md](properties.md#numeric-and-grouped-properties)), and `sim.Event` matches `lifecycle.SendEvent`.

`random.GetRandom` and `random.RandomChoice` read `crypto/rand`, which seedfall feeds from the seed, so they replay exactly and draw from the same source as `sim.Random` and `sim.RandomChoice`. Antithesis custom faults are commands its platform runs from outside your program and have no SDK call to map; mark the same spots with `sim.Buggify` instead ([buggify.md](buggify.md)).

## What you get compared with Antithesis

The same assertions and the same setup signal, run locally or in CI for free, with seed replay, shrinking, causality analysis and triage reports. What you don't get: Antithesis runs arbitrary containers in a deterministic hypervisor, while seedfall runs Go programs that build for `wasip1`.


<!-- docs/buggify.md -->

# BUGGIFY: faults inside your code

Every other seedfall fault comes from outside the process: crashes, torn writes, partitions. `sim.Buggify` lets you mark places in your own code where the simulator may force the rare path, such as a dropped reply, a retry, an error return, a minimal quorum or an extra delay. The idea comes from FoundationDB's `BUGGIFY`, which FoundationDB credits for many of its deepest bugs.

```go
v := c.apply(req)
if sim.Buggify("reply lost after apply") {
	return
}
reply(conn, v)
```

Outside the simulator `Buggify` always returns false, so the site costs one function call in production.

## Turning it on

Sites never fire unless the config asks for it:

```json
{ "faults": { "buggify": true } }
```

With `swarm` as well, each seed turns buggify on or off along with the other fault types.

## How a site decides

| Step | Rule |
|---|---|
| Enable | The first time a site is reached in a run, it is enabled with probability 0.25 and stays enabled or disabled for the rest of that run |
| Fire | Each time an enabled site is reached, it fires with probability 0.25 for `sim.Buggify(site)`, or `p` for `sim.BuggifyWithProb(site, p)` |
| Quiet | A site never fires during `sim.QuietFor`, during the recovery phase of `liveness` or the `finally` check, or, with `faults_after_setup`, before `sim.SetupComplete` |

A site is identified by its name, so keep names constant. Both decisions use random streams keyed by the seed and the site name (and, for firing, the node), so adding a site or reaching another site more often never changes when an existing site fires. Most seeds run with only some sites enabled, which explores combinations that firing every site everywhere would hide.

## Replay and shrink

Each firing is recorded as a fault with the node, the site and which hit it was, counted per node and site:

```
faults before the failure (1):
  465.631ms  buggify "reply lost after apply" fires on counter at hit #35
```

```json
{ "at": "465.631252ms", "kind": "buggify", "node": "counter", "site": "reply lost after apply", "until": "0s", "op": 35 }
```

When a schedule is replayed with `-faults`, a site fires exactly at the hits the schedule lists and nowhere else, so `seedfall shrink` removes firings like any other fault, and you can hand-edit a schedule to add or drop one. Replaying a schedule needs `"buggify": true` in the config, and with `swarm` it must be on for that seed: otherwise every site returns false. The trace shows when each site is first reached and whether it is enabled for the run, and every firing.

## Coverage

seedfall catalogs `sim.Buggify` and `sim.BuggifyWithProb` calls whose site is a string literal, and after a sweep with `buggify` on it prints how often each site was reached, enabled and fired:

```
buggify  seeds reached  seeds enabled  seeds fired  fired
                    20              6            6     88  reply lost after apply
                    20              5            5    110  slow apply
```

A site marked `never reached` (with its location) is code no seed ran; `never fired` means it ran but never fired: no seed enabled it, or its rate was too low for the hits it got, so sweep more seeds or raise its probability. Neither fails the sweep: pair a site with a `sim.Sometimes` on the path it opens when you want that path to be required. The same counts are in `buggify_sites` in `run -json` and in the MCP `seedfall_run` result.

## Structured randomness

`sim.Random()` returns a random `uint64` and `sim.RandomChoice(items)` returns one element of a slice (the zero value for an empty slice). Inside the simulator both read `crypto/rand`, which seedfall feeds from a stream keyed by the seed, the node and its restart count, so a choice replays with the seed. `RandomChoice` rejects out-of-range draws, so every element is equally likely. Outside the simulator they use `crypto/rand`.

```go
if sim.BuggifyWithProb("slow apply", 0.5) {
	time.Sleep(sim.RandomChoice([]time.Duration{time.Millisecond, 5 * time.Millisecond, 50 * time.Millisecond}))
}
```

The Antithesis SDK's `random.GetRandom` and `random.RandomChoice` read the same source, so Antithesis-instrumented code gets the same replayable choices with no changes. See [antithesis.md](antithesis.md).

## Example

[`examples/buggify`](../examples/buggify) is a counter service whose client retries an increment when the reply does not arrive. Without buggify nothing ever drops a reply and every seed passes; with it, `reply lost after apply` makes the retry apply twice and the sweep fails, and the fixed server, which remembers applied request ids, passes.

## Limits

- A site's name is its identity: two call sites with the same name share one enable decision and one hit count per node.
- Sites named by a non-literal string still fire and are recorded, but cannot be cataloged in advance.
- `seedfall cause` re-randomizes when sites fire after each branch point, not which sites are enabled, so a seed's enabled set is fixed for that seed.


<!-- docs/cause.md -->

# Causality analysis

`seedfall shrink` tells you which faults are *needed* for a failure. `seedfall cause` tells you *when the failure became likely*, and which event made it so.

```sh
seedfall cause -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1
```

```
seed 1 fails at t=2.891820635s: client#1: acknowledged write lost: k96=v96, server now answers "NONE"

chance of failing when everything after a moment is re-randomized (20 futures each):

         0s     5%  ██
  292.108ms     5%  ██                              <- after 292.108ms  partition [client] from the rest until 627.143ms
  722.955ms     0%
  757.268ms     0%
  757.268ms    75%  ███████████████████████         <- after 757.268ms  crash server during disk op #56, restart at 1.121388s
  1.084433s    75%  ███████████████████████
    1.7052s    65%  ████████████████████
    1.7052s   100%  ██████████████████████████████  <- after 1.7052s  crash server, restart at 1.942589s
  2.711082s   100%  ██████████████████████████████

biggest jump: 0% -> 75% at 757.268ms  <- after 757.268ms  crash server during disk op #56, restart at 1.121388s

440 runs in 24.296s
```

(Abridged: the full output has one row per moment.)

Read it from top to bottom. Before anything happens, a random future of this world fails 5% of the time. The partition changes nothing, so it is a bystander. The crash in the middle of disk operation #56 takes the odds from 0% to 75%: that is when the torn record lands on disk. The second crash makes the failure certain. Even before reading any code, you know which event to look at.

## How it works

For each moment *T*, seedfall replays the seed exactly up to *T*. At the first scheduler step at or after *T*, it re-keys every random stream: scheduling, network latency, disk tearing, I/O faults, what `random_get` hands each node (so `crypto/rand` and `sim.Random`, but not Go's runtime-seeded `math/rand`), and the remaining fault schedule. Then it lets the run continue into a new future. Running many such branches from the same moment estimates the probability of failing from that state.

This needs no snapshots. Because replay is exact, "the state at *T*" is reproduced by running the seed to *T*. That is the same property Antithesis's multiverse debugging relies on, with deterministic replay standing in for VM snapshots.

Moments are chosen evenly across the run (`-points`, default 16), plus just before and just after every fault. Each moment gets `-branches` futures (default 20), so the default costs a few hundred runs, all in parallel.

Branches are also the basis of [feedback-guided exploration](explore.md), which keeps branching from runs that reached something new.

## From an agent

The MCP server exposes the same analysis as `seedfall_cause`, returning the curve as JSON with the faults between consecutive moments. See [agents.md](agents.md).


<!-- docs/ci.md -->

# Running seedfall in CI

## GitHub Actions

```yaml
jobs:
  simulate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: kunalgoesbyken/seedfall@main
        id: seedfall
        with:
          config: seedfall.json
          seeds: 1-500
          check: "true"
          comment: "true"
```

The inputs below other than `config`, `profile`, `seeds`, `check`, `go-version`, `report` and `artifact-name` are newer than v0.2.0, hence `@main` until the next release.

### Inputs

| Input | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `command` | `run` | `run`, `verify` or `mutate` ([below](#verify-and-mutate)) |
| `config` | `seedfall.json` | Path to the world description |
| `profile` | | Profile from the config's `profiles` to merge over it ([config.md](config.md#profiles)) |
| `seeds` | | Seed or inclusive range. Empty uses the command's own default: `run` sweeps `1-200`, `mutate` `1-100`, and `verify` as many fresh seeds as 95% confidence needs |
| `rotate-seeds` | `false` | With `run`, move `seeds` forward by its own width for each workflow run ([below](#rotating-seeds)) |
| `check` | `false` | With `run`, run every seed twice and fail at the first host call or trace line that differs |
| `args` | | Extra flags for the command, separated by spaces, such as `-timeout 10m`, `-only fsync_noop` or `-seed 1`. Quoting is not interpreted |
| `version` | | seedfall release to download, or `latest` ([below](#which-seedfall-runs)) |
| `go-version` | `stable` | Go version for building your nodes, and seedfall when it is built from source |
| `report` | `true` | With `run`, sweep every seed and upload an HTML triage report. `false` stops at the first failure |
| `artifact-name` | `seedfall-report` | Name of the uploaded artifact, also used to keep each job's cache and pull request comment apart. Make it unique per job in a matrix |
| `cache` | `true` | Keep the run history and compiled modules between runs ([below](#history-between-runs)) |
| `comment` | `false` | Post or update one pull request comment with the outcome. Needs `pull-requests: write` |
| `webhook` | | Slack or Discord incoming webhook URL, best from a secret. Posts the report's new and regressed findings with `seedfall report notify` |
| `file-issues` | `false` | File a GitHub issue for each finding without an open one, with `seedfall report issue` |

An input that does not apply is an error rather than being ignored: `check` or `rotate-seeds` with `verify` or `mutate`, and `comment` with `report: "false"`.

The job fails if any seed or [pinned regression](verify.md#pinned-regressions) fails. The triage report (see [reports.md](reports.md)) is uploaded as an artifact, together with the [failure artifacts](reports.md#failure-artifacts) under `failures/`.

### Outputs

| Output | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `status` | `passed`, `failed`, or `error` when seedfall could not finish, for example a config that does not build. With `report: "false"` a `run` that cannot start also reads `failed`, because nothing distinguishes the two |
| `failing-seed` | With a `run` report, the seed to look at first: a pinned regression that fails again, else the first regressed, new, then ongoing finding. Empty on a clean run |
| `findings` | With a `run` report, how many findings the report has |
| `report-path` | The HTML report on the runner, or the Markdown from `verify` or `mutate`. Runner temp is cleared when the job ends |

```yaml
      - if: failure() && steps.seedfall.outputs.status == 'failed'
        run: echo "replay with seed ${{ steps.seedfall.outputs.failing-seed }}"
```

The job summary shows the same Markdown as the [pull request comment](#pull-request-comments), with seedfall's output folded below it. When seedfall cannot finish, such as a config that does not build or a `mutate` baseline that already fails, the summary says so with the last lines of output. Problems also appear as error annotations on the run and the pull request's changed files. A finding from a property with a constant message is annotated at its source line, from the same catalog that reports properties that were never reached. Other failures, such as a crash or a `sim.Assert`, are annotated without a file. GitHub only shows a limited number of annotations per step, so failing regressions come first, then regressed, new and ongoing findings, then unmet properties.

### Which seedfall runs

With `version` empty, the action uses the release that matches the ref in `uses:`, so `@v1.2.3` downloads v1.2.3 for the runner's platform and checks it against the release's `checksums.txt`. A checksum mismatch fails the job. If the ref has no release, such as a branch, a commit or a release older than the automated pipeline like v0.2.0, seedfall is built from the action's source instead. Windows runners and `uses: ./` always build from source.

Set `version: v1.2.3`, or `latest`, to run a specific release regardless of the ref. An explicit version never falls back: a missing release fails the job, and it needs a Linux or macOS runner and a released action. Go is set up either way, because seedfall compiles your nodes with it.

### History between runs

New, ongoing, resolved and regressed need the run history ([reports.md](reports.md#history-new-ongoing-resolved-regressed)), so with `cache` on the action restores and saves `.seedfall/history.jsonl` and `.seedfall/cache` next to the config, with `actions/cache`. It saves even when the sweep fails, since that is the run whose history matters most.

The key is the config file's hash, the `artifact-name`, the branch and the run, and restoring falls back to the newest entry for that config and name from this branch, then from any branch the run can read, so a pull request starts from its base branch's history. Changing the config starts a new history. An `extends` parent is not part of the hash. Keep `artifact-name` unique per job, or jobs in a matrix overwrite each other's history.

Set `cache: "false"` if you keep `.seedfall/history.jsonl` some other way, such as committing it.

### Pull request comments

`comment: "true"` posts one comment per job and edits it on later pushes, so a pull request does not collect one per run. It lists new, regressed and resolved findings, ongoing ones, failing pinned regressions and unmet properties, each failure with its replay command, and links the workflow run. It is the job summary's Markdown, so with `verify` or `mutate` it is the proof or the mutant table, and when seedfall cannot finish it says so. A clean run also updates it, so a stale failure does not linger. Only a comment written by the token's own account is edited, so a comment someone else posts with the same marker is left alone. The comment never includes seedfall's raw output; that stays in the job summary.

The job needs `pull-requests: write`. Pull requests from forks run with a read-only token, so the action logs a warning and the job's result is unaffected. `seedfall report comment` does the same from any CI, and `seedfall report github` writes the annotations and outputs ([reports.md](reports.md#github)).

### Verify and mutate

`command: verify` runs [`seedfall verify`](verify.md), and `args` names what to verify:

```yaml
      - uses: kunalgoesbyken/seedfall@main
        with:
          command: verify
          config: seedfall.fixed.json
          args: -seed 1 -faults testdata/torntail.faults.json -mutate
          comment: "true"
```

`command: mutate` runs [`seedfall mutate`](mutate.md) and fails if a mutant survives:

```yaml
      - uses: kunalgoesbyken/seedfall@main
        with:
          command: mutate
          seeds: 1-50
          args: -only fsync_noop,net_dup_chunk
```

Both write Markdown to the job summary and the artifact (`proof.md`, `mutants.md`). `failing-seed` and `findings` stay empty, because neither command writes a triage report.

### Rotating seeds

`rotate-seeds: "true"` keeps exploring new schedules. Run number `n` sweeps the range `n - 1` widths after `seeds`: with `seeds: 1-200`, run 1 sweeps 1-200, run 2 201-400, and run 8 1401-1600. Re-running a job keeps its run number, so it sweeps the same seeds. Every failure names its seed, so it stays exactly reproducible, and [pinned regressions](verify.md#pinned-regressions) still replay on every run.

Outside the action, `seedfall run -seeds 1-200 -rotate N` sweeps the Nth range after `-seeds`, and refuses a rotation past the largest seed.

### Nightly sweep

A template for a scheduled sweep, with alerts and issues for new and regressed findings:

```yaml
name: nightly-simulation
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 3 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  simulate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 60
    permissions:
      contents: read
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: kunalgoesbyken/seedfall@main
        with:
          seeds: 1-500
          rotate-seeds: "true"
          args: -timeout 45m
          webhook: ${{ secrets.SEEDFALL_WEBHOOK }}
          file-issues: "true"
```

The history is what limits alerts to new and regressed findings, so leave `cache` on. The message links the workflow run, and each issue names the seed, the replay command, the seedfall version and the commit ([notifications and issues](reports.md#notifications-and-issues)).

### Several configs

Run a matrix with a unique `artifact-name` per job:

```yaml
jobs:
  simulate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - { name: storage, config: examples/ledger/seedfall.json, seeds: 1-60 }
          - { name: upgrade, config: examples/upgrade/seedfall.json, seeds: 1-50 }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: kunalgoesbyken/seedfall@main
        with:
          config: ${{ matrix.config }}
          seeds: ${{ matrix.seeds }}
          artifact-name: seedfall-${{ matrix.name }}
```

This repository's own [`ci.yml`](../.github/workflows/ci.yml) sweeps several examples this way, and runs `verify` and `mutate` too.

## Machine-readable output

`seedfall run -json` sweeps every seed in the range and prints one JSON object per line as each seed finishes, then a summary object. Seeds finish in parallel, so lines are not in seed order.

```sh
seedfall run -c seedfall.always.json -seeds 1-100 -json | jq -c 'select(.type == "seed" and .passed == false)'
```

```json
{"type":"seed","seed":1,"passed":false,"finished":false,"failure":{"class":"assert","node":"client"},"reason":"client#1: acknowledged write lost: k96=v96, server now answers \"NONE\"","virtual_seconds":2.8918212,"faults":3,"host_calls":6810,"determinism_hash":"53786fa3165d442b"}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `type` | `seed` or `summary` |
| `seed`, `passed`, `finished` | The seed, whether it passed, and whether the workload finished before the time horizon |
| `failure` | `class`, plus `node` and `property` when known, the same key the triage report groups by |
| `reason` | The failure message |
| `virtual_seconds` | Simulated time the run covered |
| `faults` | Faults that happened during the run |
| `host_calls`, `determinism_hash` | How many host calls the run made, and the running hash over them ([determinism check](properties.md#determinism-check)). It covers only simulated values, so the same seed and guest binary should give the same hash on any machine, and a CI matrix can compare it across operating systems to check |

Before the seed lines comes one `{"type": "regression", ...}` line per [pinned regression](verify.md#pinned-regressions) and `-seeds-file` seed, with `source`, `seed` and `passed`, plus `failure`, `reason`, `classification` and `artifacts` when it fails again.

The summary has `passed`, `failed`, `unfinished`, `regressions_failed`, `unmet_properties` and `properties`, the same coverage table `seedfall_run` returns over MCP, with a `problem` on each property that was never reached or never true and a `margin` on each numeric property. With `faults.buggify` on it also has `buggify_sites`: each `sim.Buggify` site with `seeds_reached`, `seeds_enabled`, `seeds_fired`, `fired` and a `problem` of `never reached` or `never fired`, which does not change the exit code. The exit code is 1 if any seed or regression failed or any property is unmet. `-json` cannot be combined with `-report`.

## Time budgets

`seedfall run -timeout 10m` stops starting seeds after ten minutes of wall-clock time, so a CI job can use a wide range and take whatever fits:

```sh
seedfall run -seeds 1-1000000 -timeout 10m -report .seedfall/report.html
```

Seeds already running finish, so the sweep can run slightly past the limit, and [pinned regressions](verify.md#pinned-regressions) always run and count toward it. The run prints `stopped: time limit reached after N of M seeds`, the same text is `stopped` in the JSON summary, report and `seedfall_run` result, and the exit code is decided as usual: 0 if every seed that ran passed and every property was met. A property that needs more seeds than fit fails as `never reached`, as it would with a shorter range, so give the sweep enough time, or [pin](verify.md#pinned-regressions) a seed that reaches the rare path. Each seed stays exactly replayable, but which seeds ran depends on the machine's speed, so compare runs by seed and not by count.

## Rotating seeds outside GitHub

`seedfall run -seeds 1-200 -rotate N` sweeps the Nth range of the same width after `-seeds`, so any CI system can pass its build number and explore new seeds on each run while every failure stays replayable by seed. `-rotate 0` is the plain range. The run prints `rotation N: seeds A-B`, and the report's `seeds` is the rotated range. MCP's `seedfall_run` takes the same value as `rotate`.

## `go test`

```go
import "github.com/kunalgoesbyken/seedfall/seedfalltest"

func TestDurabilityUnderCrashes(t *testing.T) {
	seedfalltest.Sweep(t, "seedfall.json", "1-100")
}
```

`Sweep` first replays every [pinned regression](verify.md#pinned-regressions) for the config. A failure reports the seed, the reason, the trace tail, the classification, a replay command and the [failure artifacts](reports.md#failure-artifacts) folder. A `Sometimes` property that is never satisfied also fails the test.

Three more helpers turn known bugs into tests, each replaying for the config's full duration and expecting a pass:

```go
func TestPinnedRegressions(t *testing.T) {
	seedfalltest.Pinned(t, "seedfall.json")
}

func TestTornTailStaysFixed(t *testing.T) {
	seedfalltest.Replay(t, "seedfall.json", "testdata/torntail.faults.json")
}

func TestKnownSeeds(t *testing.T) {
	seedfalltest.Seeds(t, "seedfall.json", []uint64{1, 9})
}
```

`Pinned` runs each schedule in `seedfall-regressions/` as a subtest, and skips when there is none. `Replay` takes any schedule file with a `seed`, such as one written by `seedfall shrink`. `Seeds` runs each seed with its own faults as a subtest. `examples/kvlog/seedfall_test.go` uses all four.

## Speed

Runs are independent, so a sweep scales with cores: `seedfall run -j N` defaults to every CPU. Light servers take tens of milliseconds per seed; a 3-node hashicorp/raft cluster takes a few seconds. Each guest is compiled once per process and every seed reuses the compiled module, so per-seed cost is booting the nodes and running them. Compiled modules are also cached in `.seedfall/cache`, one entry per set of guest binaries, and only the 8 most recently used entries are kept, so the cache stays bounded however often you rebuild. Add that directory to your CI cache to skip compilation; the first build of a large guest such as nats-server takes about a minute.


<!-- docs/compat.md -->

# Storage engines that need mmap or flock

Some storage libraries don't build or run for `GOOS=wasip1` because they call `mmap`, `flock` or other syscalls that WASI doesn't have. With `compat_overlay`, seedfall gives them `wasip1` versions at build time, either a shim for that exact library or the [generic `mmap` and `flock` shim](#the-generic-mmap-and-flock-shim), so you test the library you ship, unmodified:

```json
{ "compat_overlay": true }
```

| Library | Without `compat_overlay` | With it | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `go.etcd.io/bbolt` v1.5 | doesn't build: no `MaxMapSize` for `GOARCH=wasm`, then `bolt_unix.go` needs `syscall.Flock` and `unix.Mmap` | runs; 300 seeds pass, `NoSync` is caught, and it found a [missing directory fsync](findings/bbolt-create-dir-fsync.md) | [`examples/bboltkv`](../examples/bboltkv) |
| `github.com/cockroachdb/pebble/v2` v2.1 | doesn't build: `vfs` has no `wasip1` file system (its generic lock file refers to an undefined `defFS`), `rawalloc` has no `maxArrayLen` for `wasm`, and prometheus/procfs v0.10 calls `syscall.Statfs` | runs; needs `strict_dirs` (see below) | [`examples/pebblekv`](../examples/pebblekv) |
| `github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4` v4.9 | builds, but `Open` fails: ristretto's `mmap` returns `ENOSYS` on `wasip1` | runs, with small memtable and value log sizes | [`examples/badgerkv`](../examples/badgerkv) |
| `github.com/blevesearch/mmap-go` v1.0.4 | doesn't build: its only mapping code is `//go:build` unix | runs through the generic shim; a writable mapping, `msync` and `mmap_early_writeback` work | [`examples/mmapwal`](../examples/mmapwal) |
| `github.com/edsrzf/mmap-go` v1.2.0 | builds, then `mmap` returns `ENOTSUP` from its `wasm` file | runs through the generic shim, which replaces the `wasm` file | swap the import in [`examples/mmapwal`](../examples/mmapwal) |
| `github.com/gofrs/flock` v0.13 | builds, then returns `ErrUnsupported` | runs through the generic shim, which replaces `flock_others.go` | [`examples/mmapwal`](../examples/mmapwal) |
| `golang.org/x/exp/mmap` | runs without a shim, reading the whole file | runs through the generic shim, with a real shared mapping | |
| `github.com/hashicorp/memberlist` v0.7 | doesn't build: `go-sockaddr` has no route lookup for `wasip1` | runs, with `net_overlay`; the shim answers as `go-sockaddr` does on other platforms without a route table, and a node binds and advertises its own IP | [`examples/memberlist`](../examples/memberlist) |

## What the shims do, and why crash results stay real

A shim only replaces calls that WASI can't make. Every write still goes to a file, and every durability point is still a real fsync on seedfall's simulated disk, so crashes, torn writes and fsync errors behave as they do for any other code.

- **Read-only `mmap`** (bbolt) becomes a heap copy of the file, re-read on every remap. bbolt writes pages with `pwrite` and syncs with `fdatasync`, never through the mapping. A `MAP_SHARED` mapping sees those writes immediately, so the shim copies each successful `pwrite` into the heap image too. The file stays the only source of truth after a crash.
- **Shared `mmap`** (badger through ristretto's `z` package, the generic shim) becomes a heap buffer that seedfall's disk knows about. A `pwrite` to the file updates every shared mapping of it, and pages written through a writable mapping reach the page cache at `msync`, at `munmap`, when the file is read with `pread` or mapped again, when it is fsynced, and when the process exits cleanly. `fsync` and `fdatasync` make every dirty page of the file durable. `MS_SYNC` flushes only the range it is given, then fsyncs the file; `MS_ASYNC` does not fsync. Truncating a file clears any part of a mapping past the new size. A `MAP_PRIVATE` mapping is a snapshot. Dirty pages that were never `msync`ed are lost on a crash unless [`mmap_early_writeback`](#early-writeback-of-mapped-pages) keeps them.
- **`flock` and file locks** become an in-process lock table. Each node is one process, and a crash starts a fresh process, so this matches what the lock guarantees.
- **`madvise`, `mlock` and disk-usage queries** are no-ops or report "unsupported". They are hints that don't change what is on disk.
- **Route lookups** (`go-sockaddr`) report that no route is known, as the library does on `js` and `plan9`. Only the automatic choice of a private IP depends on them.

## The generic mmap and flock shim

Most libraries put their mapping code in a file constrained to unix, and it calls `unix.Mmap`, `syscall.Mmap`, `unix.Flock` or `syscall.Flock`. You don't need a shim for each one. With `compat_overlay`, seedfall adds `Mmap`, `Munmap`, `Msync`, `Mlock`, `Munlock`, `Madvise` and `Flock` to `syscall` on `wasip1`, and a matching `golang.org/x/sys/unix`. It then finds files in your dependencies that are excluded on `wasip1`, would build on Linux, and call one of those four functions, and compiles them for `wasip1`. If such a file conflicts with a stub the library already builds on `wasip1`, like `gofrs/flock`'s `flock_others.go`, the stub is removed, but only when the file declares everything the stub declares. It does not touch your own module, or a file whose name ends in `_linux`, which normally assumes much more of Linux.

A file that uses anything else missing on `wasip1`, such as `unix.Fallocate`, fails to compile and the build error names the symbol. Run `seedfall init -n` to see which dependencies are covered: every `wasip1_blockers` entry has a `shim` line naming the shim or saying `none: needs a shim`, and `compat_shims` lists every dependency `compat_overlay` will touch, including ones like `gofrs/flock` that compile but fail at run time. `init` turns on `compat_overlay` when it finds any. `flock` is held by a table inside the node's process, keyed by inode: a lock is released by `LOCK_UN`, by closing the file descriptor that holds it, or when the process dies. A blocking `Flock` retries on a virtual 1 ms sleep; because `syscall` cannot import `time`, the overlay reaches `time.Sleep` through one `go:linkname`, the only one in seedfall.

## Early writeback of mapped pages

A kernel can write back any dirty page of a shared mapping at any time, so a program must not assume unsynced mapped data stayed volatile. With `"mmap_early_writeback": 0.5` in `faults`, each dirty page a crash finds in a writable shared mapping is treated as already written back with that probability, so it survives the crash where it would otherwise be lost. Each page is recorded as a `mmap_early_writeback` fault with the node and a `mapped page #N` count, so it replays, shrinks and edits like any other runtime disk fault. [`examples/mmapwal`](../examples/mmapwal) shows a checkpoint-and-checksum design that assumes unsynced pages can't reach the disk: it passes without the fault and fails with it.

Written-back pages are the page's content at the moment of the crash. A page written back earlier and dirtied again would have older content on a real kernel; that outcome is not generated.

## How it works

The shims are Go files embedded in seedfall, one directory per import path under [`engine/compat`](../engine/compat). At build time seedfall runs `go list -deps` for your nodes. For each dependency package with a shim, it copies the dependency's module into `.seedfall/compat`, adds the shim files, and removes every file the shim replaces. It builds with `-modfile` pointing at a copy of your `go.mod` that has a `replace` for each copied module. Your `go.mod`, `go.sum` and module cache are not touched. (`go build -overlay` can't be used here: Go refuses overlays for files in the module cache.)

Nothing is patched by text. A file is replaced when it declares something the shim declares, and then every top-level function, method, type, variable and constant it declares must be in the shim. If a new release adds a declaration to a replaced file, the build stops with an error that names it:

```
compat overlay: go.etcd.io/bbolt/bolt_unix.go declares fdatasync2, which the wasip1 shim does not provide; this version is not supported yet
```

Adding support for another library is adding a directory of `.go.txt` files. The generic shim adds `seedfall_mmap_wasip1.go` to `syscall` with the same `-overlay` mechanism as `net_overlay`, so the first build after a Go upgrade recompiles the standard library's `syscall` once.

## Pebble and directory fsyncs

Pebble records which manifest is current with an empty marker file. It creates the file and fsyncs the directory, but never fsyncs the empty file itself. On a real filesystem the directory fsync makes it durable. seedfall's default disk model drops every file that was never fsynced on a crash, so pebble would fail on its first restart with `database already exists and is not pristine`. Run pebble with `"strict_dirs": true`, where directory fsyncs decide which entries survive, as on a real filesystem.

## Not covered

- A mapping whose bytes are only read by another process. Each node is one process, so a mapping is only ever coherent with the node's own `pwrite` calls.
- Two mappings of one file see each other's writes only after one of the flushes above, because there is no page fault to hook.
- Mapping a file after its last name is unlinked: `Mmap` returns `EBADF`.
- `seedfall inspect` shows mapped writes only once they have reached the page cache, for the same reason.
- `mremap`, and code that needs more of `syscall` or `x/sys/unix` than the functions above. The build error names what is missing.
- Libraries seedfall doesn't have a verified shim for: `github.com/boltdb/bolt`, `github.com/hashicorp/raft-boltdb` before its `v2` (which uses bbolt), `github.com/dgraph-io/ristretto` before `v2`, and `github.com/cockroachdb/pebble` before `v2` (a `v2`-style shim made it build, but acknowledged writes were lost on restart, so it isn't shipped).
- Libraries that need cgo, such as RocksDB bindings or `mattn/go-sqlite3`.


<!-- docs/config.md -->

# Config files, profiles and seeded disks

One `seedfall.json` can hold every variant you test: a base config, named profiles that change a few fields, fault presets instead of hand-tuned rates, and one-off overrides from the command line. Nodes can start from an existing disk instead of an empty one, get files from the host, and restart into a new version of their program.

## Layers

A config is built from up to four layers, each merged over the one before:

1. the file named in `"extends"`, if any, itself built the same way
2. the file you pass with `-c`
3. the profile you pass with `-profile name`
4. every `-set path=value`, in order

Merging works the same way at every layer:

- objects merge key by key, so `{"faults": {"crash_on_io": 0.1}}` changes one rate and keeps the rest
- lists of named entries, such as `nodes` and `workloads`, merge by `name`: an entry with a known name merges into it, a new name is appended
- anything else, including `args` and other lists, replaces the value

Fields that no layer sets keep their defaults, as listed in the `seedfall://schema/config` MCP resource.

### extends

```json
{
  "extends": "seedfall.json",
  "nodes": [{ "name": "server", "args": ["-sync", "always", "-repair"] }],
  "faults": { "bitrot_per_sec": 0.5 }
}
```

`extends` names another config file, relative to the file that extends it, and can chain. A file that extends itself, directly or through others, is an error. Paths inside the config, such as `pkg`, `wasm`, `files` and `disk`, are resolved from the directory of the file you pass with `-c`, so keep extended files in the same directory as the configs that use them. `examples/kvlog` keeps one file per variant this way, each a few lines over `seedfall.json`, because the getting started guide and CI name those files.

### profiles

```json
{
  "nodes": [{ "name": "counter", "pkg": "./counter" }],
  "workload": { "name": "client", "pkg": "./client" },
  "faults": { "buggify": true },
  "profiles": {
    "fixed": { "nodes": [{ "name": "counter", "args": ["-dedupe"] }] },
    "off": { "faults": "none" }
  }
}
```

```sh
seedfall run -c seedfall.json -profile fixed -seeds 1-20
```

A profile is a partial config merged over the file. Asking for a profile that does not exist fails and lists the ones that do. Every command that takes `-c` takes `-profile`, and so do the MCP tools (`"profile": "fixed"`). `seedfall init` writes three starter profiles: `strict`, `resilient` and `everything`.

A profile is part of the config's identity everywhere seedfall prints or saves it:

- replay and shrink commands carry it: `replay: seedfall replay -c seedfall.json -profile fixed -seed 2`
- failure artifacts go to `.seedfall/failures/seedfall.fixed-seed-2/`, the same folder a separate `seedfall.fixed.json` would use
- `seedfall pin` records the profile and `-set` overrides in the pinned file (`"profile": "fixed"`), and a pinned schedule is replayed only by runs with the same config file, profile and overrides
- `-set` overrides add a short hash of the overrides to artifact folder and pinned file names, `seedfall.fixed.set-1a2b3c4d-seed-2`, so a run with overrides never replaces the files of a run without them
- reports, proofs and the hook print the full config reference

The Claude Code hook reads the profile from `$SEEDFALL_HOOK_PROFILE`.

### -set

```sh
seedfall run -set faults.crash_per_sec=2 -set duration=10s -seeds 1-50
seedfall run -set 'nodes.server.args=["-sync","always"]' -seeds 1-50
seedfall replay -seed 7 -set faults=resilient
```

`-set path=value` overrides one value after every other layer, and can repeat. The path is a dot-separated list of keys. Inside a list, a part is either the `name` of an entry or its index, so `nodes.server.env.MODE` and `nodes.0.env.MODE` both work. Missing objects along the path are created. The value is read as JSON when it parses as JSON (`2`, `true`, `["-x"]`, `{}`) and as a plain string otherwise (`10s`, `resilient`). To set a string that looks like JSON, quote it: `-set 'nodes.server.env.PORT="7000"'`.

## Fault presets

```json
{ "faults": "resilient" }
{ "faults": { "preset": "high_availability", "crash_per_sec": 2, "clog_per_sec": 0 } }
```

A preset fills in a documented fault level. Fields set next to it override it, and the string form is shorthand for `{"preset": name}`. Each level adds to the one before:

| Preset | Adds |
|---|---|
| `none` | no faults |
| `durability` | `crash_per_sec` 0.5, `crash_on_io` 0.002, `torn_writes`, `reorder_writes`, `strict_dirs`, `mmap_early_writeback` 0.1 |
| `resilient` | `pause_per_sec` 0.1, `slow_per_sec` 0.1, `reset_per_sec` 0.1, `clock_jump_per_sec` 0.05 |
| `high_availability` | `partition_per_sec` 0.2, `clog_per_sec` 0.2, `swizzle_per_sec` 0.05, `udp_loss` 0.01, `udp_dup` 0.01 |
| `everything` | `fsync_eio` 0.01, `write_eio`, `write_enospc`, `read_eio`, `read_corrupt`, `lost_write` and `misdirected_write` 0.005 each, `corrupt_on_crash`, `bitrot_per_sec` 0.05, `buggify` |

Durations, topologies and clog modes keep their defaults, and every rate is per node per second, per disk operation for the I/O faults, or per datagram for `udp_loss` and `udp_dup`, as in [faults](faults.md). The levels are seedfall's own, named after the fault tolerance levels Antithesis offers, not a copy of them. `high_availability` and `everything` include partitions, clogs and swizzles, which need at least two nodes that take faults, workload included. `everything` includes faults such as corrupted reads that only a system with checksums can survive.

A layer that names a preset starts its faults from that preset, and fault fields from earlier layers are dropped, so a profile with `"faults": "none"` turns every fault off even when the base config sets rates. A layer without a preset merges its fault fields as usual. On the command line, `-set faults=none` replaces the faults the same way, while `-set faults.preset=none` changes only the preset and keeps the fault fields set so far, which still override it. The preset in effect shows up as `faults.preset` in the triage report JSON and in the HTML report's fault table.

## Seeded disks and files

Every node starts with an empty disk unless its entry says otherwise:

```json
{
  "name": "ledger",
  "pkg": "./v1",
  "disk": "image",
  "files": { "etc/ledger.conf": "fixtures/atomic.conf" }
}
```

- `disk` names a host directory. Its files, directories and symlinks are copied onto the node's disk, the directory itself becoming `/`.
- `files` maps a path on the node's disk to a host file. A file listed here replaces the same path from `disk`.

Both are read from the host once, when the config loads, and copied into memory, so a run never touches the host disk and stays deterministic. The copied files are durable and synced before the node first starts, as if an earlier life had written and fsynced them: a crash never loses them, and `seedfall inspect` shows them as durable from t=0. Directories leading to them are durable too, even with `strict_dirs`. Symlinks and other special files in `disk` are rejected. The trace opens with a line per seeded node, `ledger's disk starts with 2 durable files, 86 bytes`, and the config hash in failure artifacts covers the bytes of every seeded file, so changing a fixture changes `config_sha256`.

`seedfall inspect -out dir` exports each node's durable disk as `dir/<node>/`, in exactly the layout `disk` reads, so a failing state can become the starting point of new runs:

```sh
seedfall inspect -seed 21 -out state
seedfall run -set nodes.ledger.disk=state/ledger -seeds 1-20
```

## Upgrades

```json
{ "name": "ledger", "pkg": "./v1", "upgrade_to": "./v2" }
```

`upgrade_to` names a second Go package for the node. seedfall builds both, the node starts as `pkg`, and every start from its first restart on runs `upgrade_to` instead, over whatever the old version left on disk. Restarts come from crash faults, `crash_on_io` and `supervise`. The trace marks the switch with `start ledger#2, upgraded to ./v2`. `upgrade_to` takes a package, not a prebuilt `wasm` file, and `seedfall mutate -app` mutates only `pkg`.

Together with `disk`, this tests the upgrade path FoundationDB's restart tests cover: real old data, a crash, and the new version's recovery code. [examples/upgrade](../examples/upgrade) seeds a v1 ledger, upgrades it to v2 on the first crash, and catches an in-place migration that a crash leaves half done.


<!-- docs/explore.md -->

# Feedback-guided exploration

A plain sweep draws a fresh random seed every time. A failure that needs two rare things to happen in the same run, each with odds of one in a thousand, needs on the order of a million seeds. `seedfall explore` looks for that kind of failure with feedback: it keeps the runs that reached something new, and spends further runs going deeper from there instead of starting over.

```sh
seedfall explore -c seedfall.json -seeds 1-8 -rounds 30 -batch 8
```

```
round 1   runs 8     +4 signals (4)  +625 functions (625)  corpus 4  failures 0  551ms
    new: property "level 1 reached" = true
    new: property "level 2 reached" = true
    new: property "level 3 reached" = true
    new: property "level 4 reached" = true
round 2   runs 16    +0 signals (4)  +0 functions (625)  corpus 4  failures 0  935ms
round 3   runs 24    +1 signals (5)  +0 functions (625)  corpus 5  failures 0  1.289s
    new: property "level 5 reached" = true
round 4   runs 32    +1 signals (6)  +2 functions (627)  corpus 5  failures 1  1.628s
    new: property "level 6 reached" = true

stopped: failure found
FAIL seed 6 at t=923.003008ms (924 scheduler steps, 56ms real)
  client#1: the vault opened after 6 consecutive lucky draws
```

That is [examples/explore](../examples/explore): 20 plain seeds never reach level 6 (and the sweep passes), while exploration finds it in 32 runs. A failure is reported the usual way, and the artifact is an ordinary schedule file.

## How it works

Round 1 runs the `-seeds` range and any entries left in the corpus by earlier runs. Every run reports **signals**:

| Signal | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `property "msg" = true` | a property fired with this outcome, optionally `during crash,partition`: the fault kinds with an open window when it first fired |
| `fault crash server` | a fault of this kind applied to this node, including a `buggify` firing with its site |
| function | a function reached for the first time, per node, counting every function in the binary (the Go runtime included, so some of them are the runtime reacting to the run). This is coarse, function-entry coverage, not basic blocks |

A run that adds a signal or a function joins the corpus as a schedule: its seed, recorded faults and branches. Every further round draws `-batch` children, one at a time from the exploration's own seed:

- pick a corpus entry, more often when it holds rare signals
- with odds 3 of 5, branch at the moment just after one of its signals fired, more often a rare one, and re-randomize the future. This is the checkpoint step: a run that reached the rare state continues from there, so a rare state followed by another rare event no longer needs both to happen in the same attempt
- with odds 1 of 5, re-key one stream (`sched`, `net`, `disk`, `disklatency` or `random`) from a random moment
- otherwise add, remove or shift a fault

Branching uses the machinery [`seedfall cause`](cause.md) already had, with branches now recorded in the run and chained, so a child of a child branches again. A branch at virtual time *T* re-keys the streams at the first scheduler step at or after *T*. Nothing is snapshotted: replay is exact, so reaching *T* again means re-running the seed.

The exploration stops at the first of these:

| Flag | Stops after |
|---|---|
| a failure | the first failing run, unless `-keep-going` |
| `-rounds N` | N rounds |
| `-budget 10m` | that much wall-clock time, checked between rounds |
| `-until-novelty N` (default 8) | N rounds in a row that added nothing |

## Determinism

The choices come from `-explore-seed` (default 1) and every result is merged in a fixed order, so a given corpus and flags produce the same rounds at any `-j` as long as a `-budget` does not cut them short: a `-budget` depends on the machine's speed, so use `-rounds` for an exploration that must repeat exactly in CI.

Every failure is a seed plus a schedule file, so nothing is lost for the rest of the tools:

```sh
seedfall replay  -seed 6 -faults .seedfall/failures/seedfall-seed-6-explore-504fa1fb9883/faults.json
seedfall shrink  -seed 6 -faults .seedfall/failures/seedfall-seed-6-explore-504fa1fb9883/faults.json
seedfall inspect -seed 6 -faults .seedfall/failures/seedfall-seed-6-explore-504fa1fb9883/faults.json
seedfall pin     -seed 6 -faults .seedfall/failures/seedfall-seed-6-explore-504fa1fb9883/faults.json
```

Those commands and the report's replay and shrink lines use the file because the seed alone would not reproduce the run. See [the schedule format](faults.md#editing-a-schedule).

## Corpus

Corpus entries are written to `.seedfall/corpus/<config>/<seed>-<id>.json` and replayed in the first round of the next `seedfall explore`, so a search keeps building where it left off. Pass `-corpus dir` to keep them somewhere committed, like Go fuzz testdata. An entry whose faults no longer fit the config (a node was renamed, for example) or that cannot be read is skipped and counted as stale. Delete the directory to start over.

## What re-keying does not reach

Re-keying a run changes the random streams seedfall owns: the scheduler, the network, the disk, I/O faults, buggify firings and what `random_get` returns to the guest, which reaches `crypto/rand` and `sim.Random`. Go's `math/rand` and `math/rand/v2` top-level functions are seeded once, when the process starts, and keep their own sequence, so a branch does not change what they return in a process that is already running. Workload randomness that should re-roll on a branch has to come from `crypto/rand` or `sim.Random`.

## Stopping a plain sweep

`seedfall run -until-novelty N` stops a sweep once N batches of seeds in a row added nothing, so a wide range does not need to be run in full once coverage has flattened out. `-batch` sets the seeds per batch (default 20) and the verdict for each seed is the same as without the flag; only how many seeds run changes, and the point a run stops does not depend on `-j`:

```sh
seedfall run -seeds 1-5000 -until-novelty 5 -batch 50
```

```
round  runs  new signals  signals  new functions  functions
  1     4     3            3        624            624
  2     8     1            4        1              625
  3     12    0            4        0              625
stopped: seed range finished
```

The same growth table is in the JSON output (`exploration`), `seedfall_run` and the **Exploration** section of the [triage report](reports.md).

## Throughput

Every sweep reports runs per second and virtual time simulated per wall second, the kind of efficiency numbers a deterministic simulation lives on. They are in the last lines of `seedfall run`, the JSON summary as `seeds_per_second` and `virtual_seconds_per_wall_second`, and the report header.

Numbers from one Windows 11 machine, `-j 2`, seedfall built with this repository's Go toolchain:

| Example | Seeds | Time | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `examples/kvlog` `seedfall.fixed.json` | 20 | 1.84 s to 2.12 s, 39 to 45x virtual time | without feedback instrumentation |
| `examples/kvlog` `seedfall.fixed.json` | 20 | 1.90 s to 2.13 s | with `-until-novelty`, which adds the function bitmap: no measurable slowdown |
| `examples/natscluster` | 3 | 15.2 s at `-j 1` | a 3-node cluster, about 5 s a seed |

A CPU profile of kvlog (10 seeds, `-j 1`, taken with a one-off build because `-cpuprofile` is refused on Windows) spent 55% of its samples in the guest's compiled code, 22% in wazero's call path to and from the guest, and 3.7% instantiating modules; the per-step watchdog timer did not appear in the top of the profile.

`seedfall run -cpuprofile cpu.pprof` is meant to write a Go pprof profile on platforms where Go's profiler can unwind through wazero's compiled code; it has not been verified on Linux or macOS. seedfall refuses it on Windows: the Go runtime crashes unwinding those frames, consistently with parallel guests and intermittently at one guest, reported with a `fatal error` from `runtime.sigprof`.

There is no snapshotting. `seedfall cause` and every branched run re-execute the seed from the start, in parallel on `-j` workers.

## From an agent

The MCP tool `seedfall_explore` takes the same options and returns the rounds, the stop reason and the failure. `seedfall_run` accepts `until_novelty` and `batch`. See [agents.md](agents.md).


<!-- docs/faults.md -->

# Configuration and faults

A world is described in a JSON file, `seedfall.json` by default. Paths inside it are relative to the file. One file can extend another, hold named profiles selected with `-profile`, take `-set path=value` overrides and start from a fault preset such as `"faults": "resilient"`; see [config.md](config.md).

```json
{
  "nodes": [
    { "name": "n1", "pkg": "./node", "args": ["-id", "n1"] },
    { "name": "n2", "pkg": "./node", "args": ["-id", "n2"] }
  ],
  "workload": { "name": "client", "pkg": "./client" },
  "duration": "60s",
  "latency": ["1ms", "5ms"],
  "supervise": true,
  "faults": {
    "crash_per_sec": 0.5,
    "restart_after": ["10ms", "500ms"],
    "partition_per_sec": 0.2,
    "partition_for": ["50ms", "1s"],
    "torn_writes": true,
    "crash_on_io": 0.005,
    "fsync_eio": 0.01,
    "strict_dirs": true,
    "clock_skew": "200ms",
    "pause_per_sec": 0.2,
    "clock_jump_per_sec": 0.05,
    "buggify": true,
    "swarm": true
  }
}
```

## World

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `nodes[]` | | Crashable nodes. Each has a `name`, then either `pkg` (a Go package, built for wasip1 automatically) or `wasm` (a prebuilt module), plus optional `args`, `env`, `faults`, `disk`, `files` and `upgrade_to`. `disk` and `files` copy a host directory and host files onto the node's disk before it first starts, durable and synced, and `upgrade_to` names a package the node runs from its first restart on ([seeded disks](config.md#seeded-disks-and-files), [upgrades](config.md#upgrades)). `"faults": false` keeps every fault away from the node: it is never crashed, paused, slowed or skewed, its disk never fails, and partitions and clogs never cut its links, like Antithesis's fault exclusions. `sim.Buggify` sites in its own code still fire |
| `workload` | | The checker. Same fields as a node. It takes none of the per-node faults (crashes, pauses, clock skew and jumps, slowdowns, resets, disk faults) unless `faults.include_workload` or its own `"faults": true` says so; partitions and clogs reach it like any node. The run passes when it exits 0 |
| `workloads[]` | | Several workloads instead of, or next to, `workload`. Each is a client like `workload`, and the run passes when every one of them has exited 0. See [Faults on the workload](#faults-on-the-workload) |
| `finally` | | A check that starts only after every workload has exited 0, with all faults stopped and the network healed. Same fields as a node; it never takes faults. The run passes when it exits 0, and its properties count like any other. See [properties.md](properties.md#liveness-recovery-and-finally-checks) |
| `liveness.within` | `0s` (off) | Liveness mode. At `duration` the faults stop, partitions, clogs, slowdowns and pauses end, and crashed nodes restart at once; then the workload (and the `finally` check, if any) must finish within `within`, or the run fails with class `liveness` |
| `duration` | `30s` | Virtual-time horizon, and with `liveness` the end of the fault period. A run that reaches it without failing counts as passed and is reported as "hit the time horizon"; with `liveness`, reaching it starts the recovery phase instead |
| `latency` | `["1ms", "10ms"]` | Per-chunk network delay range |
| `links[]` | | Per-link latency overrides, each `{"from": "n1", "to": "n2", "latency": ["20ms", "80ms"]}`. Links are one-way; leave out `from` or `to` to match any node, so `{"to": "n3", ...}` slows everything sent to `n3`. The first matching entry wins. See [Network faults](#network-faults) |
| `faults_after_setup` | `false` | Suppress all faults until a node calls `sim.SetupComplete()` |
| `supervise` | `false` | Restart a node that exits with an error, after `restart_after`. Go panics (exit code 2) still fail the run, and so does a workload that exits with an error, even under `include_workload` |
| `net_overlay` | `false` | Route plain `net.Listen` / `net.Dial` through the simulated network. See [networking.md](networking.md) |
| `compat_overlay` | `false` | Build dependencies that need `mmap` or `flock` with `wasip1` shims: a shim for bbolt, pebble or badger, or the generic shim for any dependency that calls `Mmap` or `Flock`. See [compat.md](compat.md) |
| `watchdog` | `30s` | Real-time limit for one node to run without yielding. Catches busy loops and livelocks. With `preempt.loops`, a busy loop parks like any other node and a run that never finishes fails on `liveness` instead, which does not depend on the host |
| `preempt.strategy` | `none` | When the running goroutine is preempted inside a node: `none` only at the end of a 4,194,304-call time slice, `random` after a seeded 1 to 4,096 counted calls, `pct` at `depth` - 1 seeded change points per node, each recorded as a `preempt` fault, `calls` every `preempt.calls` counted calls. See [how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md#strategies) |
| `preempt.interleave` | `false` | Shorthand for `"strategy": "random"`. While it is `true`, `strategy` can only be `random` or `none`, and `none` still means `random`, so a profile that switches strategy sets `interleave` to `false` |
| `preempt.depth` | `3` | `pct`: the bug depth d to look for, giving d - 1 change points per node |
| `preempt.steps` | `1048576` | `pct`: the change points are drawn over each node's first `steps` counted calls. The trace's last `pct:` line shows how many each node ran |
| `preempt.calls` | `4096` | `calls`: counted calls between preemptions, at most 4,194,304 |
| `preempt.loops` | `false` | Count loop iterations as well as function calls, so a loop without calls is preempted, uses virtual time and lets other nodes run. Costs guest CPU. See [how-it-works.md](how-it-works.md#loops) |

Every node sees the environment variables `SEEDFALL=1` and `SEEDFALL_NODE=<name>`, so `sim.Enabled()` and `sim.Node()` work.

## Faults

All faults come from the seed. Faults that depend on what the program does, such as which disk operation a crash lands on, are recorded when they happen so that shrinking and replay are exact.

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `preset` | | Start from a built-in fault level, `none`, `durability`, `resilient`, `high_availability` or `everything`, each adding to the one before; fields set next to it override it, and `"faults": "resilient"` is shorthand for `{"preset": "resilient"}`. The values each level sets are in [config.md](config.md#fault-presets) |
| `crash_per_sec` | `0` | Rate of crashes per node, at random points in time |
| `restart_after` | `["10ms", "1s"]` | Downtime after a crash, and the delay before a supervised restart |
| `partition_per_sec` | `0` | Rate of network partitions. A partition splits all nodes, workload included, into groups that cannot reach each other. A new partition replaces the previous one |
| `partition_for` | `["50ms", "2s"]` | Partition duration. TCP traffic across the cut is held and delivered after the heal; UDP datagrams are dropped |
| `partition_topologies` | `["half"]` | Shapes a partition can take; each partition picks one at random. `half` (two random sides), `one` (isolate one node), `majority` (a random majority against the rest), `majorities_ring` (every node sees a majority, and no two nodes see the same one) and `random_groups` (two or more random groups). See [Network faults](#network-faults) |
| `clog_per_sec` | `0` | Rate of clogs. A clog hits one direction of one link, or everything a node sends, receives, or both, and lasts `clog_for` |
| `clog_for` | `["100ms", "2s"]` | Clog duration, also the length of a swizzle |
| `clog_modes` | `["stop", "slow", "jam"]` | Modes a clog can take; each clog picks one at random. `stop` refuses new connections and holds traffic, `jam` holds connections and traffic without any error, `slow` adds `clog_delay` to every message. `stop` and `jam` drop UDP datagrams instead of holding them |
| `clog_delay` | `["10ms", "200ms"]` | Extra latency per message of a `slow` clog, drawn once per clog |
| `swizzle_per_sec` | `0` | Rate of swizzles (FoundationDB's swizzle-clogging): a random subset of nodes is clogged one node at a time, then unclogged in a different random order |
| `reset_per_sec` | `0` | Rate of connection resets per node. Every open connection of the node is reset at once, as if a middlebox dropped them; the process keeps running and both ends see `ECONNRESET` |
