| `udp_loss` | `0` | Probability that a UDP datagram is dropped. Each loss is recorded as a `udp_drop` fault with the sender and its datagram number. See [UDP datagrams](#udp-datagrams) |
| `udp_dup` | `0` | Probability that a UDP datagram is delivered twice, the copies with independent latencies. Each one is recorded as a `udp_dup` fault |
| `slow_per_sec` | `0` | Rate of slowdowns per node: a gray failure where the node stays up but everything it does takes longer |
| `slow_for` | `["500ms", "5s"]` | Slowdown duration |
| `slow_factor` | `10` | Largest slowdown. Each slowdown picks a factor between 1 and this value |
| `torn_writes` | `false` | A crash keeps a random in-order prefix of unsynced writes, possibly ending in a partial write |
| `reorder_writes` | `false` | A crash writes dirty pages back out of order, as the kernel does between fsyncs, within the limits of `fs_model`. This finds a commit record or header that reaches the disk before the data it points to. Combine with `torn_writes` to also tear the last write kept in each page. See [File system models](#file-system-models) |
| `fs_model` | `ext4_ordered` | Which crash states `reorder_writes` may produce: `ext4_ordered`, `page_independent` or `dir_reorder`, which needs `strict_dirs`. Setting it without `reorder_writes` is an error. See [File system models](#file-system-models) |
| `crash_on_io` | `0` | Probability that a node crashes *during* each disk operation. This is how you hit the window between a write and its fsync |
| `fsync_eio` | `0` | Probability that a file fsync fails with `EIO`. The unsynced writes stay readable but are dropped from durable storage, and the next fsync succeeds (Linux "fsyncgate" semantics) |
| `disk_bytes` | `0` | Size of each node's disk in bytes; `0` means unlimited. A write that does not fit writes what fits and returns the short count, and the next write fails with `ENOSPC`. See [Disk faults](#disk-faults) |
| `write_eio` | `0` | Probability that a file write fails with `EIO` and writes nothing |
| `write_enospc` | `0` | Probability that a file write fails with `ENOSPC` and writes nothing, however much space is free, as with a quota or a thin-provisioned volume |
| `read_eio` | `0` | Probability that a file read fails with `EIO` |
| `read_corrupt` | `0` | Probability that a file read returns one flipped bit. The disk holds the right bytes, so reading again returns them |
| `lost_write` | `0` | Probability that a file fsync succeeds but one 4 KiB page it should have written keeps its old content on disk. The program keeps reading the new content until a crash |
| `misdirected_write` | `0` | Probability that a file fsync succeeds but one page lands at another page offset of the same file, overwriting what was there, while the intended page keeps its old content |
| `corrupt_on_crash` | `false` | Each crash flips one bit in every file whose pending writes cover bytes that are on disk after the crash, somewhere in those bytes, as a sector half-written when the power failed |
| `bitrot_per_sec` | `0` | Rate of bit rot per node: one bit of durable data, in a random file at a random offset, flips |
| `disk_latency` | `["0s", "0s"]` | Extra time each fsync takes, drawn per fsync. Slow nodes stretch it |
| `mmap_early_writeback` | `0` | Probability that a dirty page of a writable shared mapping is already written back when a node crashes. Needs a shared mapping through `compat_overlay`. Recorded as a `mmap_early_writeback` fault. See [compat.md](compat.md#early-writeback-of-mapped-pages) |
| `strict_dirs` | `false` | Directory entries survive a crash only after the parent directory is fsynced (strict POSIX) |
| `clock_skew` | `0` | Each node's wall clock is offset by a seeded amount in `[-skew, +skew]`. The monotonic clock is untouched, so timers and `time.Since` are unaffected |
| `pause_per_sec` | `0` | Rate of process pauses per node. A paused node stops running, like a long GC pause or a stalled VM, then resumes without crashing. Its connections stay open and messages queue up |
| `pause_for` | `["100ms", "3s"]` | Pause duration |
| `clock_jump_per_sec` | `0` | Rate of wall-clock jumps per node. Each jump moves the node's wall clock forward or back by up to `clock_jump_max`; the monotonic clock is untouched |
| `clock_jump_max` | `10s` | Largest clock jump in either direction |
| `buggify` | `false` | Let `sim.Buggify` and `sim.BuggifyWithProb` sites in your code fire. Each site is enabled in a quarter of runs and then fires at its own rate; every firing is recorded as a `buggify` fault with its node, site and hit number. See [buggify.md](buggify.md) |
| `include_workload` | `false` | Give the workloads the per-node faults too: crashes, pauses, clock skew and jumps, slowdowns, connection resets and disk faults. A crashed workload restarts as a fresh process after `restart_after`, with the same name and its disk as the crash left it. See [Faults on the workload](#faults-on-the-workload) |
| `swarm` | `false` | Swarm testing. Each seed turns every fault type on or off and rescales its rate between 0 and 2× the configured value, so faults that hide each other get explored separately |

## Faults on the workload

By default the workload is the one process that never crashes, so a client's own retry, idempotency and session logic is never tested: what happens when a client restarts halfway through a write and sends it again? Set `"include_workload": true` to change that:

```json
"workload": { "name": "client", "pkg": "./client" },
"faults": { "include_workload": true, "crash_per_sec": 0.3, "pause_per_sec": 0.3 }
```

- A crashed workload restarts as a fresh process after `restart_after`, like a node. It keeps its name, so `sim.Node()` and any client id derived from it stay the same, and it finds its disk as the crash left it. A client that saves its progress there can resume; one that keeps it in memory starts over.
- A workload crash does not end the run. The run passes only when the last incarnation of every workload exits 0.
- Operations the crashed workload had recorded with `sim.Put`, `sim.Get`, `sim.Invoke` or `sim.Txn` and not yet completed stay open, and the trace says how many (`client#1 died with 2 operations in flight, their outcome is unknown`). The history check treats an open write as one that may take effect at any time after it started, and drops open reads, so the check stays sound under every [model](properties.md#other-models).
- Per node, `"faults": true` or `false` overrides the default: `true` on one of several workloads faults only that one, and `false` on a node keeps it out of every fault, network faults included.

`workloads[]` runs several clients side by side, each its own process, so one can crash while the others keep going:

```json
"workloads": [
  { "name": "writer", "pkg": "./client", "args": ["-mode", "write"], "faults": true },
  { "name": "reader", "pkg": "./client", "args": ["-mode", "read"] }
]
```

[`examples/liveness`](../examples/liveness) has a client that saves its progress and resends the add in flight after a crash. Without request deduplication on the server, one crash during an add applies it twice.

## Network faults

Every network fault is directional underneath: it decides what happens to traffic from one node to another. A connection needs both directions to open, so a stopped direction either way refuses a dial, and a jammed one holds it.

| Mode | New connections | Data in flight | Errors the program sees |
|---|---|---|---|
| partition, or clog `stop` | refused | held, delivered after the heal | `ECONNREFUSED` on dial |
| clog `jam` | accepted only after the clog lifts | held, delivered after the clog lifts | none, only timeouts |
| clog `slow` | accepted `clog_delay` later when the slow direction points at the listener | arrives `clog_delay` later, in order | none |

A clog targets one of four shapes, chosen at random: one link in one direction (`n1 -> n2`), or a node's inbound, outbound, or inbound and outbound traffic. A one-way partition, where `n1` can hear `n2` but `n2` cannot hear `n1`, is a `stop` clog on one link or an outbound clog on one node. Faults stack: a slow clog over a partition adds its delay to the held traffic.

Partition topologies follow Jepsen's nemeses. `half` is the original random split and stays the default, so existing seeds keep their schedules. `majority` needs at least 3 nodes and `majorities_ring` at least 4, workload included; the config is rejected otherwise. A ring partition is written as overlapping groups, and two nodes can talk only if some group holds both.

A slowdown by factor F stretches everything the node waits for: its timers and sleeps take F times as long, every message it sends or receives takes F times its latency, and a goroutine that spins is parked F times as long. The node still reads the true time, so it sees its own timeouts fire late, the way an overloaded machine does. CPU work between two waits stays free, as it is for every node in seedfall.

`sim.QuietFor` and the recovery phase of `liveness` heal every partition, clog and slowdown at once.

In a fault schedule, the new kinds look like this:

```json
{ "at": "1.2s", "kind": "partition", "groups": [["n1", "n2"], ["n2", "n3"], ["n3", "client"], ["client", "n1"]], "until": "2s" }
{ "at": "1.5s", "kind": "clog", "from": "n1", "to": "n2", "mode": "stop", "until": "3s" }
{ "at": "1.6s", "kind": "clog", "node": "n3", "dir": "out", "mode": "slow", "delay": "80ms", "until": "2.4s" }
{ "at": "2.1s", "kind": "net_reset", "node": "n2", "until": "2.1s" }
{ "at": "2.5s", "kind": "slow", "node": "n1", "factor": 4.5, "until": "6s" }
```

`dir` is `in`, `out` or `both`. A swizzle shows up as a run of `both` clogs in `stop` mode. Like every other planned fault, each one replays and shrinks on its own, appears in the trace, `seedfall cause` and the report, and joins swarm testing.

### UDP datagrams

TCP traffic is a byte stream, where the kernel retransmits and deduplicates, so a program never sees a packet dropped or repeated on a connection. A UDP program does. `udp_loss` and `udp_dup` are probabilities per datagram, drawn from their own stream of the seed, so they take no draws from any other fault:

```json
{ "faults": { "udp_loss": 0.05, "udp_dup": 0.02 } }
```

A partition or a clog that stops or jams a link also drops a datagram sent across it, rather than holding it for the heal, and a `slow` clog delays it. Datagrams that a link or a missing socket drops are consequences of the rest of the schedule, so they are not faults of their own: only `udp_loss` and `udp_dup` choices are recorded. They count per sender node, from 1, across restarts:

```json
{ "at": "2.1s", "kind": "udp_drop", "node": "n1", "to": "n2", "op": 17, "until": "0s" }
{ "at": "2.2s", "kind": "udp_dup", "node": "n2", "to": "n3", "op": 9, "until": "0s" }
```

`op` is the number of the datagram the sender sent, and the fault fires on that datagram whatever its destination; `to` is a record of where it went. Both replay exactly, shrink like any fault recorded at runtime, can be edited with `seedfall faults`, and join swarm testing. They do not apply when `faults` is off for either end of the datagram, or during a quiet period or the recovery phase. Semantics of sockets and addresses are in [networking.md](networking.md#udp).

## Disk faults

## File system models

`reorder_writes` turns on out-of-order writeback at a crash. `fs_model` says which states a crash may then leave behind. A model that is too weak reports bugs your file system cannot produce; one that is too strong misses bugs it can. The models follow Table 1 of ALICE ([All File Systems Are Not Created Equal](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/osdi14/osdi14-paper-pillai.pdf), OSDI '14), which measured these properties on real file systems.

| `fs_model` | File contents | Directory operations (`strict_dirs`) | Matches |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ext4_ordered` (default) | Appends and truncates of one file persist as an in-order prefix, split at 4 KiB page boundaries. Overwrites of existing bytes persist per page in any order, independently of the appends. Bytes past the surviving file size are not kept | An in-order prefix of the pending operations, under `torn_writes` | ext4 `data=ordered` |
| `page_independent` | Any subset of the dirty pages of a file, in order within each page. A later appended page can survive without an earlier one, leaving zeros in the gap | As `ext4_ordered` | Aggressive: useful to find code that depends on append order, but it reaches states ext4 `data=ordered` does not. ALICE records this for ext2, ext3 and ext4 in `writeback` mode, not for `ordered` |
| `dir_reorder` | As `page_independent` | Each pending operation survives independently, so a rename can persist without the create before it | ext2 and btrfs, where ALICE found directory operations persist out of order |

Details that follow from these rules:

- Models apply per file. Different files are independent, so an append to one file can survive while an earlier append to another is lost. ALICE records `Append -> Any op` failing on ext4 `ordered` for this reason (delayed allocation).
- Under `ext4_ordered` a crash that keeps an overwrite past the surviving file size keeps nothing of it, because that page was never part of the file on disk.
- A single directory operation is atomic in every model, as on btrfs. ext2 can also tear one rename so that both names or neither survive; that is not modelled.
- Plain `torn_writes` without `reorder_writes` does not use `fs_model`: it keeps an in-order prefix of all pending writes.

[`examples/symswap`](../examples/symswap) shows the difference. It publishes each generation by renaming a symlink over `current`, and fsyncs the new generation's file but not its directory entry first. Under `ext4_ordered` it passes, because a journal keeps directory operations in order. Under `dir_reorder` the rename can survive without the create, and `current` points at nothing.

Crashes, torn writes, `reorder_writes` and `fsync_eio` test what survives a crash. The faults below test what a storage engine does when the disk itself misbehaves: it fills up, it fails an operation, or it hands back or keeps the wrong bytes. These are the paths that WAL recovery and checksum code exist for, and the ones that are hardest to reach with a real disk.

```json
"faults": {
  "crash_per_sec": 0.5,
  "torn_writes": true,
  "disk_bytes": 1048576,
  "write_eio": 0.01,
  "read_eio": 0.01,
  "read_corrupt": 0.05,
  "lost_write": 0.01,
  "misdirected_write": 0.01,
  "corrupt_on_crash": true,
  "bitrot_per_sec": 0.2,
  "disk_latency": ["1ms", "20ms"]
}
```

| Fault | What the program sees | What is on disk afterwards |
|---|---|---|
| `disk_bytes` | A short write, then `ENOSPC` on the next write. Overwrites inside a file always fit, and space comes back when files shrink or are removed | What fitted |
| `write_eio`, `write_enospc` | The write fails | Nothing from that write |
| `read_eio` | The read fails | Unchanged |
| `read_corrupt` | One bit flipped in the bytes returned by one read | Unchanged |
| `lost_write` | fsync succeeds, and reads return the new content | One page has its old content; zeros if the page is new. The next fsync that rewrites the page writes it in full |
| `misdirected_write` | fsync succeeds, and reads return the new content | The intended page has its old content, and another page of the file holds the new one |
| `corrupt_on_crash` | After the restart, one flipped bit per file among the bytes that were being written | Same |
| `bitrot_per_sec` | The flipped bit, from the moment it happens, unless that byte has a pending write | One flipped bit |
| `disk_latency` | fsync takes longer | Unchanged |

How each one is modelled, and where it stops:

- **Disk usage** is the sum of every file's size on the node. Holes left by `Truncate` or by writing past the end count in full, so sparse files use more space than on ext4 or XFS. Directories and metadata use none. A `Truncate` that grows a file is never refused.
- **`ENOSPC` reaches your code as `ENOSPC`.** wazero's WASI layer has no `ENOSPC` and reports `EIO` for it, so seedfall rewrites the result of `fd_write` and `fd_pwrite` when the simulated disk was full, and `errors.Is(err, syscall.ENOSPC)` works in the guest.
- **Read and write errors** apply to file reads and writes only. Directory listings, `stat`, `open` and `Truncate` never fail.
- **Corrupted reads** flip one bit in the buffer of one read, as a bad cable or controller would. A checksum plus a retry handles them; a checksum alone turns them into an error.
- **Lost and misdirected writes** pick one dirty page of the file being fsynced. The page cache keeps the right content, because the drive acknowledged the write, so the program only notices after a crash, or never if the page is rewritten first. A misdirected write stays inside the file; writes landing in another file are not modelled. A file needs at least two pages for a misdirected write.
- **Crash corruption** damages only bytes that were being written when the node crashed. With plain crashes, unsynced writes are dropped, so it matters only where they survive: with `torn_writes`, `reorder_writes` or `crash_on_io`. If the damaged range overlapped older durable data, that data is what flips.
- **Bit rot** picks a byte uniformly over all durable data on the node, so large files are hit more often.
- **Latency** applies to file and directory fsyncs only, not to reads or writes, which go to the page cache. The whole node waits, because a wasip1 guest runs every goroutine on one thread.

Every one of them comes from the seed and replays exactly. The rates are drawn per operation, like `crash_on_io`, and each firing is recorded with its node and operation number: `disk op #N` counts the node's writes, truncates and fsyncs, and `disk read #N` counts its reads. Which page or bit is hit comes from a stream keyed by the seed, the fault kind, the node and that number, so it does not change when shrinking removes other faults. Bit rot is planned in time like a crash. In a fault schedule they look like this:

```json
{ "at": "1.942589003s", "kind": "read_corrupt", "node": "server", "op": 3, "path": "data/kv.log", "offset": 70, "until": "0s" }
{ "at": "912.496ms", "kind": "write_eio", "node": "server", "op": 67, "path": "data/kv.log", "until": "0s" }
{ "at": "2.601158s", "kind": "lost_write", "node": "server", "op": 232, "path": "data/kv.log", "until": "0s" }
{ "at": "5.259168s", "kind": "misdirected_write", "node": "server", "op": 558, "path": "data/kv.log", "offset": 4096, "until": "0s" }
{ "at": "657.015787ms", "kind": "bitrot", "node": "server", "path": "data/kv.log", "offset": 22, "until": "657.015787ms" }
{ "at": "36ms", "kind": "mmap_early_writeback", "node": "server", "op": 3, "path": "data/pages", "offset": 65536, "until": "0s" }
```

The other kinds are `write_enospc` and `read_eio`. A recorded fault fires at the operation its `kind`, `node` and `op` name, and bit rot fires at `at`. `path`, `offset` and `target` are filled in by the run so that you can read the schedule, and are left out when they are 0. `seedfall inspect` lists every damaged range of a file under `corrupted ranges`, and with `disk_bytes` shows how full each disk is. Disk usage and latency are settings, not faults, so swarm testing leaves them alone and toggles the rest.

[`examples/kvlog`](../examples/kvlog) shows each one: a corrupted read changes an acknowledged value, a checksum with a re-read fixes it, and a lost write, a misdirected write or bit rot breaks a store that keeps one copy, with or without checksums.

## Editing a schedule

A fault schedule (`.seedfall/seed-N.faults.json` from `shrink`, an artifact's `faults.json`, or a pinned regression) is a list of faults that a replay applies instead of drawing new ones. Changing one fault and replaying is the quickest way to test an explanation of a failure. `seedfall faults` makes the change and checks it:

```sh
seedfall faults -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1 -faults torntail.faults.json -remove 1 -out hypothesis.json
seedfall replay -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1 -faults hypothesis.json
```

```
seed 1, 1 faults from torntail.faults.json, wrote hypothesis.json
  1    802ms  crash server, restart at 802ms
duration 991ms
replay: seedfall replay -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1 -faults hypothesis.json
```

On kvlog's `seedfall.always.json`, seed 1 fails with `torntail.faults.json`, still fails with the crash during disk op #56 moved one operation earlier (`-shift 1=-1`), and passes once that crash is removed. That pass is within the schedule's shrunk 991ms, and the replay prints a note saying so: it shows the crash is necessary for this failure, not that the store is fixed.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-faults` | The schedule to start from. Without it, `.seedfall/seed-N.faults.json` next to the config, or, when that file does not exist, the faults seed N draws on its own, which takes one run |
| `-remove N` | Remove the fault at position N, counting from 1 as listed. Repeatable |
| `-shift N=AMOUNT` | Move fault N. A timed fault moves by a signed duration (`2=-50ms`), together with its `until`. A fault that fires at a disk operation, read, buggify hit, counted call or udp datagram (`crash_io`, `fsync_eio`, `write_eio`, `write_enospc`, `read_eio`, `read_corrupt`, `lost_write`, `misdirected_write`, `buggify`, `preempt`, `udp_drop`, `udp_dup`, `mmap_early_writeback`) moves by a signed count of those (`1=+2`), because its `at` only records when it happened. Repeatable |
| `-add JSON` | Add a fault in the format shown in this page, for example `{"at":"1s","kind":"pause","node":"server","until":"1.5s"}`. Repeatable |
| `-out` | Write the result here. Without it, the schedule is written back to the file it came from |

Positions in `-remove` and `-shift` always refer to the schedule as it was before the edit. An edited schedule drops the `shrunk_from` and `shrink_runs` that `shrink` recorded, since it is no longer what shrink found. The result is sorted by `at` and checked against the config before anything is written:

| Check | Applies to |
|---|---|
| `kind` is a fault kind seedfall knows | every fault |
| `node`, `from`, `to`, `side` and `groups` name nodes of the config | every fault |
| `at` is not negative | every fault |
| `at` is not after the end of the run: the schedule's `duration`, else the config's | every fault except those that fire at a disk operation, read, buggify hit, counted call or udp datagram, whose `at` only records when it happened |
| `until` is not before `at` | `crash`, `crash_io`, `partition`, `pause`, `clog`, `slow` |
| `side` or `groups`, not both | `partition` |
| `mode` is `stop`, `slow` or `jam`; `dir` is `in`, `out` or `both` with a `node`, or empty with two different nodes in `from` and `to` | `clog` |
| `node` is set | every kind except `partition` and `clog` |
| `factor` is at least 1 | `slow` |
| `op` is at least 1, a `buggify` fault names its `site`, and a `preempt` fault needs `preempt.strategy` `pct` in the config | faults that fire at a disk operation, read, buggify hit, counted call or udp datagram |

Without any edit, `seedfall faults` only lists and checks the schedule, and writes it only when it came from the seed's own faults, so that there is a file to edit. Over MCP, `seedfall_faults_edit` takes the same edits as JSON ([agents.md](agents.md#tools)).

A schedule file can also hold `branches`, which [`seedfall explore`](explore.md) writes for a failure it found by branching:

```json
"branches": [{ "at": "921.003003ms", "key": 257366709774643251 }, { "at": "1.2s", "key": 9, "stream": "sched" }]
```

Each branch re-keys the seed's random streams at the first scheduler step at or after `at`, in order. Without `stream` it re-keys every stream; with one of `sched`, `net`, `disk`, `io`, `udp`, `disklatency`, `mutant` or `random` it re-keys only that one. Re-keying `io` or `udp` changes nothing in a schedule, because those streams only decide faults and a schedule already fixes them; `mutant` matters only under `seedfall mutate`. `replay`, `shrink`, `inspect`, `debug`, `logs` and `pin` all honor them, and `at` values must not decrease.

## Choosing rates

Start with crashes and torn writes, then add `crash_on_io` around `0.005`, so a few hundred disk operations per run produce one or two mid-operation crashes. Add `fsync_eio`, `strict_dirs` and `reorder_writes` once the basic durability path passes. For consensus and leader-election code, add `partition_topologies` beyond `half`, then `clog_per_sec` and `slow_per_sec`: one-way links and slow leaders are the gray failures that break leases and stale-read checks. For a storage engine, add `disk_bytes` and `write_eio` to test the error paths of every write, then `read_corrupt` and `corrupt_on_crash` to test checksums. `lost_write`, `misdirected_write` and `bitrot_per_sec` lose data that a single copy cannot get back, so use them on replicated systems, or to check that a single node notices and stops instead of serving wrong data. Turn on `buggify` once you have marked sites in your code that should sometimes take the rare path. Turn on `swarm` for long CI sweeps. Use property coverage ([properties.md](properties.md)) to confirm the faults are actually reaching the code you care about.

## Durations

Every duration is a Go duration string, such as `"250ms"` or `"2s"`. Ranges are two-element arrays.


<!-- docs/getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

This walkthrough uses `examples/kvlog`, a small log-structured key-value server, to find a real durability bug, shrink it, fix it and prove the fix. It takes about five minutes.

## 1. Install

seedfall needs Go 1.25 or newer. It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows.

```sh
go install github.com/kunalgoesbyken/seedfall/cmd/seedfall@latest
seedfall doctor
git clone https://github.com/kunalgoesbyken/seedfall
cd seedfall/examples/kvlog
```

`seedfall doctor` checks the toolchain and prints a fix for anything missing. Homebrew, Scoop, an install script, a Docker image and how to verify a release are in [install.md](install.md); those paths need a release newer than v0.2.0.

## 2. Look at the world

`seedfall.always.json` runs one server and one client. It extends `seedfall.json` and changes only the server's `-sync` flag; merged, it reads (abridged):

```json
{
  "nodes": [{ "name": "server", "pkg": "./server", "args": ["-sync", "always"] }],
  "workload": { "name": "client", "pkg": "./client", "args": ["-writes", "200"] },
  "faults": { "crash_per_sec": 0.5, "torn_writes": true, "crash_on_io": 0.005 }
}
```

The server appends `key=value` lines to `data/kv.log` and fsyncs before every acknowledgement. The client writes 200 keys, then checks that every acknowledged key is still there, using `sim.Assert`. The only seedfall-specific code in the server is `sim.Listen`.

## 3. Sweep

```sh
seedfall run -c seedfall.always.json -seeds 1-100
```

```
FAIL seed 1 at t=2.891820635s (737 scheduler steps, 445ms real)
  client#1: acknowledged write lost: k96=v96, server now answers "NONE"
```

Even with an fsync before every acknowledgement, data is lost.

## 4. Shrink

```sh
seedfall shrink -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1
```

```
faults before the failure (2):
  427.268ms  crash server during disk op #56, restart at 761.268ms
     802ms  crash server, restart at 802ms
...
shrunk from 33 faults, 1m0s, 200 workload ops
         to 2 faults, 991ms, 63 workload ops
```

Shrink removed 31 faults, then made what was left simpler: the first crash restarts 30ms sooner, the second moved from 1.7s to 0.8s with no downtime, the run ends at 991ms instead of 60s, and the client, which sizes itself with [`sim.Budget`](properties.md#workload-size), sends 63 writes instead of 200.

The first crash lands in the middle of an append and leaves a torn, half-written line. On restart, recovery skips the bad line but keeps appending after it, so the next record is glued onto the garbage. The second crash forces another recovery, which can no longer parse that record.

`seedfall replay -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1` prints the full trace, and adding `-faults .seedfall/seed-1.faults.json` replays exactly the minimal schedule.

## 5. Fix and prove it

The fix is to truncate the torn tail during recovery. The server already has it behind `-repair`, and `seedfall.fixed.json` enables it:

```sh
seedfall run -c seedfall.fixed.json -seeds 1-1000
```

```
property       seeds reached  seeds true
  sometimes            1000         994  a crash interrupted the workload
  sometimes            1000         406  recovery found a torn tail

ok  1000 seeds passed (0 hit the time horizon) in 1m28.94s
```

The property table shows that the recovery path really ran: hundreds of seeds produced a torn tail, and every one was recovered correctly.

## 6. Go further

- `seedfall.fsyncgate.json` adds `fsync_eio`, and the "fixed" server fails again: a failed fsync leaves a hole in the durable log. `seedfall.rewind.json` adds the fix.
- `seedfall.strict.json` adds strict POSIX directory durability.
- Open `.seedfall/failures/seedfall.always-seed-1/timeline.html` from the failing sweep for a diagram of every crash, partition and message, or step through the run with `seedfall debug -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1 -at 1.7s` ([timeline.md](timeline.md)).
- Each of these files is a few lines that extend `seedfall.json`. In your own project you can keep such variants as profiles in one file and run them with `-profile`, or try a fault preset with `-set faults=resilient` ([config.md](config.md)).

## Your own project

1. Make your nodes reachable: either switch `net.Listen` and `net.Dial` to `sim.Listen` and `sim.Dial`, or set `"net_overlay": true` to run unmodified code ([networking.md](networking.md)).
2. Write a workload: any Go `main` package that drives your system and checks invariants with `sim.Assert`, `sim.Always` and friends ([properties.md](properties.md)).
3. Describe the world in `seedfall.json` ([faults.md](faults.md)).
4. Sweep locally, then in CI ([ci.md](ci.md)), and from your coding agent ([agents.md](agents.md)).

Your code must build for `GOOS=wasip1`. cgo is not available. Dependencies that need `mmap` or `flock` work with `"compat_overlay": true`, through a shim for bbolt, pebble and badger or the generic shim for other callers of `Mmap` and `Flock`; `seedfall init` turns it on and says which dependency is covered ([compat.md](compat.md)).


<!-- docs/gostman.md -->

# Use your Gostman collections as workloads

A [Gostman](https://github.com/kunalgoesbyken/gostman) collection already says what your API promises: each request carries checks such as `res.status equals 200` or `res.body equals {{value}}`. Gostman's Go `runner` package builds for `wasip1`, so a seedfall workload can load the collection and send it while seedfall crashes your service, tears its writes and partitions its network. A check that fails after the faults stop is a broken promise, reported with the request and the check, and replayable from its seed.

[`examples/gostman`](../examples/gostman) is a complete world: `examples/httpkv`'s server and a client that runs the collection in [`examples/gostman/collection`](../examples/gostman/collection).

## The pattern

Split the collection into two folders:

- **Write**: requests that change state. They are sent while faults run and retried until their checks pass, so a pass means the server acknowledged the change.
- **Verify**: requests that check state. They are sent after `sim.QuietFor`, when faults are paused and partitions healed. A request that gets no answer, because the server is still restarting, is sent again. A check that fails on an answer fails the seed.

The client copies the embedded collection onto its simulated disk, loads it and sends one request at a time through a single session:

```go
//go:embed collection
var Collection embed.FS

os.CopyFS(".", Collection)
collection, _ := runner.Load("collection")
session, _ := runner.NewSession(engine.Policy{})
session.Enter(collection, "", "Simulation", nil)
listed, _ := session.Catalog(collection, "Verify")
result := session.Send(ctx, listed[0].Request, listed[0].Folder, vars).Result
sim.Always(!result.Failed, "Gostman checks pass once the faults stop", details)
```

Nodes cannot read files on the host, which is why the collection is embedded. Variables passed to `Send` (`key`, `value`, `deleted_key` in the example) win over the environment, so each round uses fresh keys. The `Simulation` environment points `base_url` at `http://server:8080`, the node name; a `Local` environment points at `127.0.0.1` so the same files run with the Gostman command line.

## Run it

```sh
cd examples/gostman
seedfall run -seeds 1-120
seedfall replay -c seedfall.json -profile nofsync -seed 1
```

With fsync before every acknowledgement every seed passes. With `-fsync=false` the first seed fails once a crash drops an acknowledged write:

```
FAIL seed 1 at t=13.104695555s (108 scheduler steps, 29.398s real)
  client#1: Gostman checks pass once the faults stop: GET http://server:8080/kv/k6 (Verify/Get value)
  res.status equals 200: The value was 404
  res.body equals v6: The value was "404 page not found\n"
```

The client embeds the Gostman runner and its JavaScript sandbox, so each seed takes about a minute of real time; sweeps get their speed from running seeds in parallel.

## Use your own collection

1. Copy `examples/gostman/client` and `collection.go` next to your service's seedfall config, and put your Gostman workspace folder in `collection/`.
2. Add a `Simulation` environment whose base URL uses the node name from `seedfall.json`.
3. Put the requests that write in one folder and the requests that check in another, and pass their names with `-write` and `-verify`.
4. Enable `"net_overlay": true` so the runner's plain `net/http` client reaches the simulated network.

The example uses HTTP requests with assertions. Anything that needs the host, such as `{{$file(...)}}`, local commands or an OAuth sign-in in a browser, cannot work inside a node.


<!-- docs/how-it-works.md -->

# How seedfall works

## One process, one clock, many nodes

seedfall compiles every node with the stock Go toolchain for `GOOS=wasip1` and runs each one as its own [wazero](https://wazero.io) module instance. On `wasip1` the Go runtime is single-threaded and has no async preemption, and every source of nondeterminism reaches the outside world through three WASI calls. seedfall implements all three in the host, and adds a deterministic preemption point of its own (below):

| WASI call | seedfall behavior |
|---|---|
| `random_get` | A ChaCha8 stream derived from the seed and the node's incarnation. This fixes map iteration order, `select` choice, `math/rand` and crypto randomness. |
| `clock_time_get` | A virtual clock shared by every node. Every read advances it by one nanosecond, so two `time.Now()` calls in a row never return the same value, as on real hardware; wall and monotonic clocks advance together. With `clock_skew` and `clock_jump`, each node's wall clock is offset by a seeded amount; the monotonic clock is never skewed. |
| `poll_oneoff` | Parks the node until its earliest timer or its next network arrival. |

A node gives up control when all of its goroutines are blocked, or when it is preempted after a long run without blocking (see [Preemption](#preemption)). The scheduler runs exactly one node at a time, picks the next one by earliest wake-up time, breaks ties with the seed, and jumps virtual time forward. Ten seconds of `time.Sleep` cost no real time.

There is no `linkname`, no source rewriting and no forked runtime, so new Go releases keep working. The opt-in `compat_overlay` and `net_overlay` are the exceptions: they add wasip1 files to your build ([compat](compat.md)), and the generic `flock` shim uses one `go:linkname` to `time.Sleep`.

## Preemption

Real Go preempts a goroutine that has run for 10ms. On `wasip1` nothing does, so a goroutine that spins without a syscall would starve every other goroutine in its node, and its node would never yield. seedfall loads each Go module with a call counter added to the start of every function. After 4,194,304 counted calls without the node blocking, the counter calls back into the host, which triggers the Go runtime's own cooperative preemption path for the running goroutine (the same `stackguard0` request the runtime's `sysmon` makes on other platforms) and parks the node for 10ms of virtual time, so other nodes run too. The count is part of the execution, so preemption points are as deterministic as everything else. A burst shorter than that costs no virtual time.

### Loops

By default a loop that makes no function call is not counted, so it is never preempted: a call-free spin holds the whole simulation until the real-time `watchdog` stops it, and a long call-free computation takes no virtual time. With `"preempt": {"loops": true}` the counter also runs at the head of every wasm `loop`, which the Go compiler emits for Go loops, so loop iterations count like calls. A node that spins or computes for 4,194,304 counted calls and iterations is then parked for 10ms of virtual time like any other: other nodes keep running, timers and leases on other nodes expire, and a spin that never ends fails deterministically on `liveness` (or runs to the horizon) instead of on the host-dependent watchdog. [`examples/busyloop`](../examples/busyloop) shows both: a leader whose lease expires during a call-free checksum, which only fails with `loops`, and a spin-wait that fails as `liveness` with `loops` and as a real-time `timeout` without.

Two limits. The Go runtime on `wasip1` can switch goroutines only at a function entry, so a goroutine in a call-free loop still keeps the other goroutines of its own node from running until it makes a call; `loops` parks the node, it cannot hand the CPU to a sibling goroutine. And the extra check on every iteration costs guest CPU, which is why it is off by default.

### Strategies

`preempt.strategy` decides when, inside a time slice, the running goroutine is preempted:

| Strategy | Preempts the running goroutine | Randomness |
|---|---|---|
| `none` (default) | only at the end of a 4,194,304-call time slice | none |
| `random` (`"interleave": true` is shorthand) | after a seeded random 1 to 4,096 counted calls, again and again | per instance, from the seed |
| `pct` | at `depth` - 1 change points per node, drawn from the seed over the node's first `steps` counted calls | per node, from the seed, recorded as faults |
| `calls` | every `calls` counted calls | none |

`random` finds shallow races quickly: a check-then-act window that any preemption opens shows up within a few seeds ([`examples/interleave`](../examples/interleave), `interleave.json`). But it preempts every goroutine every few thousand calls, so no goroutine ever runs long without being interrupted. A bug that needs one goroutine to stop inside a window while another runs a long stretch to completion is almost never hit.

`pct` is probabilistic concurrency testing (Burckhardt, Kothari, Musuvathi and Nagarakatte, ASPLOS 2010), as in shuttle's `check_pct`. A run is left alone except at `depth` - 1 seeded change points; at each one the running goroutine is preempted and goes to the back of the Go run queue, and whatever runs next keeps running until it blocks or its time slice ends. For a priority scheduler with n threads and k steps, PCT finds any bug of depth d (one that needs d ordering constraints) with probability at least 1/(n·k^(d-1)) per run. In `examples/interleave`, a checkpointer that copies a journal up to its reserved length instead of its committed length fails on 20 of seeds 1-20 with `pct` at depth 2, on 2 of 20 with `random`, and on none with `none`, because the bug needs the checkpointer to format a long header without being interrupted (`journal.json`).

Every change point that fires is recorded as a `preempt` fault with its node and counted call (`op`), and the trace says so:

```
    0.000s  preempt: pct, depth 2, change points per node: 1, drawn over the first 300000 counted function calls
    0.000s  fault preempt journal#1's running goroutine at counted call 259662
    0.000s  pct: journal ran 271681 counted calls, change points fired: 1
```

In the schedule file it is

```json
{ "at": "10ns", "kind": "preempt", "node": "journal", "until": "0s", "op": 259662 }
```

so replay is exact, `shrink` drops change points the failure does not need, and `seedfall faults` can move one (`-shift 1=-1000`) or remove it to test an explanation. A schedule's `preempt` faults replace the seed's own change points, and they fire only when the config's strategy is `pct`. The last trace line shows how many counted calls each node ran: set `steps` near that number, because change points drawn beyond it never fire.

The bound is a guide for choosing `depth` and `steps`, not a guarantee seedfall gives. seedfall picks only the change points. It cannot see goroutines from the host, so it does not assign them priorities: which goroutine runs after a preemption is the Go scheduler's choice, under the seed's random source. Change points are drawn per node, k is counted in calls (and loop iterations with `loops`), and preemption takes effect at the goroutine's next function call. None of the strategies is a data race detector: they find races that change behaviour, not unsynchronized accesses that happen not to. Run your tests under `go test -race` as well.

## Determinism

Scheduling, network latency, disk tearing, fault timing and I/O faults each draw from their own seeded stream. Removing one fault therefore barely disturbs the rest of the run, which is what makes shrinking work. The same seed produces the same trace byte for byte across processes and machines. `seedfall run -check` verifies this on every seed.

## Disk

Each node gets an in-memory file system mounted at `/` with an explicit durability model. Your code uses plain `os.File`.

- Writes land in the page cache immediately and are visible to reads.
- `Sync` makes the file's pending writes durable.
- A crash keeps only durable data. A file that was never synced disappears.
- With `torn_writes`, a crash also keeps a random in-order prefix of the pending writes, possibly ending in a partial write.
- With `reorder_writes`, a crash writes back dirty pages out of order, as kernel writeback does between fsyncs. Each pending write is split into 4 KiB pages. What may survive depends on `fs_model` ([File system models](faults.md#file-system-models)). The default, `ext4_ordered`, keeps appends and truncates of a file as an in-order prefix and lets overwrites of existing pages survive per page. `page_independent` keeps a random in-order prefix of the writes to each page, with pages chosen independently, and `dir_reorder` also lets each pending directory operation survive independently. With `torn_writes` as well, the last write kept in each page can be partial. Which pages survive is drawn from a stream keyed by the crash itself, its time or its `crash_on_io` disk operation, so shrinking away other faults does not change it.
- `Sync` and `Datasync` behave the same: both make every pending write to the file durable, and neither makes the file's directory entry durable, which is what `strict_dirs` models.
- With `strict_dirs`, creating, renaming or unlinking a file survives a crash only after its parent directory is fsynced. This is strict POSIX, the model used by ALICE and CrashMonkey. Without it, directory entries are durable as soon as they are made, which matches ext4 and XFS in practice.
- With `fsync_eio`, a file `Sync` can fail with `EIO`. The unsynced writes stay readable but are dropped from durable storage, and the next `Sync` succeeds. These are Linux's post-2018 "fsyncgate" semantics.
- Hard links share one inode and count their links, symbolic links are followed by `open`, `stat` and intermediate path components, and `Lstat`, `Readlink`, `Link` and `Symlink` behave as on Linux, including `ELOOP` after 40 hops. A new link is a directory operation like any other: with `strict_dirs` it survives a crash only after its parent directory is fsynced. Symlinks are durable with their directory entry, because a program cannot fsync one.
- `Chtimes` stores times on the file, reads update the access time as `relatime` does, and the times a file had at its last fsync are what a crash restores. Directories report no times. `Chmod` is not modelled: WASI has no call for it, Go's `wasip1` `os.Chmod` only checks that the file exists, and `Stat` reports fixed permission bits.
- With `disk_bytes`, each node's disk has a fixed size. A write that does not fit is cut short and the next one fails with `ENOSPC`.
- `write_eio`, `write_enospc`, `read_eio` and `read_corrupt` fail or corrupt single reads and writes. `lost_write` and `misdirected_write` make a successful fsync leave one page with its old content, or put it at the wrong offset, while the page cache keeps the right bytes. `corrupt_on_crash` flips a bit in the bytes being written at a crash, `bitrot_per_sec` flips durable bits over time, and `disk_latency` makes every fsync wait. Each per-operation fault is recorded with the node's disk operation or disk read number, so it replays and shrinks like `crash_on_io`. See [Disk faults](faults.md#disk-faults).

See [faults.md](faults.md) for every fault type.

## Network

UDP sockets are queues of datagrams with their own seeded latency, sorted by arrival, so they reorder; a held link drops them rather than holding them, and `udp_loss` and `udp_dup` choices are recorded per sender datagram so they replay and shrink like the disk faults. Connections are ordered byte streams with seeded per-chunk latency. Partitions and `stop` or `jam` clogs hold traffic until they heal, `slow` clogs and slow nodes add latency, and a crashed node's connections are reset, as are a live node's when a `net_reset` fault fires. Every fault is a rule on one direction of a link, so one-way partitions fall out of the same code. Every connection is a virtual file registered with Go's own network poller, so blocking reads, deadlines and `Accept` behave exactly like `net`, and nothing polls. See [networking.md](networking.md).

## Crashes and restarts

Every incarnation of a node is a fresh module instance. A crash kills the whole process at a host call, including in the middle of a disk operation with `crash_on_io`, then applies the disk durability model. A restart instantiates the module again over the surviving disk. With `supervise`, a node that exits with an error is restarted the way systemd or Kubernetes would restart it.

## Checking

A run fails when:
- any node calls `sim.Fail`, fails `sim.Assert` or `sim.Always`, or reaches `sim.Unreachable`;
- a `sim.Eventually` condition is still false at its deadline, or, with `liveness`, the workload or the `finally` check has not finished within `liveness.within` of the recovery phase (liveness);
- the workload or the `finally` check exits non-zero;
- a node exits or panics, unless `supervise` restarts it (Go panics always fail);
- every node is blocked with no timer or pending message (deadlock);
- a node runs longer than `watchdog` of real time without yielding (livelock or busy loop; with `preempt.loops`, a spinning node parks like any other and fails on `liveness` instead);
- the recorded `sim.Put` / `sim.Get` / `sim.Invoke` history is not linearizable under the configured model, or the `sim.Txn` history has an isolation anomaly.

A sweep also fails when a cataloged property is never reached, or a `Sometimes` is never true, in any seed.

See [properties.md](properties.md).

## Shrinking

`seedfall shrink` replays a failing seed under smaller and smaller variations and keeps a change only while the run still fails the same way: same class, node, property and message, ignoring numbers. It never trades the bug for a different one, and every schedule it keeps is one it actually ran. It works in passes:

1. **Remove faults by delta debugging** (ddmin). Try half the schedule, then each half on its own, then quarters, eighths and so on down to removing single faults. In `examples/kvlog`, seed 1 goes from 33 faults to the 2 it needs in 16 runs. The last round removes one fault at a time, so the result is 1-minimal: removing any fault left makes the failure go away or change.
2. **Cap the workload** if it sizes itself with [`sim.Budget`](properties.md#workload-size), by bisecting the operation count.
3. **Trim the duration** by bisecting the run's horizon down toward the failure.
4. **Simplify each fault**: shorten crash downtimes, partitions, pauses, clogs and slowdowns (`until` moves toward `at`), shrink clock jumps toward zero, take nodes off the cut side of a partition (a partition into groups keeps its groups), and move planned faults earlier. Faults recorded at run time, such as a crash during a disk operation, keep their operation index; only their downtime shrinks.

Passes 2 to 4 repeat, with another removal round after each, until nothing changes. Times are bisected to within two milliseconds. The shrinker makes no random choices of its own, so a seed always shrinks to the same schedule.

Candidates of one round run at once on `-j` workers (all cores by default), and the shrinker takes the first one that fails, in the order it would have tried them one by one. The schedule and run count are the same for any `-j`. `-budget` stops early: a number (`-budget 300`) counts those runs, so the result is still reproducible, while a duration (`-budget 10m`) is wall-clock time and depends on the machine. With more than one job, a round can also start runs whose results are thrown away. When the budget runs out, shrink saves the smallest failing schedule so far and says it may not be minimal.

The output shows each improvement with the runs used so far and the faults left, then the sizes before and after:

```
  run   16    2 faults  removed 1 of 3 faults
  run   26    2 faults  sim.Budget capped at 107 of 200 operations
  run   43    2 faults  duration 1.965s instead of 1m0s
  ...
shrunk from 33 faults, 1m0s, 200 workload ops
         to 2 faults, 991ms, 63 workload ops
in 191 runs, 14.296s
```

The schedule is saved to `.seedfall/seed-N.faults.json`:

```json
{
  "seed": 1,
  "faults": [
    { "at": "427.268419ms", "kind": "crash_io", "node": "server", "until": "761.268419ms", "op": 56 },
    { "at": "802ms", "kind": "crash", "node": "server", "until": "802ms" }
  ],
  "duration": "991ms",
  "ops": 63,
  "shrunk_from": { "faults": 33, "duration": "1m0s", "ops": 200 },
  "shrink_runs": 191
}
```

`replay`, `inspect` and `verify` take it with `-faults`. `duration` replaces the config's `duration` and `ops` caps `sim.Budget`; leave either out to use the config. A bare JSON array of faults, the format older versions wrote, still works. A replay that passes only because the shortened `duration` ended it before the workload finished prints a note saying so, and `verify` replays schedules for the config's full duration, so a cut-short run never counts as proof of a fix.

## Speed

Virtual time never waits on the wall clock. When every node is blocked, the scheduler jumps straight to the next timer, message or fault; the only real-time limit is the `watchdog`. Real time therefore goes to three things:

- **Guest CPU.** Nodes run as wasm compiled to native code by wazero, with a check on every loop iteration so the watchdog can stop a busy loop. That check costs about a third of guest CPU and is what makes livelocks reportable instead of hanging the run. `preempt.loops` adds seedfall's own counter to every loop head as well. Host calls (clock, `poll_oneoff`, files, network) are a few percent.
- **Booting nodes.** Every start and restart is a fresh module instance: wazero sets up memory and data segments, then the Go runtime and your `main` run. For nats-server this is 0.1-0.3s per start, so short seeds with many crashes are dominated by boots.
- **Compiling, once.** Each guest is compiled once per process and shared by every seed and every node that runs the same binary. Compiled code is cached in `.seedfall/cache`, so later processes only load it. The cache keeps the 8 most recently used sets of binaries and deletes older ones, so rebuilding a guest many times does not fill the disk.

A busy 3-node NATS JetStream cluster under crashes and partitions simulates about 2.5-3x faster than real time; a JetStream node that mostly waits on its client about 7x. Seeds are independent, so `seedfall run -j N` runs N at once.


<!-- docs/inspect.md -->

# Inspecting the disk at the moment of failure

`seedfall replay` tells you what happened. `seedfall inspect` shows you what is on disk when it goes wrong: every file on every node, how much of it is durable, which bytes a crash would lose, which directory entries are not durable yet, and where the last crash tore a write.

```sh
seedfall inspect -c rosedb.json -seed 1
```

```
seed 1 failed at t=3.12130224s: client#1: acknowledged entry 27 lost: server now answers "VAL e141-1111111111111111111111"
disk state at t=3.12130224s, the moment of failure

node server (directory entries are durable once made; torn_writes: a crash may also keep a prefix of the pending writes)
  path                                                   size    durable  state
  data/                                                     -          -  durable
    wal/                                                    -          -  durable
      000000001.SEG                                      4029       4029  durable
        ^ torn by the crash at t=427.268199ms: kept 60 of a 73-byte write at offset 2019
      000000002.SEG                                      3979       3979  durable
      000000003.SEG                                      2054       2054  durable
  2 dirs, 3 files: 10062 bytes durable, 0 bytes pending, 0 entries lost on crash, 0 removed entries that come back

node client (directory entries are durable once made; torn_writes: a crash may also keep a prefix of the pending writes)
  empty disk
```

The crash at 427ms left a 60-byte fragment of entry 26 at offset 2019, and every later entry was appended after it. That is the rosedblabs/wal bug in [findings](findings/rosedblabs-wal-torn-tail.md), visible without reading any code.

## Usage

```sh
seedfall inspect [-c seedfall.json] -seed N [-faults file.json] [-at DURATION] [-node name] [-cat path | -out dir]
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-seed` | Seed to replay |
| `-faults` | Replay with a fault schedule from `seedfall shrink` |
| `-at` | Snapshot at this virtual time instead of at the failure, for example `-at 4.4s`. The snapshot is taken at the last scheduler step at or before it. If the run fails or ends first, the snapshot is taken there. |
| `-node` | Only this node |
| `-cat` | Print the durable content of one file: text as is, binary as a hex dump. The file must exist in the durable image. |
| `-out` | Write each node's durable disk image to `dir/<node>/`, so you can open it with the library's own tools, or start new runs from it with `"disk": "dir/<node>"`, a path relative to the config's directory ([seeded disks](config.md#seeded-disks-and-files)); the command prints that path. The target must not exist yet. |

The run is the same as `seedfall replay`: same seed, same faults, same trace. Inspecting changes nothing about it.

## Reading the output

Each file has its live size (what the program reads now) and its durable size (what survives a crash), and one state:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `durable` | The live content and the durable content are the same, and the name survives a crash |
| `PENDING: N bytes lost on crash at [a,b) ...` | These byte ranges of the live content differ from the durable content: they were written but not fsynced |
| `PENDING truncate` | The file was truncated but not fsynced; a crash restores the old bytes |
| `NOT DURABLE: never fsynced` | Without `strict_dirs`, a file that was never fsynced disappears on crash |
| `NOT DURABLE: entry vanishes on crash` | With `strict_dirs`, the directory entry is not durable until the parent directory is fsynced, even if the file's data is |

A `^ torn by the crash at t=...` line under a file says the last crash kept only part of one write: how many bytes of it, and at which offset. Those partial bytes are now durable and are what recovery code has to cope with.

With `reorder_writes`, a `^ the crash at t=... wrote back pages out of order` line lists the writes that were pending at the last crash, numbered in program order, and says which of them reached the disk: `kept`, `lost`, or `partial` when only some of its pages did. A later write marked `kept` above an earlier one marked `lost` is the reordering your recovery code has to survive. The same list is in `last_writeback` in the MCP inspect output.

With the [disk faults](faults.md#disk-faults), a `^ corrupted ranges` list under a file shows every range a disk fault damaged: a `lost write` or `misdirected write` that a successful fsync left with its old content, a bit flipped by `bit rot` or by `crash corruption`, and each `corrupted read` that returned a flipped bit while the disk held the right bytes. It is a history: an entry stays after the program overwrites the range or a later fsync rewrites the page in full. The last 8 are shown, and the full list is in `damage` in the MCP inspect output. With `disk_bytes`, a `disk_bytes: N of M bytes used` line follows the totals.

```
    kv.log                                               5727       5727  durable
      ^ corrupted ranges:
        t=5.259168049s misdirected write: [4096,5005) kept its old content on disk, and its page landed at offset 0 instead
```

With `strict_dirs`, a file that was unlinked or renamed away while its parent directory was not fsynced is listed separately as an entry that a crash brings back. Renaming a temporary file over an existing one without fsyncing the directory shows up as the new name `NOT DURABLE` and the old content coming back.

The durable image is the disk a crash would leave without `torn_writes` or `reorder_writes`. With `torn_writes`, a crash can also keep an in-order prefix of the pending writes and, with `strict_dirs`, of the pending directory operations. With `reorder_writes`, what it can keep depends on `fs_model`, which the node line names: `fs_model` is also a field of the MCP inspect output, and each file reports `symlink` and `links` there. With `inspect -out`, a symlink is written as a symlink; on Windows without the privilege to create one, it is written as a file holding its target. Hard links are written as separate files.

## Examples

NATS JetStream, the stream that vanishes ([finding](findings/nats-stream-meta-checksum-crash.md)):

```sh
cd examples/natsjs
seedfall inspect -c seedfall.always.json -seed 40 -faults metasum.faults.json
```

```
          EVENTS/                                           -          -  durable
            meta.inf                                      517        517  durable
            meta.sum.tmp                                    6          6  durable
              ^ torn by the crash at t=158.20724ms: kept 6 of a 16-byte write at offset 0
            msgs/                                           -          -  durable
              1.blk                                      7702       7702  durable
```

`meta.inf` exists, `meta.sum` does not, and only a torn `meta.sum.tmp` is left. NATS skips a stream without a checksum on restart, and because `meta.inf` exists it never writes `meta.sum` again, so the 1.blk messages acknowledged since are skipped on every later restart.

tidwall/buntdb, one step before the crash that empties the database ([finding](findings/tidwall-buntdb-shrink-fsync.md)):

```sh
cd examples/buntdb
seedfall inspect -c seedfall.shrink.json -seed 27 -at 4.417s -node server
```

```
  data/                                                     -          -  durable
    db                                                   1255          0  NOT DURABLE: never fsynced, vanishes on crash
```

The AOF shrink renamed its rewritten file into place without fsyncing it: 1255 bytes live, none durable. At the failure, `db` holds only the 211 bytes that the crash at 4.417s happened to keep.

## From an agent

The MCP server exposes the same snapshot as `seedfall_inspect`, with the per-file sizes, volatile byte ranges, entry durability and last tear as JSON, and optionally one file's durable content. See [agents.md](agents.md).

## Limitations

- The snapshot covers the simulated disk only, not process memory or in-flight network messages. `seedfall debug -at` stops the run at the same moment and also shows the messages in flight, the active faults and each node's live file content ([timeline.md](timeline.md#debugger)).
- The last tear is recorded per file. A later write over the same range does not clear it.
- `-cat` prints the whole file. Pipe it through `tail` for large files.


<!-- docs/install.md -->

# Installing seedfall

seedfall ships as a single binary, and it builds your nodes with Go. Anything that runs nodes, including `run`, `replay`, `shrink` and the matching MCP tools, needs Go 1.25 or newer because it builds them first. Reading a finished report with `seedfall findings`, and `version`, `help` and `schema`, need only the binary.

**Which of these work today.** The Homebrew, Scoop, install script and Docker paths install from a release built by `.github/workflows/release.yml`. v0.2.0 predates that workflow and has only bare binaries, with no archives or `checksums.txt`, so until a newer release is cut use `go install`. The pipeline's signing, SBOM, cask, manifest and image steps have not run yet, so the commands below that depend on them are what the configuration is set up to produce, not something checked against a published release.

## Homebrew

```sh
brew install kunalgoesbyken/tap/seedfall
```

The cask depends on Go. seedfall binaries are not notarized by Apple, so on macOS the cask clears the quarantine flag on its own binary after installing; without that, Gatekeeper would refuse to start it.

## Scoop (Windows)

```powershell
scoop bucket add seedfall https://github.com/kunalgoesbyken/homebrew-tap
scoop install seedfall
```

The manifest depends on Go.

## Install script (Linux and macOS)

```sh
curl -fsSL https://seedfall-lemon.vercel.app/install.sh | sh
```

It picks the archive for your OS and architecture, checks its SHA-256 against the release's `checksums.txt`, and installs to `~/.local/bin`. Set `SEEDFALL_VERSION=v0.3.0` to pin a release, `SEEDFALL_INSTALL_DIR` to change where it goes, and `SEEDFALL_BASE_URL` to download from a mirror. It stops with an error on a checksum mismatch. The script is `scripts/install.sh`; read it first if you prefer.

## Docker

```sh
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" ghcr.io/kunalgoesbyken/seedfall run -seeds 1-200
```

The image is built on the official `golang` image, so it can build your nodes with no local Go. Files the container writes, including `.seedfall/`, belong to root unless you pass `--user`.

## go install

```sh
go install github.com/kunalgoesbyken/seedfall/cmd/seedfall@latest
```

This needs Go 1.25 or newer and always works, including for releases before the automated pipeline.

## Check the install

```sh
seedfall version
seedfall doctor
```

`seedfall version` (or `--version`, with `-json` for a script) prints the release, commit, build date, Go version and platform. A build without VCS data, such as `go install` of a tagged module, has no commit or date lines. The same version goes into `report.json`, each `.seedfall/history.jsonl` entry, failure artifacts, pinned regressions and the `seedfall verify` proof block, so a bug report can name the exact build.

`seedfall doctor` checks the Go version, that `GOOS=wasip1` builds, that `net_overlay` patches and builds against the installed Go, that the Go build cache and the current directory are writable, and the free memory. It prints a fix for anything wrong and exits 1 only if a check fails; a warning, such as low memory or an unsupported `net_overlay`, leaves it at 0. `-json` prints the same checks, as does the `seedfall_doctor` MCP tool. Free memory is measured on Linux and Windows and reported as `skip` elsewhere.

`seedfall help` lists every command, and `seedfall help run` prints one command's flags and defaults. `-h` and `--help` work too and all of these exit 0.

## Verifying a release

Each automated release publishes `checksums.txt`, a Sigstore bundle `checksums.txt.sigstore.json` signed keylessly by the release workflow, an SBOM per archive, and a GitHub build provenance attestation.

Verify the signature on the checksums, then an archive against them:

```sh
cosign verify-blob checksums.txt \
  --bundle checksums.txt.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/kunalgoesbyken/seedfall/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/v' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c checksums.txt
```

Or check provenance with the GitHub CLI:

```sh
gh attestation verify seedfall_linux_amd64.tar.gz --repo kunalgoesbyken/seedfall
```

The install script checks SHA-256 only, which catches a corrupted download but not a tampered release; use one of the commands above for that.

## Cutting a release

Pushing a `v*` tag runs the release workflow, which builds linux, darwin and windows on amd64 and arm64 with GoReleaser, signs, attests, publishes the GitHub release and pushes the Homebrew cask, the Scoop manifest and the image. The repository needs a `HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN` secret with write access to `kunalgoesbyken/homebrew-tap`, which holds both the `Casks/` directory and the Scoop `bucket/`. Release notes are grouped from commit subjects starting with `Add` or `feat` and `Fix` or `fix`. A tag with a prerelease suffix, such as `v0.3.0-rc1`, is marked as a prerelease and leaves the cask, the Scoop manifest and the `latest` image alone.


<!-- docs/mutate.md -->

# Mutation testing your checks

A sweep that passes is only meaningful if your workload would notice when a guarantee breaks. `seedfall mutate` tests that directly: it weakens the simulated disk, network or clock under your nodes, one guarantee at a time, and checks whether your sweep catches it.

```sh
seedfall mutate -c seedfall.always.json -seeds 1-30
```

```
baseline: seeds 1-30 pass

  fsync_noop     killed     seed 1: client#1: stream EVENTS lost after restart, 133 acknowledged messages gone
                 file fsync returns success without making anything durable

  dirsync_noop   not exercised (the operation never ran, or has no effect in this configuration)
                 directory fsync does nothing (matters with strict_dirs)

  osync_ignored  killed     seed 1: client#1: stream EVENTS lost after restart, 133 acknowledged messages gone
                 writes to O_SYNC and O_DSYNC files are no longer synchronous

every exercised mutant was killed
```

That run is NATS JetStream (`examples/natsjs`). Both guarantees NATS relies on are protected by the workload: when either one silently stops working, acknowledged messages are lost and the sweep fails.

## Mutants

| Mutant | What breaks |
|---|---|
| `fsync_noop` | File `fsync` reports success but makes nothing durable |
| `dirsync_noop` | Directory `fsync` does nothing. Only observable with `strict_dirs`, where directory entries need it to survive a crash |
| `osync_ignored` | Writes to files opened with `O_SYNC` or `O_DSYNC` stop being synchronous |
| `fsync_corrupts` | File `fsync` makes the data durable with one bit flipped: the first byte of the last write it covers. Reads see the right data until a crash, then the flipped one |
| `rename_not_atomic` | A rename over an existing file is not durable until the next successful fsync of any file or directory on that disk. A crash before then loses both names, so neither the old nor the new version exists after the restart. A rename to a new name is unchanged |
| `truncate_not_durable` | `fsync` makes writes durable but skips truncations, including `O_TRUNC`. Reads see the shorter file until a crash, then the old length comes back with the old bytes past the new data |
| `net_drop_after_close` | When a connection is closed, the last chunk written to it that the peer has not read yet is dropped, so the peer sees end of file without it |
| `net_dup_chunk` | 5% of connection writes, chosen from the seed, arrive twice in a row |
| `monotonic_jump` | `clock_jump` faults move the monotonic clock along with the wall clock, so `time.Since` and timers see time run backwards or leap ahead. Needs `clock_jump_per_sec` |

Mutants need no changes to your code. Each one weakens only the nodes that take faults: the disk mutants their disks, the network mutants the data they receive, and `monotonic_jump` their clocks. The workload is affected only with `include_workload`, and the `finally` check never. A run with a mutant replays exactly like any other: the duplicated writes come from their own seeded stream.

Run some of them with `-only`:

```sh
seedfall mutate -c seedfall.json -seeds 1-20 -only net_dup_chunk,truncate_not_durable
```

`-md mutants.md` also writes the result as a Markdown table, for a pull request or job summary; the [GitHub Action](ci.md#verify-and-mutate) uses it. `-only` picks among these runtime mutants and cannot be combined with `-app`. Over MCP the tool is `seedfall_mutate`, with `config`, optional `seeds` (default `1-100`) and `only`. It returns each mutant's `outcome`, the `killed_by_seed` and `reason` when killed, the `seeds_passed` and how many times the operation was `weakened`.

### The new mutants on `examples/ledger`

```
$ seedfall mutate -c seedfall.json -seeds 1-20
baseline: seeds 1-20 pass

  fsync_noop            killed     seed 1: client#1: ledger total covers every acknowledged deposit: {"left":4660,"right":5506,"unacked":1831}
  ...
  truncate_not_durable  SURVIVED   20 seeds passed although the operation was weakened 5 times
                        fsync makes writes durable but not truncations, so a crash brings back the old length and the bytes past it

  net_dup_chunk         killed     seed 18: client#1: ledger total holds no deposit that was never sent: {"left":8387,"right":8119}
                        a seeded 5% of connection writes are delivered twice, which TCP never does
  ...
1 mutants survived: your workload does not notice those guarantees disappearing
```

A duplicated `ADD` is applied twice and the upper bound on the total catches it. `truncate_not_durable` survives because the ledger cuts off a torn final entry with `Truncate` at every start, so a truncation that does not persist only brings back bytes that the next recovery drops again: a survivor you can explain as equivalent. In `examples/liveness`, `rename_not_atomic` survives 991 weakenings for a similar reason: when a crash loses the client's progress file, the client resends adds the servers have already deduplicated.

## Source mutants

The mutants above break the world under your program. `-app` breaks the program itself: seedfall parses the Go files of every node package (not the workload or the `finally` check), lists every place it can make one of three changes, picks `-mutants` of them (default 10) with the first seed of the range, and rebuilds the node once per mutant through a `go build -overlay`, so your files are never touched:

| Change | What it does |
|---|---|
| `flip_comparison` | Negates one comparison: `<` and `>=`, `>` and `<=`, `==` and `!=` |
| `skip_error_return` | `if x != nil { ...; return ... }` becomes `if false && x != nil`, so the early return never runs |
| `skip_sync` | `f.Sync()` becomes a call that returns `nil` without syncing |

```
$ seedfall mutate -c seedfall.fixed.json -seeds 1-10 -app -mutants 4
baseline: seeds 1-10 pass

  server/main.go:95     SURVIVED   10 seeds passed (or the mutated code never ran)
                        complete < len(data) -> complete >= len(data)

  server/main.go:97     killed     seed 1: server#2 crashed: module closed with exit_code(2)
                        err != nil -> err == nil

  server/main.go:157    killed     seed 1: client#1: acknowledged write lost: k61=v61, server now answers "NONE"
                        err != nil -> err == nil

  server/main.go:197    SURVIVED   10 seeds passed (or the mutated code never ran)
                        cmd[0] == "PUT" -> cmd[0] != "PUT"

2 mutants survived: your workload does not notice those guarantees disappearing
```

That is `examples/kvlog`. The survivor at line 197 is a real blind spot: with the comparison flipped, the server answers every `PUT` with an error, the client counts no write as acknowledged, and nothing asserts that writes are ever acknowledged, so the sweep still passes. The survivor at line 95 only changes the condition of a `sim.Sometimes`, which records coverage and never fails a seed.

seedfall cannot tell whether a mutated line ever ran, so a source mutant has no "not exercised" verdict: a survivor may be dead code. A mutant that does not compile (for example a `Sync` method with no error result) is reported as `did not build` and does not count as a survivor. The same seed range and `-mutants` count pick the same mutants every time. Each mutant costs one `go build` and one sweep, so start with a small count. `seedfall verify -app-mutants N` adds the same mutants to a proof ([verify.md](verify.md)), and over MCP `seedfall_mutate` takes `app` and `mutants`.

## Verdicts

- **killed**: some seed failed, so your workload notices this guarantee disappearing. That is the goal.
- **SURVIVED**: every seed passed even though the operation was weakened. Either your checks miss the broken guarantee (acknowledged data loss, a duplicated request, a timeout computed from a clock that ran backwards), or your faults never hit the window where it matters. Raise `crash_per_sec` or `crash_on_io`, lengthen the run, or strengthen the invariant. `seedfall mutate` exits non-zero when any mutant survives.
- **not exercised**: the weakened operation never ran, or had no effect in this configuration. For example, `dirsync_noop` without `strict_dirs`.

The baseline must pass first; otherwise mutants would be killed by the existing bug.


<!-- docs/networking.md -->

# Networking

seedfall gives every node a simulated network: ordered TCP byte streams and unordered UDP datagrams with seeded latency, per-link latency overrides, partitions that hold TCP traffic until they heal and drop UDP datagrams, one-way clogs that stop, jam or slow a link, slow nodes, and connection resets when a peer crashes or a reset fault fires. Node names are host names, so a node named `server` is reachable at `server:7000`.

How each network fault behaves and how to configure it is in [faults.md](faults.md#network-faults).

There are two ways to connect your code to the simulated network.

## Option 1: `sim.Listen` and `sim.Dial`

```go
import "github.com/kunalgoesbyken/seedfall/sim"

ln, err := sim.Listen("tcp", ":7000")
conn, err := sim.Dial("tcp", "server:7000")
pc, err := sim.ListenPacket("udp", ":7100")
```

They return a standard `net.Listener`, `net.Conn` and `net.PacketConn`. Outside the simulator they call `net.Listen`, `net.Dial` and `net.ListenPacket`, so production builds are unaffected. This works on every Go version seedfall supports, and it is how most of the examples are written. A connection also has `CloseRead` and `CloseWrite`, reached with a type assertion to an interface that declares them.

If a library takes a custom dialer or listener, pass these in. hashicorp/raft's `NewNetworkTransport` accepts a `StreamLayer` built on them, and NATS clients accept `nats.SetCustomDialer`.

## Option 2: zero code changes with `net_overlay`

```json
{ "net_overlay": true }
```

With `net_overlay`, unmodified programs that call `net.Listen`, `net.Dial`, `net.ListenPacket`, `net.ListenUDP` and `net.DialUDP` use the simulated network, and so do `net/http` servers and clients, and libraries such as hashicorp/raft's stock `NewTCPTransport` and hashicorp/memberlist. `examples/httpkv` is a plain `net/http` server and client with no seedfall imports in the server, and `examples/memberlist` is an unmodified memberlist cluster gossiping over simulated UDP.

How it works: on `wasip1`, Go's `net` package uses an in-process fake network. At build time, seedfall reads that package from your own `GOROOT` and builds an overlay with `go build -overlay`. It makes four exact-text patches: `socket()` is renamed so a seedfall version can wrap it, `accept()` gets a hook for seedfall listeners, and `setReadBuffer` and `setWriteBuffer` accept any size for simulated sockets, because the simulated queues have no size. Then it adds one file to package `net` that sends TCP and UDP sockets to the simulator. Node names resolve through a simulated `/etc/hosts`, and `localhost` means the node itself.

If a future Go release changes those internals, the build fails with a clear "this Go version is not supported yet" error instead of misbehaving. Verified on Go 1.27.

## Addresses, port 0 and half-close

Both options behave the same way:

- Listening or binding on port 0 picks a free port from `49152`..`65535`, in a sequence kept per node, and `Addr()` or `LocalAddr()` returns the real port.
- Every dial takes its own port from the same range, so an accepted connection's `RemoteAddr()` is the dialer's real address and matches the dialer's `LocalAddr()`. Under `net_overlay` an address is the node's IP from the simulated `/etc/hosts`, such as `10.77.0.2:49152`. Through `sim` it is the node name, such as `client:49152`.
- `CloseWrite` sends EOF to the peer after the data already written, and the other direction keeps working. Writing after `CloseWrite` fails with `EPIPE`. `CloseRead` makes every later read return EOF.

## UDP

A UDP socket on one node talks to any other through the same link table as TCP, and every datagram draws its own latency, so datagrams overtake each other whenever the latency range allows it.

| Condition | What happens to a datagram |
|---|---|
| Partition, or clog `stop` or `jam`, in the sending direction | Dropped. Nothing holds it for the heal |
| Clog `slow` | Arrives `clog_delay` later |
| Slow node | Latency is stretched, as for TCP |
| No socket bound to the address when it is sent, or one connected to a different address | Dropped. A connected sender gets the equivalent of ICMP port unreachable: unless a partition or clog cuts the path back, its next read or send after a round trip fails with `ECONNREFUSED`, once. An unconnected sender hears nothing |
| `udp_loss` | Dropped, recorded as a `udp_drop` fault |
| `udp_dup` | Delivered twice with independent latencies, recorded as a `udp_dup` fault |

Datagram boundaries are kept: a read returns one datagram and discards whatever does not fit in the buffer. A socket's queue has no limit, so `SetReadBuffer` and `SetWriteBuffer` succeed and change nothing, and a sender is never blocked. A crash closes the node's sockets and drops what was queued for them, and `net_reset` faults do not touch UDP, because a datagram socket has no connection to reset. Multicast is not simulated, and `WriteMsgUDP` with out-of-band data and raw reads with flags return `ENOTSUP`.

## Seeing the traffic

`-net-trace` on `run`, `replay`, `logs` or `debug` adds every dial, accept, message sent and message read to the trace, with its connection, size, send and arrival time, and whether a partition or clog held it.
