UDP sockets show up as `binds udp`, each datagram as `udp <socket>` lines, and a lost one says why. Every failure's `timeline.html` draws the same messages as arrows between nodes. See [timelines and logs](timeline.md).

## Without either

Go's unmodified `net` package on `wasip1` is an in-process fake. A `net.Listen` succeeds but can never be reached from another node. If nodes cannot reach each other, enable `net_overlay` or switch to `sim`.


<!-- docs/properties.md -->

# Properties, linearizability and determinism

## Failing a run

```go
sim.Fail("replica diverged")
sim.Assert(got == want, fmt.Sprintf("acknowledged write lost: %s=%s", key, want))
```

`Fail` and `Assert` stop the run with a message. Outside the simulator they panic, so the same code works in ordinary tests.

## Properties with coverage

A green sweep only means something if the dangerous paths actually ran. Properties are tracked across every seed and printed after a sweep:

```go
sim.Always(len(log) >= committed, "log never shrinks below the commit index", len(log), committed)
sim.Sometimes(tornTail, "recovery found a torn tail")
sim.Reachable("a node restored from a snapshot")
sim.Unreachable("two leaders in the same term", term)
```

| Function | Fails the seed when | Fails the sweep when |
|---|---|---|
| `Always(cond, msg, details...)` | `cond` is false | it was never reached |
| `AlwaysOrUnreachable(cond, msg, details...)` | `cond` is false | |
| `Unreachable(msg, details...)` | it is called | |
| `Sometimes(cond, msg, details...)` | | it was never reached, or `cond` was never true |
| `Reachable(msg, details...)` | | it was never reached |
| `Eventually(cond, msg, within)` | `cond()` is still false after `within` of virtual time, as a `liveness` failure | it was never reached |

```
property       seeds reached  seeds true
  sometimes             400         400  a crash interrupted the workload
  sometimes             400         172  recovery found a torn tail

ok  400 seeds passed (0 hit the time horizon) in 1m32s
```

A property is identified by its message, so keep messages constant and pass changing values as details. Details appear in the failure message but do not create a new property. A `Sometimes` that is never satisfied means your faults never reached that path: raise a fault rate, lengthen `duration`, or change the workload.

Properties are evaluated in any node, not only the workload. Outside the simulator, `Always`, `Unreachable` and `Eventually` panic on violation and the others do nothing.

### Numeric and grouped properties

The comparison and grouped forms match the [Antithesis SDK](antithesis.md) and say more than a plain boolean:

```go
sim.AlwaysGreaterThanOrEqualTo(len(log), committed, "log never shrinks below the commit index")
sim.SometimesGreaterThan(backlog, 100, "the queue backs up past 100")
sim.AlwaysSome(map[string]bool{"primary": p >= 0, "backup": b >= 0}, "some replica answers")
sim.SometimesAll(map[string]bool{"crashed": crashed, "recovered": recovered}, "a crashed node caught up")
```

| Function | Same as |
|---|---|
| `AlwaysGreaterThan(left, right, msg, details...)`, also `OrEqualTo` | `Always(left > right, ...)` (`>=`) |
| `AlwaysLessThan(left, right, msg, details...)`, also `OrEqualTo` | `Always(left < right, ...)` (`<=`) |
| `SometimesGreaterThan(left, right, msg, details...)`, also `OrEqualTo` | `Sometimes(left > right, ...)` (`>=`) |
| `SometimesLessThan(left, right, msg, details...)`, also `OrEqualTo` | `Sometimes(left < right, ...)` (`<=`) |
| `AlwaysSome(named, msg, details...)` | `Always` that at least one value in the `map[string]bool` is true |
| `SometimesAll(named, msg, details...)` | `Sometimes` that every value in the map is true |

`left` and `right` are any Go number type. On failure the details are JSON, `{"left":41,"right":40}` for the comparisons and the named booleans for the grouped forms, with any extra details under `"details"`.

For the comparisons seedfall also keeps a margin: `left - right` for `GreaterThan`, `right - left` for `LessThan`, so a positive margin is on the true side. An `always` comparison reports its smallest margin over every hit and seed, which is how close it came to failing; a `sometimes` comparison reports its largest, which is how close it came to being true. A margin of 0 on an `OrEqualTo` assertion means the boundary was hit exactly:

```
property       seeds reached  seeds true
  always                 20          20  no acknowledged add is lost  (smallest margin 0)
  sometimes              20           0  the queue backs up past 100  (largest margin -37)  <- never true (client/main.go:41)
```

The margin is also in `-json`, the MCP `seedfall_run` result (`margin`) and the HTML report.

### Events

```go
sim.Event("client resumed", map[string]int{"next add": done})
```

`sim.Event(name, details)` records a moment in the run without asserting anything. The details are encoded as JSON. Each event is a trace line (`event client resumed from client#2: {"next add":39}`), so it sits in order between the faults and the program output, and `seedfall_replay` returns the run's events as a list. Outside the simulator it does nothing. `lifecycle.SendEvent` from the Antithesis SDK is recorded the same way.

### The property catalog

Before a sweep, seedfall scans the Go source of every node and the workload for calls to these functions, including the numeric and grouped forms, with a constant message, so it knows about properties even if no seed ever executes them. A property that is never reached is reported with its location and fails the sweep:

```
property       seeds reached  seeds true
  reachable               0           0  compaction ran  <- never reached (node/main.go:12)
  always                  5           5  invariant holds

FAIL 1 properties were never reached or never true in 5 seeds
```

An `Always` that never runs proves nothing, so it has to be reached too. Calls whose message is not a string literal are still tracked once they run, but they cannot be cataloged in advance.

## Liveness: recovery and finally checks

Safety properties say nothing bad happens. Liveness properties say something good eventually happens, and they can only be checked once the faults stop. A cluster with a stuck leader, or a node that never reconnects after a network blip, passes every safety check: it just stops making progress, and a run that stops making progress only hits the time horizon.

Liveness mode adds a recovery phase to every run:

```json
"duration": "20s",
"liveness": { "within": "10s" }
```

For the first `duration`, faults fire as usual. Then the recovery phase starts: every remaining fault is suppressed, every partition, clog and slowdown ends, paused nodes resume, and crashed nodes restart at once instead of waiting out their downtime. From then on the workload has `within` of virtual time to finish. If it does not, the run fails with class `liveness`:

```
FAIL seed 1 at t=15s (2255 scheduler steps, 404ms real)
  liveness: client did not finish within 10s of the recovery phase starting at 5.000s

trace:
    4.172s  fault reset 1 connections of primary#1
    5.000s  recovery: the fault period ended; faults stop, partitions, clogs, slowdowns and pauses end, 0 crashed nodes restart now, everything must finish by 15.000s
   15.000s  FAIL  liveness: client did not finish within 10s of the recovery phase starting at 5.000s
```

That failure shrinks like any other: `seedfall shrink` cuts it to the faults that leave the system stuck, here a single connection reset. Liveness failures are grouped apart from safety failures in reports, as `liveness · client`.

### Eventually

`sim.Eventually` checks a condition that must become true, rather than one that must always hold:

```go
sim.Eventually(func() bool { return leader() != "" }, "a leader is elected", 5*time.Second)
```

It calls `cond` until it returns true, sleeping `within/100` of virtual time between calls, and returns true. If `cond` is still false after `within`, the run fails with class `liveness`, the property's message and `not true within 5s`. It is a property like the others: it is cataloged from the source, shows up in the coverage table as `eventually`, and fails the sweep if no seed ever reaches it. Outside the simulator it uses real time and panics when the condition never holds.

### Finally checks

A `finally` program runs once, after every workload has exited 0, the way Antithesis runs `finally_` commands:

```json
"workload": { "name": "client", "pkg": "./client" },
"finally": { "name": "check", "pkg": "./check" }
```

When the last workload exits, the recovery phase starts (if `liveness` has not started it already) and then the check starts. It never takes faults, it sees every node through a healed network, and the run passes when it exits 0. With `liveness`, it too must finish within `within` of the recovery phase. Its properties are cataloged and counted like the workload's, so this is the place for end-state checks: replicas converge, every acknowledged write is readable, nothing was applied twice.

```go
var p, b int
sim.Eventually(func() bool {
	p, b = count("primary:7000"), count("backup:7000")
	return p >= 0 && p == b
}, "primary and backup report the same count", 5*time.Second)
sim.AlwaysLessThanOrEqualTo(p, adds, "no add is applied twice")
sim.AlwaysGreaterThanOrEqualTo(p, adds, "no acknowledged add is lost")
```

[`examples/liveness`](../examples/liveness) shows all three: a primary that never reconnects to its backup fails liveness mode, a server without request deduplication fails the finally check once the client is crashed mid-request, and the fixed pair passes.

### Quiet periods

`sim.QuietFor(d)`, called from any node, starts a quiet period from inside the program: it suppresses every fault for `d` of virtual time and heals any active partition, lifts every clog and ends every slowdown. Unlike the recovery phase, nodes that are already down still restart on schedule. The trace records each suppressed fault. `examples/raftkv/client` uses this to check that the cluster recovers after the workload.

```go
sim.QuietFor(10 * time.Second)
started := time.Now()
waitUntilServed()
sim.Always(time.Since(started) < 10*time.Second, "cluster serves reads again within the quiet period")
```

## Faults at your own code sites

`sim.Buggify("site")` returns true at seeded points when `faults.buggify` is on, so the simulator can force a retry, an error return or a delay inside your code. A quiet period stops sites from firing too. See [buggify.md](buggify.md).

## Waiting for setup

With `"faults_after_setup": true`, no faults fire until some node calls `sim.SetupComplete()`. Use it when bootstrapping, such as electing the first leader or creating a stream, is not what you want to test.

## Workload size

Wrap the number of operations your workload performs in `sim.Budget` so that `seedfall shrink` can make it smaller:

```go
writes := flag.Int("writes", 200, "number of writes")
flag.Parse()
n := sim.Budget(*writes)
for i := range n {
	// one operation
}
```

`sim.Budget(n)` returns `n` in normal runs and outside the simulator. When a shrunk schedule sets `ops`, it returns at most that many, and the trace says so: `client#1: sim.Budget capped at 63 of 200 operations`. Shrink only tries this when a node called `sim.Budget` in the failing run, and bisects the cap down to the fewest operations that still fail the same way. Use the returned value everywhere the count matters, including messages and checks such as "all `n` writes were acknowledged". `examples/kvlog/client` does this.

## Linearizability

Workloads can record operations from any number of concurrent clients. When the workload finishes, seedfall checks the history with [Porcupine](https://github.com/anishathalye/porcupine) against the model named in `seedfall.json` (`kv` when there is no `checker`).

```go
op := sim.Put(clientID, "k1", "v7")
reply, err := client.Put("k1", "v7")
switch {
case err != nil:          op.Unknown()
case reply == "redirect": op.Failed()
default:                  op.Ok("")
}

op = sim.Get(clientID, "k1")
value, err := client.Get("k1")
if err != nil {
	op.Unknown()
} else {
	op.Ok(value)
}
```

- `Ok(output)` means the operation took effect. For a read, `output` is what was read, with `""` meaning absent.
- `Unknown()` means it may or may not have taken effect, such as a timeout. Unknown writes may land any time after they start; unknown reads are dropped.
- `Failed()` means it definitely did not take effect, such as a redirect to the leader.

On a violation, seedfall writes an interactive timeline to `.seedfall/seed-N.history.html`.

### Other models

`sim.Put` and `sim.Get` are shorthands for `sim.Invoke(client, f, key, value)`, which records any operation. Pick the model in `seedfall.json`:

```json
"checker": { "model": "queue" }
```

| Model | Operations: `sim.Invoke(client, f, key, value)`, then `op.Ok(output)` | Checked as |
|---|---|---|
| `kv` (default) | `put` with a string value; `get` with the string read as output, `""` for absent | A linearizable register per key |
| `cas` | `put` and `get` as in `kv`, plus `cas` with value `[]string{old, new}` and output `true` if it swapped, `false` if the value was not `old` | A linearizable compare-and-set register per key, for locks and leases |
| `append` | `append` with a string value; `read` with the whole list as output, a `[]string` | A linearizable append-only log per key |
| `queue` | `enqueue` with a string value; `dequeue` with the item taken as output, `""` when empty | A linearizable FIFO queue per key: no item lost, delivered twice or out of order |
| `set` | `add` with a string value; `read` with the members as output, a `[]string` in any order | A linearizable grow-only set per key |
| `counter` | `add` with an integer value; `read` with the integer read as output | A linearizable counter per key |
| `list-append` | `sim.Txn(client, mops...)`, see [transactions](#transactions) | Serializability, with Elle-style anomaly detection |

Every model checks each key on its own. An unknown `dequeue` stays in the history with any result allowed, since it may have removed an item; unknown pure reads (`get`, `read`) are dropped. An operation the model does not have, or an input or output of the wrong type, fails the run as an `assert` that names the operation, for example `history (model queue): operation "put" is not one of dequeue, enqueue`, so a typo cannot silently weaken the check.

```go
op := sim.Invoke(client, "cas", "leader-lock", []string{"", me})
swapped, err := locks.CompareAndSwap("leader-lock", "", me)
if err != nil {
	op.Unknown()
} else {
	op.Ok(swapped)
}
```

### Transactions

With `"checker": {"model": "list-append"}`, workloads record transactions over append-only lists, the workload Elle uses, and seedfall infers the dependencies between them:

```go
mops := []sim.Mop{sim.Read("x"), sim.Append("y", "c1-17")}
op := sim.Txn(client, mops...)
err := db.Txn(func(tx *Tx) {
	mops[0].Value = tx.List("x")
	tx.Append("y", "c1-17")
})
if err != nil {
	op.Unknown()
} else {
	op.Ok(mops)
}
```

`Ok` takes the same micro-ops back, with every read's `Value` set to the list it returned (a `[]string`). Appended values must be unique per key. seedfall takes each key's version order from its longest read, builds write-write, write-read and read-write edges between transactions, finds the strongly connected components with Tarjan's algorithm, and searches them breadth-first for one short cycle of each kind:

| Anomaly | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `G0` | A cycle of write-write edges: two transactions' appends interleave in different orders on different keys |
| `G1a` | A committed transaction read an append made by a transaction that `Failed()` |
| `G1b` | A transaction read a list ending in an intermediate append of another transaction, which appended to that key again later |
| `G1c` | A cycle of write-write and write-read edges with at least one write-read edge |
| `G-single` | A cycle with exactly one read-write edge, such as read skew |
| `G2` | A cycle that needs two or more read-write edges, such as write skew |
| `internal` | A transaction's read does not match its own earlier reads and appends |
| `incompatible-order` | Two reads of a key where neither is a prefix of the other, such as after a lost append |
| `duplicate-elements` | A read that contains the same element twice |
| `duplicate-append` | The same value appended to a key twice, which makes the history impossible to analyse |
| `garbage-read` | A read returned an element nobody appended |

A history with any of these fails as `isolation`, with one explained example of each kind in the trace:

```
G-single: T4 -rw z-> T0 -wr z-> T6 -ww y-> T4; T4 (client 4, ok) [r z ["4-0"], append y "4-1", r y ["3-0" "1-1" "4-1"]]; T0 ...
FAIL  history of 121 transactions is not serializable: G-single, G2, internal
```

`Tn` is the transaction's `id` in the history file. The check is serializability, not strict serializability: real-time order between transactions is not used. Transactions that returned `Unknown()` or never returned count as possibly committed: their appends are used once someone reads them, and their reads are ignored.

### History files

Every failing `run`, `replay` and `shrink`, and every passing `replay`, writes the recorded history to `.seedfall/seed-N.history.jsonl`, one event per line in Jepsen's invoke and completion shape:

```json
{"index":0,"type":"invoke","process":1,"f":"enqueue","key":"q","value":"1-0","time":8,"id":0}
{"index":4,"type":"ok","process":1,"f":"enqueue","key":"q","value":null,"time":648261,"id":0}
```

`type` is `invoke`, then `ok`, `info` (unknown) or `fail`; an operation that never returned has no completion line. `time` is virtual nanoseconds, and `id` pairs an invocation with its completion. A completion's `value` is the output for `ok` and the input otherwise. For `list-append`, `value` holds the micro-ops as `[f, key, value]` triples, the same layout as Elle's list-append micro-ops (seedfall's keys and values are strings). Over MCP, the failure view names the files as `history_file` and `timeline_file`.

Re-check a stored history, or check it against a different model, without running anything:

```sh
seedfall check -history .seedfall/seed-1.history.jsonl -model queue
```

It prints the verdict and every anomaly, writes the timeline next to the history file (or to `-timeline`) on a linearizability violation, and exits 1 when the history fails. The MCP tool is `seedfall_check`.

### Your own Porcupine model

For a data type none of the models cover, read a history file in Go and check it with your own [Porcupine](https://github.com/anishathalye/porcupine) model:

```go
f, _ := os.Open(".seedfall/seed-1.history.jsonl")
ops, err := engine.ReadHistory(f)
ok := porcupine.CheckOperations(myModel, engine.PorcupineOperations(ops))
```

`PorcupineOperations` drops failed operations and gives unknown and pending ones a return time after the end of the history. Each operation's `Input` and `Output` are its `engine.HistoryOp`, with the raw JSON `Value` and `Output` and the `Status`; your `Step` should accept any output when `Status` is not `ok`.

## Determinism check

```sh
seedfall run -seeds 1-200 -check
```

Every seed runs twice, and the sweep fails if the two runs diverge. Run it in CI to make sure nothing in your program escapes the simulator.

The comparison does not wait for a difference to reach the trace. Every run keeps a running hash over its host calls: clock reads, `random_get` lengths, sleeps and `poll_oneoff`, file opens, stats, reads, writes, truncates, syncs, renames, links, symlinks and directory changes, `mmap`, `msync` and `munmap` calls, network listens, dials, accepts, reads, writes and closes, and the `sim` property, event, history, `Buggify`, `SetupComplete`, `QuietFor` and `Budget` calls, each with its node instance, arguments and virtual time. The hash is saved every 4,096 calls. When the two runs differ, seedfall finds the first window of 4,096 calls where they differ, runs the seed twice more recording that window, and reports the first call that differs, in the form `host call N: <call in one run> vs <call in the other>, after <last common call>; host calls <window> (...)`. Each call reads as instance, call, target, argument and virtual time, for example `server#1 random_get(8) at 1.204s` or `server#1 fd_write data/log(37) at 1.204s`. Every `-check` failure is a `nondeterminism` failure.

If the extra runs do not reproduce the difference, the report names the window instead. If the host calls agree but the traces do not, it falls back to the first differing trace line.

The final hash is printed at the end of `seedfall replay` (`determinism hash 4c9ab008f72df649 over 9126 host calls`) and is the `determinism_hash` field of every `-json` seed line and of `seedfall_replay`. The hash covers only simulated values, so two machines that build the same guest binary should get the same hash for the same seed; comparing the field from CI runs on different machines checks that. A different Go toolchain or source tree produces a different binary and may change the hash.


<!-- docs/reports.md -->

# Triage reports

```sh
seedfall run -c seedfall.json -seeds 1-500 -report .seedfall/report.html
```

With `-report`, a sweep keeps going after the first failure, groups every failing seed into findings, and writes an HTML report plus a JSON version next to it (`report.json`). The terminal prints a summary:

```
16 of 60 seeds failed, 1 findings, in 4.867s
  new       assert · client                             16 seeds  e.g. seed 1  bug
report: .seedfall/report.html
```

## Findings

Failures are grouped by what failed, not by message text: the failure class (`property`, `assert`, `crash`, `exit`, `watchdog`, `deadlock`, `liveness`, `linearizability`, `isolation`, `nondeterminism`), the node, and, for properties, the property name. Use `sim.Always` with a constant message to get one finding per invariant.

For each finding the report shows:
- how many seeds failed and the rate, with findings under 1% marked rare;
- up to ten example seeds;
- ready-to-run `replay` and `shrink` commands;
- the faults before the failure and the trace of the lowest failing seed. seedfall re-runs that seed to get them, which works because replays are exact;
- that seed's [timeline](timeline.md), embedded from its artifact folder, with a link to open it on its own.

## Classification

Every finding, and the failure `seedfall run` stops at, gets a class that says whether it is worth blocking on:

| Class | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `bug` | Replaying the seed fails again with the same trace. A real, reproducible failure of the system under test |
| `nondeterministic` | The replay diverges from the original run: something in the harness or the system leaks host nondeterminism. The first diverging trace line is shown |
| `timeout` | The real-time watchdog fired. This depends on host speed and load, not only on the seed. With `preempt.loops` a busy loop fails on `liveness` instead |

```
FAIL seed 1 at t=2.892s ...
class: bug
```

Classification replays only the failure that `run` reports and one representative seed per finding, so it adds one run per finding, never one per seed. It appears in the terminal summary, in the HTML report, as `classification` in `report.json`, and in the MCP `seedfall_run` and `seedfall_replay` results, so CI and agents can block on `bug` and quarantine the rest.

## History: new, ongoing, resolved, regressed

Every report appends a line to `.seedfall/history.jsonl`, keyed by config path. Findings are classified against that history:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `new` | Never seen before for this config |
| `ongoing` | Seen in earlier runs and still failing |
| `not seen` | Absent from this run, but not enough clean seeds yet to be sure it is fixed |
| `resolved` | Absent for enough consecutive clean seeds to be 95% confident it is fixed |
| `regressed` | Failing again after it was resolved |

"Enough" depends on how often the finding used to fail. A finding that failed in a fraction *p* of seeds needs *n ≥ ln(0.05) / ln(1 − p)* clean seeds, counted across runs since it was last seen. A bug that failed 1 seed in 4 is resolved after 11 clean seeds; one that failed 1 seed in 100 needs 299.

```
  new       assert · client          16 seeds  e.g. seed 1
  ongoing   assert · client          15 seeds  e.g. seed 61
  not seen  assert · client          not seen in 5 seeds, but 11 are needed to be 95% sure it is fixed
  resolved  assert · client          not seen in 20 seeds since it failed 15 of 60
  regressed assert · client           6 seeds  e.g. seed 1
```

Keep `.seedfall/history.jsonl` between CI runs (cache or commit it) to get this classification on every pull request. The [GitHub Action](ci.md#history-between-runs) caches it for you.

## Reading findings back

`seedfall findings` reads the last report and the run history without running anything:

```sh
seedfall findings                          # .seedfall/report.html
seedfall findings -status new,regressed    # only what needs attention
seedfall findings -report ci/report.json -json
```

```
.seedfall/report.html: 1 of 6 seeds failed (seeds 1-6 of seedfall.always.json), 3 runs in history
  new       assert · client                              1 seeds  16.67%  e.g. seed 1
            client#1: acknowledged write lost: k96=v96, server now answers "NONE"
            replay: seedfall replay -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1
```

It lists each finding with its status, failing seeds, rate, example seed, reason and replay command, then the earlier findings this run did not see (`resolved` or `not seen`) and the properties that were never reached or never true. `-status` takes a comma-separated list of the statuses above and applies to both lists, `-history` points at a history file other than the one the report names, and `-json` prints the same object the `seedfall_findings` MCP tool returns, with every finding's example failure, trace tail, shrink command and artifacts folder, and every run of that config in the history.

## Properties and fault profile

The report also lists every property with how many seeds reached it and how many saw it true, flagging properties that were never reached or never true, and the fault profile the sweep ran with. Its header names the seedfall version, the Go version and, when the config is in a git repository, the commit it was run at. Schedules pinned with `seedfall pin` are replayed before the sweep and listed in a **Regressions** section ([pinned regressions](verify.md#pinned-regressions)); a regression that fails again fails the run.

## Exploration and throughput

A report from `seedfall run -until-novelty` or `seedfall explore -report` has an **Exploration** section: one row per batch or round with the runs so far, the new signals and functions it added, and the corpus size, so you can see where coverage flattened out, plus why it stopped. Every report's header and JSON (`seeds_per_second`, `virtual_seconds_per_wall_second`) also state throughput. A finding that needs a schedule to reproduce, as `seedfall explore` findings do, carries `schedule_file` in its example and its replay and shrink commands use it; `seedfall verify -report` replays that schedule instead of the bare seed ([explore.md](explore.md)).

## Utilization

A report from `seedfall run` has a **Utilization** section (`utilization` in `report.json`, in the `-json` summary and in the `seedfall_run` result) that answers whether to keep sweeping:

- `batches` splits the seeds that ran into up to ten ranges of nearly equal size, with how many new property outcomes each added. An outcome is a property being reached, being true or being false, and it counts toward the lowest seed that showed it, so the table is the same whatever order parallel runs finished in.
- `speedup_min`, `speedup_median` and `speedup_max` are virtual seconds per real second for one seed, including time spent waiting for a CPU under `-j`.
- `advice` is one sentence, also printed as `utilization:` at the end of the run, saying whether the last batches still added outcomes: more seeds are likely to help if the last batch did, may help if a new outcome came in the later half, and are unlikely to if the later half was quiet. Under ten seeds it says there are too few to compare. It is a heuristic over property outcomes only: it cannot see a bug no property or invariant catches, so read `No new property outcome` as "this config has stopped widening coverage", not as "no bugs remain".

`seedfall explore` reports have the Exploration section instead, because its runs are branches of earlier runs rather than a seed range.

On a terminal, `seedfall run` also shows a progress line on stderr, updated every second and erased when the sweep ends: seeds done, seeds per second, failures, estimated time left and virtual speedup. With `-until-novelty` the estimate is an upper bound, since the sweep can stop early. It is off with `-json`, with `-v`, and when stderr is not a terminal, so piped output and CI logs stay clean.

## Failure artifacts

Every failure seedfall reports gets a folder you can attach to an issue or upload from CI:

```
.seedfall/failures/seedfall.always-seed-1/
  report.json            what failed, classification, seedfall and Go versions, config hash, commit, replay command
  trace.txt              the full trace
  faults.json            the run's fault schedule, replayable with seedfall replay -faults
  history.jsonl          the recorded operations, when the workload records any
  linearizability.html   the timeline, on a linearizability violation
  timeline.html          a space-time diagram of nodes, messages, faults and operations with a trace explorer
  timeline.mmd           the same run as a Mermaid sequence diagram
  disk/<node>/           each node's durable disk image at the failure, as inspect -out exports it
```

`timeline.html` and `timeline.mmd` are described in [timelines and logs](timeline.md). The HTML triage report embeds each finding's `timeline.html` under the finding, linked relative to the report, so keep the report and `.seedfall/failures/` together when you move or upload them.

seedfall writes it by replaying the failing seed once more and capturing the disks at the failure, so it costs one run per reported failure, not one per seed. `seedfall run` writes it for the failure it stops at, `run -report` for the example seed of each finding (the report links it), `replay` for a failing replay, `shrink` for the minimal schedule, and a failing [pinned regression](verify.md#pinned-regressions) for itself. The folder is named after the config and the seed, `<config>-seed-N`, so two configs in one directory keep separate folders. `<config>` is the file name without `.json`, then `.<profile>` for a profile and `.set-<hash>` for `-set` overrides, a short hash of the overrides in order, as in `seedfall.fixed.set-1a2b3c4d-seed-2`. A run from the seed alone goes to `<config>-seed-N`; a replay from a schedule file to `<config>-seed-N-schedule`, a shrunk schedule to `<config>-seed-N-shrunk` and a pinned one to `<config>-seed-N-pinned`, so they do not overwrite each other. A new failure of the same seed replaces the folder. `run -json` writes artifacts only for failing regressions, not for every failing seed.

`report.json` has `reproduced`, which is false when the replay did not fail the same way as the reported run, `classification` ([above](#classification)), `seedfall_version` (from the binary's build information), `config_sha256` (of the resolved config after `extends`, the profile and `-set`, plus the bytes of every file seeded onto a node's disk), `commit` (`git rev-parse HEAD` in the config's directory, so uncommitted changes are not reflected) and `replay`, a command that replays `faults.json` exactly:

```sh
seedfall replay -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1 -faults .seedfall/failures/seedfall.always-seed-1/faults.json
```

Over MCP, failures from `seedfall_run`, `seedfall_replay` and `seedfall_shrink` carry the folder as `artifacts_dir`.

## Notifications and issues

Two commands turn a report into alerts and issues, so a nightly sweep needs no glue code:

```sh
seedfall report notify -report .seedfall/report.html -webhook "$SEEDFALL_WEBHOOK" -link "$CI_RUN_URL"
seedfall report issue  -report .seedfall/report.html -repo owner/name
```

`report notify` posts one message with the report's `new` and `regressed` findings, each with its failing seeds, rate, example seed, reason and replay command, to an incoming webhook. The body is `{"text": ..., "content": ...}`, the fields Slack and Discord incoming webhooks read, and the message is cut to Discord's 2000-character limit with a count of the findings left out. `-webhook` defaults to `$SEEDFALL_WEBHOOK`, and errors never print the URL, which holds the webhook's secret. Each finding sent is recorded in `.seedfall/history.jsonl` against the report it came from, so posting the same report twice sends nothing the second time; an `ongoing` finding is never sent. Because new and regressed come from that history, keep the file between CI runs (see [above](#history-new-ongoing-resolved-regressed)), or every run's findings are new and every run notifies. `-dry-run` prints the message instead.

`report issue` files one GitHub issue per finding with the [`gh` CLI](https://cli.github.com), titled `seedfall finding: <key>`, for example `seedfall finding: assert · client`. The body has the counts, status and class, the reason, the replay and shrink commands, the example seeds, the faults before the failure, the trace tail, the artifacts folder, and the seedfall version, commit and Go version. Before filing, it reads the titles of the repository's 1000 most recent open issues and skips a finding whose title is among them, so a finding has one open issue whether or not the history is saved, and gets a new one if it comes back after its issue was closed. `gh` needs to be logged in, or `GH_TOKEN` set, with permission to write issues. `-dry-run` prints each issue without calling `gh`.

The HTML report has a **Copy issue markdown** button on every finding with the same body, and the text itself under it, for filing by hand in any tracker.

## GitHub

Two more commands read a report for GitHub, and the [GitHub Action](ci.md#github-actions) runs both:

```sh
seedfall report github  -report .seedfall/report.html
seedfall report comment -report .seedfall/report.html -repo owner/name -pr 12 -marker storage -link "$RUN_URL"
```

`report github` prints one `::error` workflow command per problem, most urgent first: pinned regressions that fail again, regressed, new and ongoing findings, then properties that were never reached or never true. A finding from a [property](properties.md) with a constant message, and an unmet property, carry the `file` and `line` of the call, as a path relative to the working directory. Run it from the repository root. A location outside that directory, such as a dependency in the module cache, is left off. It then appends `failing-seed` and `findings` to `-output`, default `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, or prints them when neither is set. `-md file` also writes the Markdown that `report comment` would post, for a job summary or a later `report comment -body file`.

`report comment` posts the report to a pull request as a [`gh`](https://cli.github.com) comment, or `-body file` posts a Markdown file instead, such as a `verify -md` proof, with `-link` added at the end. It lists new, regressed, resolved and ongoing findings with replay commands, failing pinned regressions and unmet properties, with the most urgent sections first. Each comment starts with a hidden marker from `-marker`, and a later call with the same marker edits that comment instead of adding one, so give each job in a matrix its own. Failure text sits inside code spans so it cannot mention anyone or inject Markdown, and a comment too long for GitHub is cut with a note. `-dry-run` prints the comment.


<!-- docs/testing.md -->

# Testing seedfall itself

seedfall is only useful if its own model of crashes, faults and replay is right, so that model has its own tests. This page lists what they check and how to run them.

## What the tests check

| Area | Test file | What it proves |
|---|---|---|
| Disk durability | `engine/memfs_test.go` | Synced writes survive a crash, unsynced writes and never-synced files do not, `O_SYNC` makes every write durable, an unsynced truncate is undone |
| Torn writes | `engine/memfs_test.go` | A torn crash keeps an in-order prefix of the pending writes, the last one possibly cut mid-way, and records the tear |
| Out-of-order writeback | `engine/memfs_test.go` | Writes split at 4 KiB page boundaries, pages persist independently (a later page can survive without an earlier one), and writes to one page persist in order |
| fsync `EIO` | `engine/memfs_test.go` | A failed fsync drops the pending writes while they stay readable, and a retried fsync does not bring them back |
| Disk faults | `engine/diskfaults_test.go` | `disk_bytes` cuts a write short and then refuses it, flagged so the guest gets `ENOSPC`, while overwrites still fit; a failed write writes nothing but counts as a disk operation; a corrupted read flips the returned buffer and never the stored data; a lost write keeps the old page on disk (zeros for a new page) and a misdirected write puts the page at another offset, while the page cache keeps the new content, and rewriting the page later writes it in full; crash corruption flips exactly one bit inside the bytes that were being written; bit rot flips one stored bit; `fsync_corrupts` flips only the durable copy; a misdirected write is chosen from the seed and operation number and replays from its recorded fault |
| File system calls | `engine/memfs_test.go` | `OpenFile` flags, `Mkdir`, `Rename`, `Unlink`, `Rmdir` and `Readdir` return the POSIX errors and results |
| `strict_dirs` | `engine/namespace_test.go` | New entries need the parent directory fsynced to survive, a rename reverts without a directory fsync, and a torn crash recovers an in-order prefix of directory operations |
| Fault schedules | `engine/faults_test.go` | Schedules are identical for the same seed and differ across seeds, stay inside the time horizon and in order, never crash the workload unless asked, and never plan runtime-only faults; swarm rates stay in `[0, 2 x rate)`, swarm mixes are deterministic per seed, and partition sides are never empty |
| Network faults | `engine/netfaults_test.go` | Every partition topology has the promised shape (a ring gives each node a distinct majority), the default `half` topology keeps the old schedule, a one-way clog holds one direction only, `jam` accepts late without an error, `slow` adds its delay, per-link latency overrides apply one way, a reset breaks both ends, including connections waiting to be accepted, while the listener stays open, a slow node stretches its latency and timers, `sim.QuietFor` heals clogs, swizzles clog one node at a time and unclog in random order, and bad settings, including network faults on a single-node config, are rejected |
| Scheduler | `engine/sched_test.go` | The next step is the earliest one; at the same time a planned fault goes before a restart and a restart before a resume; every resume due at that time is a candidate for the seeded scheduler; a paused node waits for its pause to end |
| Shrinking | `engine/shrink_test.go`, `cmd/seedfall/shrink_test.go` | Against a fake runner, `Shrink` keeps the original failure, ignores a different failure, and returns a 1-minimal schedule; delta debugging finds one needed fault among 64 in fewer runs than removing one at a time; downtimes, clock jumps, partition sides and fault times shrink to just what the failure needs, while faults recorded at run time keep their operation; the duration and a `sim.Budget` workload are trimmed, and a workload without `sim.Budget` is left alone; the result and run count are the same for 1, 3 and 8 jobs; a run or time budget stops it with the failure intact; failure matching ignores numbers only. Schedule files round-trip, the older fault arrays still read, and a passing replay gets a note only when a shortened duration ended it before the workload finished |
| Network | `engine/net_test.go` | Messages on one connection arrive in order under random latency, reads wait for arrival, a partition holds messages until it heals, close delivers EOF after data, and a crash resets every connection |
| Linearizability | `engine/history_test.go` | Every model (`kv`, `cas`, `append`, `queue`, `set`, `counter`) accepts and rejects known histories, including unknown, pending and failed operations; operations a model does not have, and inputs or outputs of the wrong type, are rejected; a history survives the JSONL round trip and re-checks the same; a custom Porcupine model checks a history through `PorcupineOperations` |
| Transactional anomalies | `engine/elle_test.go` | The list-append checker finds `G0`, `G1a`, `G1b`, `G1c`, `G-single`, `G2`, internal inconsistency, incompatible orders, duplicate elements and appends, and garbage reads in minimal histories, passes serializable ones and reads of unknown transactions, explains the cycle, and rejects malformed transactions |
| End to end | `engine/guest_test.go` | A small guest in `engine/testdata/guest` runs under crashes, partitions, torn writes, out-of-order writeback, crashes during disk operations and pauses: two runs of a seed give byte-identical traces, `-check` passes, a sweep finds the same failing seeds with 1 or 4 jobs, a failure replays exactly from its saved fault schedule, and a shrunk schedule keeps the failure, replays exactly and is 1-minimal. `sim.Budget` caps the client's writes when a schedule sets `ops`, the trace shows the cap, the run is shorter and replays exactly. Under clogs, swizzles, resets, slow nodes and partition topologies, two runs of a seed and a replay of its fault schedule give byte-identical traces. Under every disk fault the same holds, a full disk and `write_enospc` reach the guest as `syscall.ENOSPC`, and a failure caused by a lost write shrinks to a schedule that keeps the lost write and replays exactly |
| Liveness and workload faults | `engine/liveness_test.go` | Against the guest: with `liveness`, a workload that never finishes fails as `liveness` at `duration + within` and without it only hits the horizon; the recovery phase restarts a node that would stay down and heals a partition, so the workload finishes; a `finally` check starts only after the workload, with no fault after it, and its `sim.Eventually` counts as a property; an `Eventually` that never holds fails as `liveness` with its message; `include_workload` crashes and pauses the client, open operations are reported and stay sound for linearizability, and a replay of the recorded faults is byte-identical; every one of several workloads must finish. Without the guest: `supervise` never restarts a workload that exits with an error, `"faults": false` keeps a node out of every planned fault and every partition, the workload is a fault target only when asked, configs with `workloads[]`, `finally` and `liveness` are validated, and `sim.Eventually` is cataloged |
| Assertions and events | `engine/assertions_test.go`, `sim/sim_test.go` | The catalog finds numeric and grouped assertions with their message at the right argument; Antithesis guidance records keep the smallest margin for `always` and the largest for `sometimes`, and guidance without an assertion creates nothing; `lifecycle.SendEvent` becomes a trace event; margins aggregate across seeds; outside the simulator the numeric and grouped forms fail with JSON details and `sim.Event` does nothing |
| Determinism hash | `engine/hostcalls_test.go` | The host-call hash is stable, checkpointed every 4,096 calls and sensitive to field boundaries, and a divergence report names the first differing call with the call before it, including a run that ends early |
| Mutants | `engine/mutation_test.go` | `rename_not_atomic` loses both names in a crash before the next fsync in loose and strict mode, but not a rename to a new name or one a later fsync closed; `truncate_not_durable` brings back the old tail; `net_drop_after_close` drops only an unread last chunk; `net_dup_chunk` duplicates a seeded share of writes and replays them identically; network mutants skip nodes that take no faults; `monotonic_jump` moves the monotonic clock only when active; `-only` parses and rejects typos. `engine/appmutant_test.go`: source mutants find comparisons, early error returns and `Sync` calls and still parse, the selection is seeded and ordered, and a mutant's overlay merges with the `net_overlay` one |
| Preemption | `engine/preempt_test.go` | Strategy validation; loop counting adds the countdown after every `loop` header while decoding LEB immediates, `br_table` and `0xfc` opcodes, and rejects unsupported opcodes; the loop-counted guest compiles; with `preempt.loops` a call-free loop of three time slices takes at least 30ms of virtual time and without it almost none; `pct` finds a goroutine race, records its change points as `preempt` faults that replay exactly, an empty schedule fires none, shrinking keeps one, every change point fires at its counted call across time-slice parks and sleeps and replays the same, and a `preempt` fault is rejected unless the strategy is `pct`; `calls` preempts deterministically |
| Confidence math | `report/report_test.go` | `SeedsToConfirm` and the detectable failure rate against known values, findings moving through new, ongoing, not seen, resolved and regressed across runs, and the JSON report against a golden file |
| Proof rendering | `verify/verify_test.go` | How many seeds a proof needs, and the text and Markdown proof blocks against golden files |

`scripts/regress.sh` then runs every example against its expected pass or fail result, replays saved fault schedules, and checks that replays are identical.

## Running them

```sh
go test ./...                 # everything, including the wasip1 guest build
go test -short ./...          # skip the tests that build and run a wasip1 guest
go test -race ./...           # what CI runs; needs cgo
go test ./report ./verify -update   # rewrite golden files after an intended change, then review the diff
go run honnef.co/go/tools/cmd/staticcheck@latest ./...
go run golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest ./...
bash scripts/regress.sh       # every example; takes hours
```

govulncheck also reports standard library vulnerabilities, so run it with the latest Go patch release, as CI does with `go-version: stable`.

## CI

| Workflow | When | What |
|---|---|---|
| `ci.yml` | every push to `main` and every pull request | gofmt, `go vet`, staticcheck and govulncheck; `go test -race ./...` on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows; and two example sweeps through the GitHub Action with `-check` |
| `regress.yml` | nightly, or by hand | `bash scripts/regress.sh` |
| `codeql.yml` | every push to `main`, every pull request, weekly | CodeQL analysis of the Go code |

Dependabot opens weekly updates for the root module and the GitHub Actions. The examples are left alone on purpose: each pins the library version its findings were made against.


<!-- docs/timeline.md -->

# Timelines, logs and time-travel debugging

A failing seed replays exactly, so you can look at it as many times and in as many ways as you like. seedfall gives you four views of one run:

| View | Command | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| Timeline | `seedfall replay -html timeline.html`, and `timeline.html` in every [failure artifact](reports.md#failure-artifacts) folder | A space-time diagram: one lane per node, every connection and message as an arrow, fault intervals shaded, recorded operations as bars, properties and events as markers, next to a filterable trace |
| Sequence diagram | `seedfall replay -html timeline.mmd`, and `timeline.mmd` in every artifact folder | The same run as a Mermaid `sequenceDiagram`, for an issue or a pull request |
| Logs | `seedfall logs -seed N -node server -grep re -from 1s -to 2s` | The trace filtered by node, pattern and virtual time, with app output interleaved with engine events and slog JSON parsed into fields |
| Debugger | `seedfall debug -seed N -at 1.7s` | A prompt paused at a moment of the run: node states, the live disk, in-flight messages and active faults, then step, run until a pattern, or branch into a different future |

`seedfall trace grep` finds a pattern and shows the lines of every node around each match, and `seedfall trace diff` compares two traces and shows where they first part ways. Logs, trace search and the debugger are also MCP tools, and the timeline is in every artifact folder the MCP tools name.

## The trace

Every run already traces node starts, crashes, faults and checks, plus every line each node writes to stdout or stderr, stamped with the virtual time it was written:

```
    0.000s  start server#1
    0.000s  server#1| serving 0 keys on :7000
    0.292s  fault partition [client] | rest, heals at 0.627s
    0.757s  fault crash server#1 during disk op 56, restart at 1.121s
```

`server#2` is the second process started on node `server`, after its first crash. With `-net-trace` on `run`, `replay`, `logs` or `debug`, the trace also has every connection, message sent and message read:

```
    1.120s  net client#1 dials server:7000, refused
    1.121s  start server#2
    1.121s  server#2| serving 26 keys on :7000
    1.130s  net client#1 dials server:7000 conn 57, arrives 1.132s
    1.130s  net client#1 -> server#2 conn 57: 12 bytes, arrives 1.132s
    1.132s  net server#2 accepts conn 57 from client#1
    1.132s  net server#2 <- client#1 conn 57: 12 bytes sent at 1.130s
    1.132s  net server#2 -> client#1 conn 57: 3 bytes, arrives 1.137s
```

A message sent while a partition or a clog holds the link says `held by a partition or clog`, and a duplicate from the `net_dup_chunk` mutant says `a duplicate`. UDP datagrams appear as `udp <socket>` lines, and one that never arrived says `lost` and why: a partition or clog, no socket bound to the address, a socket connected to another address, or a `udp_drop` fault. `-net-trace` adds lines to the trace only: it does not change the schedule, the determinism hash or the result, so a seed fails the same way with and without it. A failure replayed with `-net-trace` writes those lines into its artifact `trace.txt` as well.

## Timeline

```sh
seedfall replay -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1 -html timeline.html
```

`timeline.html` is one self-contained file with no network fetches, so it opens from a CI artifact or an email attachment. Every failure seedfall reports also gets one in its artifact folder, next to `trace.txt`, and the [triage report](reports.md) embeds it under each finding.

The diagram has one column per node with virtual time flowing down:

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Green line | A process of the node is alive, from its start to its crash or exit, labelled with its instance (`server#2`) |
| Arrow | A connection (`connect`, purple) or a message (data, blue; EOF, yellow; reset, red) from the sender at the time it was sent to the receiver at the time it was first read. A dashed arrow was never read: it was dropped by a crash, a reset or the end of the run. Hover for the connection, size and times |
| Shaded box | A fault interval over the nodes it hits: a crash until the restart, a pause, a slowdown, a clog, a clock jump, or a partition over every lane |
| Bar | An operation recorded with `sim.Put`, `sim.Get`, `sim.Invoke` or `sim.Txn`, from invocation to completion, green when ok, red when failed, yellow when unknown. Concurrent operations of one node sit side by side |
| Dot | A `sim.Event`, the first time a `Sometimes` or `Reachable` property is true, or the first time an `Always` or `Eventually` property is checked |
| Red line | The failure, with its reason |

Rows are the distinct moments something happened, labelled with their virtual time, so a run with long idle stretches stays compact; the spacing is not proportional to time.

The trace explorer beside it lists every trace line. Above both are a node toggle per node (plus `engine` for lines that belong to no node), toggles for lives, messages, operations, faults and marks, a `from` and `to` window in Go duration syntax (`1.5s`, `200ms`), and a `grep` box that filters trace lines with a JavaScript regular expression. Clicking a trace line scrolls the diagram to its moment.

## Sequence diagram

```sh
seedfall replay -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1 -html timeline.mmd
```

A path ending in `.mmd` writes Mermaid instead of HTML:

```
sequenceDiagram
  participant p0 as server
  participant p1 as client
  Note over p0: 0.000s start server#35;1
  p1->>p0: 0.000s conn 2 connect, read 0.003s
  p1->>p0: 0.000s conn 2 10 bytes, read 0.003s
  p0->>p1: 0.003s conn 2 3 bytes, read 0.007s
  p1-->>p0: 0.007s conn 2 eof, read 0.009s
```

It has the node lives, messages (`->>` read, `-->>` an EOF or reset, `-x` never read or a lost datagram), faults, events, properties and the failure, in time order. Recorded operations are only in the HTML timeline. GitHub renders a ` ```mermaid ` block in issues and pull requests; a run with thousands of messages makes a diagram too tall to read there, so cut it to the moments around the failure first.

## Logs

```sh
seedfall logs -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1 -node server
```

```
    0.000s  start server#1
    0.000s  server#1| serving 0 keys on :7000
    0.757s  fault crash server#1 during disk op 56, restart at 1.121s
    1.121s  start server#2
    1.121s  server#2| serving 26 keys on :7000
    1.705s  fault crash server#2, restart at 1.943s
    1.943s  start server#3
    1.943s  server#3| serving 60 keys on :7000
8 of 12 trace lines; seed 1: FAIL client#1: acknowledged write lost: k96=v96, server now answers "NONE"
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-seed`, `-faults` | The run to replay, as for `replay` |
| `-node` | Only lines that belong to these nodes, comma separated: their output, starts, crashes, faults aimed at them and, with `-net-trace`, the messages they send and read. Lines about the whole run, such as a partition or the end of the workload, belong to no node and are left out |
| `-grep` | Only lines matching this Go regular expression |
| `-from`, `-to` | Only lines in this virtual time window, for example `-from 1.5s -to 2s` |
| `-json` | One JSON object per line instead of text |
| `-net-trace` | Add connections and messages to the trace first |

The summary line goes to stderr, so `seedfall logs ... > server.log` keeps only the trace. With `-json`, each line has `at`, `at_ns`, `node`, `instance`, the full trace `line` and, for a node's own output, `output`. When that output is a JSON object, such as a line from `slog.NewJSONHandler`, it is parsed into `fields`:

```json
{"at":"100.000013ms","at_ns":100000013,"node":"app","instance":"app#1","line":"    0.100s  app#1   | {\"time\":\"2026-01-01T00:00:00.100000012Z\",\"level\":\"INFO\",\"msg\":\"put\",\"key\":1}","output":"{\"time\":\"2026-01-01T00:00:00.100000012Z\",\"level\":\"INFO\",\"msg\":\"put\",\"key\":1}","fields":{"key":1,"level":"INFO","msg":"put","time":"2026-01-01T00:00:00.100000012Z"}}
```

slog's `time` field is the guest's wall clock, which seedfall simulates from 2026-01-01 (and skews or jumps under clock faults); `at` is the virtual time the line was written. Other slog handlers' text output comes through as `output` without `fields`.

## Searching the trace

`logs -grep` keeps only the matching lines. To see what happened around each match, across every node, use `seedfall trace grep`:

```sh
seedfall trace grep -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1 -e crash -context 1
```

```
     4     0.292s  fault partition [client] | rest, heals at 0.627s
>    5     0.757s  fault crash server#1 during disk op 56, restart at 1.121s
     6     1.121s  start server#2
     7     1.121s  server#2| serving 26 keys on :7000
>    8     1.705s  fault crash server#2, restart at 1.943s
     9     1.943s  start server#3
2 matches of 12 trace lines, 2 shown; seed 1: FAIL client#1: acknowledged write lost: k96=v96, server now answers "NONE"
```

Matches are marked `>`, each line carries its number in the run's trace (the same as the artifact's `trace.txt` for that run) and its virtual time, windows that touch or overlap are merged, and separate windows are divided by `--`. `-e` is a Go regular expression. `-node`, `-from` and `-to` narrow which lines can match, as for `logs`, while the context lines come from every node. `-context` sets the lines before and after each match (3 by default), `-limit` the most matches shown (200), `-net-trace` adds connections and messages first, and `-json` prints the windows as one JSON object with the same line fields as `logs -json` plus `n` and `match`.

## Debugger

```sh
seedfall debug -c seedfall.always.json -seed 1 -at 1.7s
```

`debug` replays the seed and stops before the first scheduler step after `-at` (the same moment `seedfall inspect -at` snapshots), then reads commands:

```
paused at t=1.696068226s before scheduler step 379
  server       server#2     blocked
  client       client#1     runnable at 1.702612857s
(seedfall 1.696068226s) until fault crash
    1.705s  fault crash server#2, restart at 1.943s
paused at t=1.705199634s before scheduler step 382
  server                    down until 1.942588993s
  client       client#1     runnable at 1.706780887s
(seedfall 1.705199634s) net
  conn 125  server#2 -> client#1: eof, sent at 1.705199634s, arrives at 1.706780887s
(seedfall 1.705199634s) stat server data/kv.log
data/kv.log on server: 527 bytes, 527 durable, directory entry durable: true
```

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `where` | Virtual time, the next scheduler step, and each node's state: `runnable` at a time, `blocked` with no timer or message due, `paused` or `down` until a time, `exited` |
| `log [n]` | The last `n` trace lines, 20 by default |
| `grep <regex>` | Every trace line so far that matches |
| `ls [node]` | Every node's disk, or one node's, in the [inspect](inspect.md) format: live and durable sizes, what a crash loses, torn writes and damage |
| `stat <node> <path>` | One file's size, durable size, the byte ranges a crash loses and its damage |
| `cat <node> <path>` | The file's live content, what the node reads now, as text or a hex dump (`inspect -cat` shows the durable content instead) |
| `net` | Every message still in flight with its sender, receiver, size, send and arrival time, and connections not yet accepted |
| `faults` | Active faults and the next scheduled one |
| `step [n]` | Run `n` scheduler steps, 1 by default |
| `until <regex>` | Run until a new trace line matches, then stop right after it |
| `to <duration>` | Run until the next step is after this virtual time |
| `branch [key]` | Re-randomize everything after now with this key, 1 by default: the scheduler, network and disk randomness, guest randomness and the faults still to come, as [`seedfall cause`](cause.md) does. One branch per session |
| `quit` | End the session |

Commands after `step`, `until` and `to` print the trace lines that ran and the new position. Nothing runs between commands, and the run is the same one `replay` produces, so the state you see is the state the failing run had. Once the run ends, inspection commands still work on the final state.

The debugger stops between scheduler steps, not inside a node's code: it shows what a crash at that moment would see, not a goroutine's stack. For source-level stepping, rebuild the node natively and reproduce with the faults from `faults.json`.

## Comparing traces

```sh
seedfall trace diff .seedfall/failures/seedfall.always-seed-1 after-fix.txt
```

Each side is a trace file (an artifact's `trace.txt`, or `seedfall logs` output saved to a file) or an artifact folder, which means its `trace.txt`. It prints the line where the traces first differ with the matching lines before it (`-context 3`), and exits 1, or says they are identical and exits 0. `-context` goes before the two paths. Here `a.txt` is the trace of seed 1 and `b.txt` the trace of the same seed under its shrunk schedule, both saved with `seedfall logs`:

```
$ seedfall trace diff a.txt b.txt
the traces diverge at line 4 (a.txt has 12 lines, b.txt has 12)

      0.000s  start server#1
      0.000s  start client#1
      0.000s  server#1| serving 0 keys on :7000
-     0.292s  fault partition [client] | rest, heals at 0.627s
+     0.000s  client#1: sim.Budget capped at 63 of 200 operations
```

Use it after shrinking to see where the shrunk schedule leaves the original run, after a fix to see the first moment the run behaves differently, or on two machines to find where a nondeterministic run splits (`run -check` does that for you within one machine).

## Over MCP

`seedfall_logs` takes `config`, `seed` and optionally `faults`, `node`, `grep`, `from`, `to`, `net_trace` and `limit` (200 by default), and returns the matching lines with the same fields as `logs -json`, how many matched and how many the trace has. `seedfall_trace_search` takes `config`, `seed`, `pattern` and optionally `faults`, `context`, `node`, `from`, `to`, `net_trace` and `limit`, and returns the same windows as `trace grep -json`. `seedfall_debug` takes `config`, `seed`, optionally `faults`, `at`, `net_trace` and a `commands` list run in order (`["until fault crash", "net", "ls server"]`), and returns each command's output and the final state. Failures from `seedfall_run`, `seedfall_replay` and `seedfall_shrink` name the artifact folder, which holds `timeline.html` and `timeline.mmd`. See [agents.md](agents.md#tools).


<!-- docs/verify.md -->

# Proving a fix with `seedfall verify`

`seedfall verify` is the definition of done for a change that fixes a seedfall failure, whether a person or an AI agent wrote it. It answers one question with evidence: is the failure gone, and how sure are we?

```sh
seedfall verify -c seedfall.fixed.json -seed 1 -faults .seedfall/seed-1.faults.json -mutate -md proof.md
```

```
verify seedfall.fixed.json (seedfall v1.2.3)
  pass  replay seed 1 with .seedfall/seed-1.faults.json  passes, twice, with identical host calls and traces
  pass  fresh sweep, seeds 2-300                         299 of 299 pass: 95% confidence that a failure with rate >= 0.997% would have shown up
  pass  determinism, seeds 2-11                          every seed ran twice with identical host calls and traces
  pass  mutant fsync_noop                                killed by seed 2
  pass  mutant dirsync_noop                              not exercised
  pass  mutant osync_ignored                             not exercised
  pass  mutant fsync_corrupts                            killed by seed 2
PASS
```

Against the unfixed config the same command stops at the first check and exits 1:

```
verify seedfall.always.json (seedfall v1.2.3)
  FAIL  replay seed 1 with .seedfall/seed-1.faults.json  seed 1 FAILS [bug]: client#1: acknowledged write lost: k60=v60, server now answers "NONE"
  skip  fresh sweep                                      an earlier check failed
  skip  determinism                                      an earlier check failed
FAIL
```

## What it checks

In order, stopping at the first stage that fails:

1. **Replay.** Every failing schedule you name is replayed and must pass now. Each replay runs twice and must produce identical host calls and traces, so a pass cannot be luck.
2. **Fresh sweep.** New seeds, starting after the highest seed already known, must all pass. By default verify runs as many as needed for 95% confidence that a failure with the historical rate would have shown up: *n = ⌈ln(0.05) / ln(1 − p)⌉*, the same rule the [triage report](reports.md) uses to call a finding resolved. A finding that failed 27.5% of seeds needs 10 clean seeds; when no rate is known, verify assumes a rare failure (1%) and runs 299. `-seeds` overrides the range.
3. **Determinism.** The first `-check` fresh seeds (default 10) run twice and must produce identical host calls and traces, as with `run -check`.
4. **Mutants** (with `-mutate`). The [mutants](mutate.md) run over the fresh seeds, and every exercised mutant must still be killed. This catches a "fix" that passes by weakening the checks. With `-app-mutants N`, N [source mutants](mutate.md#source-mutants) of the node packages run too, each as a row naming its line and change, and each one that builds must be killed. If the node packages cannot be read to list the source mutants, a `source mutants` row fails the proof.

Any failure is printed with its [classification](reports.md#classification), so a determinism leak is not mistaken for the bug coming back.

## What to verify

| Flags | Replays |
|---|---|
| `-seed N` | seed N with its generated faults |
| `-seed N -faults file.json` | seed N under a saved schedule, for example one written by `seedfall shrink`. Its faults and `ops` cap are kept, but it runs for the config's full `duration`: a shrunk schedule's shorter duration could end the run before the workload checks anything |
| `-report .seedfall/report.html` | every example seed of every finding in a [triage report](reports.md), plus any schedule `shrink` saved for those seeds in `.seedfall/`. The findings' failure rates set the sweep size |

`-seed` and `-report` can be combined. Point `-c` at the config of the code you changed; the report can come from an earlier run of the same or another config.

Every schedule [pinned](#pinned-regressions) for the config is replayed too, as a `replay pinned seed N with seedfall-regressions/...` row, without being named.

```
$ seedfall verify -c seedfall.fixed.json -report .seedfall/report.html
verify seedfall.fixed.json (seedfall v1.2.3)
  pass  replay assert · client seed 1                                     passes, twice, with identical host calls and traces
  pass  replay assert · client seed 1 with .seedfall/seed-1.faults.json   passes, twice, with identical host calls and traces
  pass  replay assert · client seed 12                                    passes, twice, with identical host calls and traces
  ...
  pass  fresh sweep, seeds 41-50                                          10 of 10 pass: 95% confidence that a failure with rate >= 25.9% would have shown up (historical rate 27.5%)
  pass  determinism, seeds 41-50                                          every seed ran twice with identical host calls and traces
PASS
```

## Pinned regressions

A fixed bug should stay fixed. `seedfall pin` copies a failing seed's schedule into `seedfall-regressions/`, next to the config, a directory you commit:

```sh
seedfall pin -c seedfall.fixed.json -seed 1 -faults torntail.faults.json
```

```
pinned seed 1 (2 faults, from torntail.faults.json) to seedfall-regressions/seedfall.fixed-seed-1.json
it passes now; seedfall run, verify and seedfalltest replay it first and fail if it fails again
```

Without `-faults`, pin takes the schedule `seedfall shrink` saved in `.seedfall/seed-N.faults.json`, or else the seed's own faults, recorded fault by fault so the pinned faults stay the same if the fault rates change later. The file is a schedule in the usual format with a `pinned` block: the config it belongs to, the finding and reason if it fails now, where it came from, the seedfall version and the date. It is named `<config>-seed-N.json`, so two configs in one directory can pin the same seed; `<config>` carries the profile and a hash of any `-set` overrides, as artifact folders do ([config](config.md#profiles)). Pinning a schedule that still fails is allowed, and the commands below fail until the bug is fixed, the way a test written before its fix does.

A pinned schedule keeps its faults and `ops` cap but runs for the config's full `duration`, as `-faults` does in verify, so a shrunk schedule's short duration cannot end the run before the workload checks anything. The same file replays exactly with `seedfall replay -c C -seed N -faults seedfall-regressions/<file>`.

Pinned schedules are replayed, in parallel, before anything else by:

| Where | What happens |
|---|---|
| `seedfall run` | A `regressions` table comes first. One that fails again stops the run before the sweep with its failure, classification, [artifacts](reports.md#failure-artifacts) and replay command, and exit code 1 |
| `seedfall run -report` | The sweep still runs, the report gets a **Regressions** section, and a failing regression fails the run |
| `seedfall run -json` | One `{"type": "regression", ...}` line per regression before the seed lines, with `source`, `seed`, `passed`, and on a failure `failure`, `reason`, `classification` and `artifacts`; the summary counts `regressions_failed` |
| `seedfall verify` | A `replay pinned` row each, which must pass twice |
| `seedfalltest.Sweep` and `seedfalltest.Pinned` | The test fails with the regression's failure ([ci.md](ci.md#go-test)) |
| `seedfall hook` and `seedfall_run` over MCP | The regression's failure is reported before any sweep |

A file in `seedfall-regressions/` without a `pinned.config`, for example a schedule copied in by hand, is replayed for every config in that directory. `run -pinned=false` skips them; over MCP, `skip_pinned`.

`run -seeds-file known-bad.txt` replays a list of seeds, each with its own faults, the same way before the sweep. The file holds seeds separated by spaces or lines, with `#` comments.

## The proof block

`-md proof.md` writes the result as Markdown for the pull request description:

```markdown
### seedfall verify: PASS

Config `seedfall.fixed.json`, seedfall `v1.2.3`, reproduce with `seedfall verify -c seedfall.fixed.json -seed 1 -faults .seedfall/seed-1.faults.json -mutate`

| | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| pass | replay seed 1 with .seedfall/seed-1.faults.json | passes, twice, with identical host calls and traces |
| pass | fresh sweep, seeds 2-300 | 299 of 299 pass: 95% confidence that a failure with rate >= 0.997% would have shown up |
| pass | determinism, seeds 2-11 | every seed ran twice with identical host calls and traces |
| pass | mutant fsync_noop | killed by seed 2 |
| pass | mutant dirsync_noop | not exercised |
| pass | mutant osync_ignored | not exercised |
| pass | mutant fsync_corrupts | killed by seed 2 |
```

## Flags

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `-c` | `seedfall.json` | Config of the code under test |
| `-seed` | | Failing seed to replay |
| `-faults` | | Fault schedule for `-seed` |
| `-report` | | Triage report (`.html` or `.json`) whose findings to replay |
| `-seeds` | enough for 95% confidence | Fresh seed range to sweep |
| `-check` | `10` | Fresh seeds to run twice for the determinism check |
| `-mutate` | off | Also require every exercised mutant to be killed |
| `-app-mutants` | `0` | Also rebuild the nodes with this many [source mutants](mutate.md#source-mutants), picked from the first fresh seed, and require every one that builds to be killed |
| `-md` | | Write the Markdown proof block to this file |
| `-j` | all CPUs | Parallel runs |

The exit status is 0 only when every check passes.

## From an agent

The MCP tool `seedfall_verify` takes the same inputs (`config`, `seed`, `faults`, `report`, `seeds`, `check_seeds`, `mutate`) and returns each check as structured JSON, the overall `passed` verdict, and the proof block as `markdown`. See [agents.md](agents.md).


<!-- skills/seedfall-fix-and-prove/SKILL.md -->


# Fix a seedfall failure and prove it

The fix is done when `seedfall verify` passes, not when one replay goes green. Below, `C` is the config that failed, `N` the seed, and `S` the schedule from `seedfall shrink`, `.seedfall/seed-N.faults.json`.

## 1. Fix the cause, not the symptom

Change the code that triage identified: fsync before acknowledging, truncate a torn tail during recovery, fsync the directory after a rename, stop acknowledging after a failed fsync. Do not change `C`, the workload's checks or the fault rates to make the failure go away. A fix that weakens the checks fails step 4 anyway.

## 2. Replay until it passes

```sh
seedfall replay -c C -seed N -faults S
seedfall replay -c C -seed N
```

Both must end with `seed N: ok, ... steps`. Seeds and schedules replay exactly, so a pass here is not luck. If it still fails, read the new failure: it may be the same bug further along, or a second bug the first one was hiding.

## 3. Sweep

```sh
seedfall run -c C -seeds 1-200
```

A new failure on another seed is a new finding. Triage it before going on.

## 4. Verify

```sh
seedfall verify -c C -seed N -faults S -mutate -md proof.md
```

If the failures came from a triage report, use `-report .seedfall/report.html` instead of, or as well as, `-seed`. Verify stops at the first stage that fails:

1. **Replay.** Each named schedule passes, twice, with identical host calls and traces.
2. **Fresh sweep.** Enough new seeds for 95% confidence at the failure's historical rate. Without a rate, verify assumes 1% and runs 299 seeds. `-seeds` overrides the range.
3. **Determinism.** `-check` fresh seeds (default 10) run twice with identical host calls and traces.
4. **Mutants** (`-mutate`, `-app-mutants N`). Every exercised mutant is still killed, so the fix did not pass by making the checks blind. `-app-mutants` also rebuilds the nodes with N source mutants.

It prints `PASS` or `FAIL` and exits 0 or 1. Over MCP, `seedfall_verify` with `{"config": "C", "seed": N, "faults": "S", "mutate": true}` returns the same verdict, and its `markdown` field holds the proof block.

## 5. Put the proof in the pull request

Paste `proof.md`, or the MCP `markdown` field, into the pull request description unchanged, under a heading such as `## Crash-safety proof`. It names the config, the replayed schedules, the seed ranges and the confidence, so a reviewer can rerun the exact command it shows.

## 6. Keep it fixed

- Pin the schedule as a permanent regression and commit the file:

  ```sh
  seedfall pin -c C -seed N
  git add seedfall-regressions/
  ```

  Pin takes `S` (or `-faults` another file) and writes `seedfall-regressions/<config>-seed-N.json`. Over MCP, `seedfall_pin` with `{"config": "C", "seed": N}`. It reports whether the schedule passes now; after a real fix it must. From then on `seedfall run`, `seedfall verify`, the Stop hook and `seedfalltest.Sweep` replay it before every sweep and fail if the bug comes back.
- Run the sweep from `go test` with `seedfalltest.Sweep(t, "seedfall.json", "1-100")`, and the pinned schedules alone with `seedfalltest.Pinned(t, "seedfall.json")`, from `github.com/kunalgoesbyken/seedfall/seedfalltest`, or in CI with the `kunalgoesbyken/seedfall` GitHub Action, whose `command: verify` input runs the same proof on a pull request.


<!-- skills/seedfall-properties/SKILL.md -->


# Write properties that catch real durability bugs

A passing sweep proves only what the workload checks. Find the service's promises, check each one, prove that the faults reached the dangerous paths, then break the disk on purpose and confirm the checks notice.

## 1. Find the promises

Read the code, not the README. For each item below, note the file and line:

- **Acknowledgement.** Where does the service answer OK, return 2xx or ack a producer? What must already be fsynced at that point: the data file, the directory entry, the index?
- **Recovery.** What does startup do with a torn last record, a missing file, a leftover temp file or a half-finished compaction?
- **Atomic replace.** For each write-temp-then-rename, is the file fsynced before the rename, and is the parent directory fsynced after it?
- **Deletes and compaction.** Can a crash bring back deleted data, or lose data that had been copied?
- **Replication.** When is a write committed? Can a follower serve stale reads? Can two leaders coexist?

Write each promise as one sentence, for example "every acknowledged write is readable after any number of crashes".

## 2. Turn each promise into a check

The full reference is the MCP resource `seedfall://docs/properties` (docs/properties.md).

| Promise | Check |
|---|---|
| Acknowledged writes survive | The workload records each acknowledged write, then reads it back after the faults: `sim.Assert(got == want, "acknowledged write lost: "+key)` |
| State never goes backwards | In the node: `sim.AlwaysGreaterThanOrEqualTo(len(log), committed, "log never shrinks below the commit index")`. The numeric forms (`AlwaysGreaterThan`, `AlwaysLessThan`, `SometimesGreaterThan`, ... and their `OrEqualTo` variants) put `left` and `right` in the failure and report a margin: the smallest one shows how close an `always` came to failing |
| One of several things holds | `sim.AlwaysSome(map[string]bool{"primary": p >= 0, "backup": b >= 0}, "some replica answers")`; `sim.SometimesAll(...)` for a combination that must happen at least once |
| Something must never happen | `sim.Unreachable("two leaders in the same term", term)` |
| A dangerous path actually ran | `sim.Sometimes(tornTail, "recovery found a torn tail")`, `sim.Reachable("a node restored from a snapshot")` |
| Concurrent clients see a linearizable history | Wrap each call: `op := sim.Put(client, key, value)`, then `op.Ok("")`, `op.Unknown()` on a timeout, or `op.Failed()` when it definitely did not apply. Use `sim.Get` for reads |
| A lock, queue, log, set or counter behaves like one | Set `"checker": {"model": "cas"}` (or `queue`, `append`, `set`, `counter`) in seedfall.json and record each call with `sim.Invoke(client, f, key, value)`, for example `sim.Invoke(c, "cas", "lock", []string{"", me})` then `op.Ok(swapped)`, or `sim.Invoke(c, "dequeue", "q", nil)` then `op.Ok(item)`. The table of operations per model is in docs/properties.md, Other models |
| Transactions are serializable | Set `"checker": {"model": "list-append"}`, record each transaction with `op := sim.Txn(client, sim.Read("x"), sim.Append("y", unique))`, and pass the micro-ops back with each read's `Value` set to the list it returned: `op.Ok(mops)`. Appended values must be unique per key. Failures name the anomaly (`G-single`, `G2`, ...) and the cycle |
| The system recovers | Set `"liveness": {"within": "10s"}` in seedfall.json: after `duration` the faults stop, crashed nodes restart, and a workload that does not finish within 10s fails as `liveness`. Inside a program, `sim.Eventually(func() bool { return served() }, "cluster serves reads again", 10*time.Second)` |
| The end state is right | A `"finally": {"name": "check", "pkg": "./check"}` program runs after the workload with faults stopped; check convergence and exactly-once effects there with `sim.Eventually` and `sim.Always` |
| Client retries are safe | `"include_workload": true` in `faults` crashes and pauses the workload too. Derive request ids from `sim.Node()` and saved progress, so a restarted client resends the same id, then check in `finally` that nothing was applied twice |

Rules:
- Keep messages constant string literals and pass changing values as extra arguments. seedfall catalogs literal messages before the sweep, and an `Always` or `Reachable` that no seed reaches fails the sweep.
- Add a `Sometimes` for each fault-dependent path you care about. The coverage table then proves the faults reached it.
- Use `sim.Event("name", details)` to mark a moment (a recovery finishing, a leader change) in the trace without asserting anything; triage then reads it next to the faults.
